articles.title: 2 families claim same body as Nepal flood victims remain hard to ID
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — Two families have claimed the same body recovered after the Bhotekoshi flood, forcing authorities in Pokhara to turn to DNA testing as they struggle to identify dozens of victims…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — Two families have claimed the same body recovered after the Bhotekoshi flood, forcing authorities in Pokhara to turn to DNA testing as they struggle to identify dozens of victims brought from the disaster zone.

Body No 1003 at Pokhara Academy of Health Sciences was identified by the relatives of both Gopal Dahit, a worker at the Mailung Hydropower Project, and Damodar Basyal, a tourist guide from Rupandehi who went missing after the flood.

Both families say the body’s physical features match their missing relative. With both families maintaining their claims, authorities collected DNA samples from relatives of Dahit and Basyal on Sunday for comparison with the body’s DNA. The body will remain in the morgue until the results establish its identity.

The case is not unique. Another body at the hospital has also been claimed by two families, according to Kaski District Police. Police have so far collected DNA samples from relatives of five families to determine whether the bodies they have claimed are indeed their missing relatives.

“During a disaster, there is a possibility that one family may mistakenly take away someone else’s body,” said Inspector Dipak Rijal, acting spokesperson for Kaski District Police. “That is why DNA testing is necessary.”

The confusion comes as authorities process a large number of bodies recovered after the Bhotekoshi flood. A total of 102 bodies recovered from Gorkha, Tanahun, Dhading and eastern Nawalparasi East have been brought to Pokhara.
By Sunday, 16 had been identified and handed over to relatives.
Two families, one body
Dahit’s relatives travelled from Bardiya to search for him after he disappeared following the flood.

His two sisters, a brother and a sister-in-law left Jogigaun in Barbardiya Municipality-2 on Friday. The following morning, they reached Gaindakot in Nawalparasi East, where they were shown photographs of recovered bodies.
They identified Body No 1003 as Dahit.

Police told them the body had been sent to Pokhara, and the family traveled there the same day. The physical description appeared to match the photograph they had seen, and the hospital was preparing to hand over the body on Saturday evening.
But Dahit’s elder brother, Krishna Bahadur Tharu, was still on his way to Pokhara to see the body himself. By the time he arrived on Sunday afternoon, another family had already claimed it.

Radhe Shyam Sharma Basyal had travelled to Pokhara after receiving a photograph of Body No 1003 from a relative. His younger brother Damodar had disappeared after traveling to Kerung with a group of 67 tourists from Mansarovar.
Basyal said several distinctive features in the photograph matched his brother.
“There was a mole. That matched. His lips were thick, and that matched too,” he said, showing a photograph of Damodar on his mobile phone. “He is my youngest brother. I am ready for a DNA test.”
He said the body should not be handed to either family until the identity was established scientifically.
“It may take a little longer, but tomorrow we will know for certain,” he said. “Let’s do the DNA test. Whoever it belongs to can take the body.”
Dahit’s sister Manji Tharu remains convinced that the body is her brother’s. “His teeth, forehead, lips, hands, chest and face all match,” she said outside the morgue on Sunday.
The family had planned to take the body home on Saturday but waited for Krishna to arrive.
“We were waiting for our elder brother. Now we are in a situation where we may not get the body at all,” she said.
For Dahit’s family, the search has already come at a high cost. His elder sister Saraswati Tharu said the family borrowed money from neighbours to travel in search of him.

“He had gone to work at the hydropower project only a month ago,” she said. “Our new house is still unfinished, and we had debt from building it. He went to the hydropower project to earn money to repay that debt.”
His 18-month-old daughter had only recently learned to say “Baba”. Dahit’s brother Krishna has asked authorities to keep the body preserved until the DNA results are released.
A growing identification challenge
The Bhotekoshi flood has left families searching for relatives across several districts, while authorities face the difficult task of matching unidentified bodies with missing-person reports.
Police have set up a help desk at Pokhara Academy of Health Sciences for relatives arriving in search of loved ones.

Photographs showing the bodies and their physical characteristics are displayed inside the hospital. When faces cannot be recognised, relatives have sometimes identified victims through distinctive items such as ties, tattoos, necklaces and earrings.

“Relatives are continuing to arrive,” Rijal said. The desk also helps families file reports, arranges free hearses and provides food and accommodation for those who have travelled to Pokhara to search for missing relatives.
The scale of the operation has stretched the hospital’s mortuary.

For now, however, officials say there is no immediate need to bury the unidentified victims in Pokhara. Kaski Chief District Officer Kumar Singh Gurung said relatives were still arriving from Chitwan and Nawalparasi to search for missing family members.
“Unlike Chitwan, where bodies were kept in a temporary morgue and a foul smell began spreading, we have refrigerated facilities here,” he said. “We can keep the bodies for several more days.”
The district security committee and the body management committee will wait before deciding whether to bury any bodies that remain unidentified.
For families such as the Dahits and the Basyals, however, the wait is now more immediate. Both believe they have found their missing relative. Only DNA can tell them which family is right.

Of the 102 bodies brought to Pokhara, 87 had undergone postmortem examinations by Monday morning. Five forensic specialists are working on the examinations, while two specialists from Nepal Police’s Central Forensic Science Laboratory have arrived to collect DNA samples and analyze fingerprints.
The hospital is also running out of refrigerated space.

Its morgue has 72 refrigerated compartments, but 77 bodies were being kept there after 16 had been handed over to relatives and nine transferred to Nepal Manipal Teaching Hospital. Authorities have managed the shortage by making arrangements for small bodies and fragmented remains and by installing a container inside the cold room.
Twenty-five bodies were transferred into the temperature-controlled container on Sunday.

Aryal said the facility has one of the largest and most modern mortuaries in Nepal after Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital in Maharajgunj, Kathmandu, and can preserve bodies at 2 to 6 degrees Celsius for 10 days to two weeks.
Authorities are continuing to hand over bodies as families identify them.

For bodies that remain unidentified, officials must follow the Unidentified and Unclaimed Dead Body Management (First Amendment) Directive, 2026. Authorities must photograph each body and preserve fingerprints, DNA samples, and other identifying information.

If a body remains unidentified for a prolonged period, the directive requires it to be buried at a site designated by the local government. The burial site must be kept free of construction for 12 years so that remains can be exhumed if relatives later come forward.
“We bury bodies with tag numbers and geolocation details,” Rijal said. “If relatives come looking within 12 years, the body can be exhumed and the remains handed over after DNA identification.”

For now, however, officials say there is no immediate need to bury the unidentified victims in Pokhara. Kaski Chief District Officer Kuman Singh Gurung said relatives were still arriving from Chitwan and Nawalparasi to search for missing family members.
For families such as the Dahits and the Basyals, however, the wait is now more immediate. Both believe they have found their missing relative. Only DNA can tell them which family is right. /dl

articles.title: Witness: Possible DepEd spent own funds for youth leadership summits
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines— An Army official raised the possibility on Tuesday that the Department of Education (DepEd) might have spent its own budget for youth training programs in 2023, but without…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines— An Army official raised the possibility on Tuesday that the Department of Education (DepEd) might have spent its own budget for youth training programs in 2023, but without knowing if the money was sourced from the agency’s confidential funds.

Testifying for the prosecution team, Philippine Army (PA) Col. Manaros Boransing II maintained that they did not receive any funding from the DepEd for the Youth Leadership Summit (YLS) and the Information Education Communication (IEC) activities from January to December 2023.

As then assistant chief of staff for civil-military operations of the First Infantry (Tabak) Division, Boransing supervised and monitored the two anti-communist recruitment initiatives. Meanwhile, DepEd was headed at that time by Vice President Secretary Sara Duterte.

“Binaggit nyo po kanina na wala kayong tinaggap na pera mula sa DepEd, wala ring bingay na pera ang DepEd sa AFP (Armed Forces of the Philippines) o sa First Tabak o sa unit ninyo? But would you know if DepEd spent on that activity on their own people because you collaborated with Deped on that activity? Would you know? Sabi nya kanina kasi KKB (kanya-kanyang bayad) e,” presiding officer and Sen. Francis Escudero asked during the impeachment trial of Duterte.

(You mentioned earlier that you did not receive any money from DepEd, and that DepEd also did not provide any funds to the AFP, First Tabak, or your unit. But would you know if DepEd spent money on its own personnel for that activity, since you collaborated with DepEd on it? Would you know? You said earlier that everyone paid for their own expenses.)

“Yes sir. What I know is they arrived there. They were there during the youth leadership summits and traveling as I know in the government entails expenses and permission to leave the post,” Boransing said.
When Escudero asked whether confidential funds were spent for the said activities, the witness said he had no knowledge about the source of funds.
“So you can confirm that no money was given to the AFP or any of its units or anyone in your unit but that DepEd must have spent on the activities?” Escudero asked again.
Boransing repeated that no DepEd funds were downloaded to his unit.
“But it is very possible that DepEd spent on the YLS and the IECs?” Escudero pressed on.
“Yes, Sir,” the witness answered.

Still on Escudero’s questioning, Boransing explained that the funds spent for the YLS and IECs came from the PA’s regular budget. The witness though noted that the YLS is part of a campaign so it involves civil-military, combat, and intelligence operations.
“Although I can’t comment about the intelligence operations, Sir, but they are interlink and mutually supporting so all army and AFP operations are intelligence-driven, Sir,” he further noted.
The witness also answered in the affirmative when Escudero raised the possibility that the AFP used its intelligence funds for the YLS and IECs.
On DepEd’s request, Boransing signed a certification on the agency’s participation in the summits.
But the witness told the Senate impeachment court that he had no idea that the certification would be used by DepEd to justify its use of confidential funds.
Duterte has been accused of misusing and misappropriating the confidential funds released to the Office of the Vice President and the DepEd. /jpv

articles.title: [ANALYSIS] What does ‘at least nearly proficient’ mean in Philippine education?
articles.summary: The Philippine Development Plan 2023–2028 says proficiency. The National Education and Workforce Development Plan 2026–2035 says proficiency. Why, then, does our annual budget target ‘at least nearly…

blocks.text: As Congress examines the proposed 2027 national budget, there is a seemingly technical line in the performance targets of the Department of Education (DepEd) that deserves an honest question: What does it mean when our target for Filipino learners is to be “at least nearly proficient”? This is not a semantic question. Targets reflect our aspirations. And our aspirations inform our investments.

That matters especially now. Education is receiving historically high levels of public investment. After years of chronic underinvestment, Congress and the Executive are finally putting significantly greater resources behind classrooms, teachers, textbooks, nutrition, learning recovery, and other long-standing gaps.
So what are we asking those investments to achieve?

Under DepEd’s assessment framework, a score of 75% to 89% is Proficient, while 50% to 74% is Nearly Proficient. A nearly proficient learner demonstrates the minimum level of skills expected in areas such as problem-solving, managing information, and analyzing data.

What does this mean concretely? For a Grade 6 learner, this could mean being able to understand the main idea and retrieve information from a text, but not yet consistently make deeper inferences, connect ideas, or critically evaluate what is being read. In Mathematics, the learner may solve more straightforward problems using fractions, decimals, percentages, or measurement, but may still struggle to apply these concepts independently when a problem is unfamiliar or requires several steps of reasoning.
There are valid reasons to measure this. In the middle of a learning crisis, moving a child from low proficient to nearly proficient is meaningful progress. But should it be our target?

This formulation is relatively recent. In 2017, the General Appropriations Act still measured learners who scored “average or better” in the National Achievement Test. DepEd subsequently changed its assessment methodology from “mastery” to “proficiency” in 2018. By the 2020 GAA, the performance indicator had been revised to the formulation we recognize today: the proportion of learners achieving “at least nearly proficient” in the NAT.
Six budget cycles later, it is reasonable to ask whether the indicator still captures the learning outcome we now aspire to achieve.

The Second Congressional Commission on Education’s (EDCOM 2) examination of DepEd’s own NAT data gives us reason for sobriety. Around 30.5% of Grade 3 learners were proficient or highly proficient. In Grade 6, only 19.6% were. For Grade 10 students, this is much lower at 0.74%. At Grade 12, at the end of 13 years of education, only 0.4% remain.
Department Order No. 55, series of 2016, established national assessments precisely to determine whether learners have achieved the standards expected at critical stages of basic education.
So what should a Filipino child actually know after six years of schooling? After 10? After 12? And what level of achievement should our country consider success?

Our national plans already answer that question. The Philippine Development Plan 2023–2028 — and, importantly, its 2025 Midterm Update — measures progress by the proportion of learners achieving at least Proficient in the NAT. The updated PDP did not lower this benchmark to Nearly Proficient.

The National Education and Workforce Development Plan 2026–2035 likewise carries that aspiration forward, targeting an increase in the proportion of Grade 12 learners achieving at least Proficient in the NAT from a baseline of just 0.4% to 90% in 10 years, or by 2035. Both houses of Congress have since adopted the NatPlan and the recommendations of EDCOM 2 as the country’s 10-year framework for education reform.
The PDP says proficiency. The NatPlan says proficiency. Why, then, does our annual budget target “at least nearly proficient”?

There may be a sound technical explanation. If there is, we should understand it. These targets emerge from the government’s planning and budgeting process involving DepEd, the Department of Budget and Management (DBM), and the Department of Economy, Planning, and Development (DEPDev), and are ultimately scrutinized and funded by Congress.
But neither are we suggesting that the Philippines can leap from today’s proficiency levels to our desired outcomes overnight. No serious education reform works that way.

Even the world’s strongest education systems were built over years, often decades, of sustained reform. Singapore’s transformation, for example, proceeded through successive phases of reform beginning in the 1960s. Even after becoming a top-performing system, Singapore continued improving its Programme for International Student Assessment or PISA performance between 2009 and 2022.

Our NatPlan recognizes this reality. Its 90% Grade 12 proficiency goal is for 2035, not next year. The point of a long-term target is precisely to establish the destination, then build a credible annual trajectory toward it.
We need sobriety. But sobriety is different from lowering ambition.

“Nearly proficient” can therefore remain an important measure of recovery. The 2027 GAA should report it. But it should also separately report how many learners actually reach proficient or highly proficient.
More importantly, DepEd, DBM, and DEPDev should align annual budget targets with the proficiency trajectories already established in the PDP and NatPlan — and cost what is required to achieve them.

If we need more remediation, let us prioritize it. If we need smaller early-grade classes, let us advocate for resources for them. If textbooks, teacher development, nutrition, or instructional time are the binding constraints, let us put our funds there.
Aspiration should determine targets. Targets should determine reforms. And reforms should determine where we place our investments.

The question, then, is not whether every Filipino learner can become proficient next year. We know education systems do not transform that quickly. The question is whether proficiency remains our destination — and whether every annual target and every peso we invest is moving us credibly toward it.

Our national plans already set that destination. It is only fitting that our annual targets be likewise deliberate — a tool not just for compliance, but for genuine target setting, resourcing, and accountability. – Rappler.com
Karol Mark Yee is the executive director of the Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM 2).

articles.title: United Arab Emirates says it intercepted an Iranian drone over its territorial waters
articles.summary: DUBAI, United Arab Emirates (AP) — The United Arab Emirates said that it intercepted an Iranian drone over its waters Monday, an attack that comes after the United States and Iran exchanged fire over…

blocks.text: A small boat sails past cargo ships and other commercial vessels anchored in the Strait of Hormuz off Bandar Abbas, Iran, Wednesday, Aug. 5, 2026. (Amirhosein Khorgooi/ISNA via AP, File)

DUBAI, United Arab Emirates (AP) — The United Arab Emirates said that it intercepted an Iranian drone over its waters Monday, an attack that comes after the United States and Iran exchanged fire over the weekend for the first time in a month.

Iranian officials said two people were killed and several others wounded in the U.S. attack Sunday night on Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz. Iran responded by launching missiles at U.S. sites in Jordan, which were intercepted.
During the lull in fighting, the U.S. has been ratcheting up economic pressure on Iran with the hope of forcing concessions out of Tehran, including reopening the Strait of Hormuz to shipping.

After the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28, Iran established a chokehold on the vital strait, through which a fifth of the world's traded oil passed in peacetime, slowing ship traffic to a trickle. That has roiled the global economy, raising prices worldwide for energy and other goods.

As the fighting resumed, the price of Brent crude oil, the international standard, climbed above $90, up about 25% from the start of the war, presenting a growing problem for U.S. President Donald Trump before the midterm elections.
A return to open conflict would be dangerous for the region, where Iran has targeted U.S. military bases and infrastructure in Gulf countries since the war began.
In the wake of the renewed violence, Anwar Gargash, a diplomatic adviser to the UAE’s president, said on social media that “the state of neither war nor peace cannot be a sustainable solution.”

He called for a political solution that would return normal navigation to the Strait of Hormuz, but also a “more realistic approach” than the June memo of understanding between Iran and the U.S., which, he said, “failed to outline a practical and acceptable” road map.
UAE says Iranian attack is a ‘dangerous escalation’
In a short statement earlier, the UAE Defense Ministry said it “dealt with” an Iranian drone that was detected over its waters approaching from Iran. There were no reports of damage.

“This dangerous escalation constitutes a blatant violation of the UAE’s sovereignty, security, and stability, and a direct threat to the safety of its citizens and residents,” the Foreign Ministry said.
The Defense Ministry later issued a second statement denying a claim by the Iranian army that the Al Minhad Air Base in Dubai had been targeted, saying it was false.

In the wake of the U.S. attack on Sunday, Iran's military warned that any further U.S. attacks would draw a far heavier response, including strikes on bases or other points from which attacks against Iran are launched, state-run IRNA reported.
“The U.S. military has no choice but to leave the region,” the statement from Iran’s Armed Forces General Staff and the Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters said.
Trump on Monday didn’t rule out the possibility of further strikes on Iran. “We’ll see what happens,” he told reporters.
Iran says it has right to defend itself and will ‘respond decisively’

Speaking after the first day of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization's summit in Kyrgyzstan, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said the U.S. must abide by the June memo, state television reported.
Araghchi said Iran would continue defending its rights and that the solution to ending the conflict remained “completely clear.”

The summit brings together a group billed as a counterweight to U.S. global influence, and includes Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkia was scheduled to meet with Putin on the sidelines Tuesday.
US weekend attack comes after weeks of rising economic pressure

Meantime, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent opened meetings of the Group of 20 finance ministers in North Carolina on Monday, as Washington pressures other countries to help the U.S. economically isolate Iran.
The shifting strategy centers on threats to punish any country or entity that conducts business with Tehran.
Two weeks ago, the UAE suspended all trade with Iran after saying it had come under renewed fire from Iran with two missiles splashing down harmlessly in the Persian Gulf. Iran denied the attack.
Bessent later suggested it was pressure from Washington that led to the UAE decision.
Trump stressed last week that he is “not in a hurry” to get Iran back to the negotiating table, and he continues making the case that the Islamic Republic’s leadership is on the ropes.
Appointments to Iran’s senior security leadership in the past month, however, have signaled Tehran’s defiance after weathering decades of sanctions.
US military says strike on Iranian rocket launchers 'precise’

On Sunday, U.S. Central Command said it struck Iranian launchers after observing forces with Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the Strait of Hormuz. The U.S. military said last week that it had completed clearing sea mines from the waterway’s international shipping routes.
U.S. military officials disputed Iran’s claim that the latest American strikes were an act of aggression, calling them a “limited, precise action” against what they said were minelaying forces.
Iranian state television later showed what it said were ballistic missiles being fired at American bases in Jordan, and Jordan’s military said it intercepted eight that had entered its airspace.
The last time the U.S. military confirmed targeting Iran was July 29, when it announced a “heavy wave of strikes” on dozens of Revolutionary Guard targets.

articles.title: PNP beefs up security in pumping stations pver cable theft threat
articles.summary: The Philippine National Police (PNP) tasked policemen in Metro Manila to strengthen security measures around pumping stations and other flood-control facilities following the theft of vital equipment…

blocks.text: The Philippine National Police (PNP) tasked policemen in Metro Manila to strengthen security measures around pumping stations and other flood-control facilities following the theft of vital equipment that disrupted flood mitigation operations in Metro Manila.
PNP chief Gen. Jose Melencio C. Nartatez, Jr. also warned that any person who would be caught stealing or buying the stolen items from pumping stations would be dealt with aggressive legal measures.

“The Philippine National Police strongly condemns the theft of vital components from government pumping stations. These are not ordinary property crimes because they can compromise flood-control operations and put lives and property at risk,” said Nartatez.

The directive follows the reported theft of around eight to 10 meters of grounding cable from the Navotas pumping station, which caused the facility to malfunction amid severe flooding in Metro Manila.

Malacañang earlier vowed to run after those involved in the incident, and those who would dare to steal cable and other items from pumping stations, noting the importance of the role of the facilities in addressing floods in Metro Manila.

Nartatez said police stations were directed to coordinate with the Metropolitan Manila Development Authority (MMDA), Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH), local government units, and facility operators to secure critical infrastructure, particularly in flood-prone areas.

“I have directed concerned police units to coordinate with local governments and facility operators, intensify security and conduct immediate investigations to identify and arrest those responsible,” Nartatez said.

The theft of pumping station components can disrupt the operation of facilities relied upon to reduce floodwaters, the top cop stressed, and replacing stolen equipment also requires public funds and may delay efforts to address flooding.

articles.summary: The Bureau of Internal Revenue’s (BIR) Manila regional office has destroyed 240,550 illicit vape products seized in the city and Palawan province with tax liability amounting to more than ₱1.5…

blocks.text: The Bureau of Internal Revenue’s (BIR) Manila regional office has destroyed 240,550 illicit vape products seized in the city and Palawan province with tax liability amounting to more than ₱1.5 billion.

In a statement on Tuesday, Sept. 1, BIR Commissioner Charlito Martin R. Mendoza said the destruction last Aug. 24 at DIGAMA Waste Management Facility in Porac town, Pampanga province was part of the agency’s continuing campaign against the illegal manufacture, importation, distribution, and sale of vape products.

“Enforcement does not end with seizure. We must permanently remove illicit vape products from the market and hold accountable those behind their illegal manufacture, importation, distribution, and sale,” Mendoza said.

Manila Revenue Regional Director Remir Macatangay said his office has expanded its operations from retail stores to warehouses, resulting in a major enforcement action against Tap Fog Philippines, which he described as the BIR’s largest single illicit vape operation.
He said the destruction underscores intensified efforts to prevent illicit vape products from returning to the market and to protect government revenues from tax evasion.

articles.title: Carney’s Liberals sweep 3 special elections in Canada as voters back his stand against Trump
articles.summary: TORONTO (AP) — Canada's Liberals swept three special elections Monday in a result that showed voters backing Prime Minister Mark Carney for standing up against U.S. President Donald Trump. The…

blocks.text: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney speaks as he announces a $11.3 billion contract for icebreakers at the Davie shipyard in Levis, Quebec on Monday, Aug. 24, 2026. Quebec Premier Christine Frechette, right, looks on. (Jacques Boissinot/The Canadian Press via AP)
TORONTO (AP) — Canada's Liberals swept three special elections Monday in a result that showed voters backing Prime Minister Mark Carney for standing up against U.S. President Donald Trump.
The Canadian Press, Canada’s national news agency, projected Liberal victories in Chicoutimi-Le Fjord in Quebec, Beaches-East York in Toronto and North Vancouver-Capilano in British Columbia.

Carney said the results amounted to an endorsement of his government’s approach. “At this consequential time for Canada, voters have placed their trust in our government’s plan,” he said in a statement.

The Quebec result was the most dramatic shift. Liberal Daniel Gobeil was projected to win big in Chicoutimi-Le Fjord, a district held by the opposition Conservatives since 2018. The region is home to aluminum producers, dairy farms and other industries caught in the escalating trade war.
“This victory means we can maintain Canadian unity all across the country,” Gobeil said.
The other two seats were previously held by Liberals. In British Columbia, Carney’s former deputy chief of staff Braeden Caley won North Vancouver-Capilano.
“The United States is getting a message tonight. Our leader has the support of the Canadian people,” Liberal lawmaker Hedy Fry told the Canadian Broadcasting Corp. in an interview.

U.S.-Canada trade talks collapsed Aug. 21 after the two sides failed to reach a deal, and Trump imposed 50% tariffs on roughly $20 billion in Canadian goods. Canada responded with plans for tariffs on U.S. products.

Trump has escalated his attacks on Canada since the talks failed. He signed an executive order renaming Lake Ontario “Lake America," and U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Monday that Canada had limited leverage in the dispute because the U.S. economy is roughly 13 times larger.
Trump has repeatedly talked about making Canada the 51st state.
Carney has accelerated efforts to deepen economic ties with Europe and other partners.
The Liberal sweep would bring Carney’s party to 173 seats in the 343-seat House of Commons, further strengthening its position in Parliament.
The special elections were called after the lawmakers who previously held the three seats resigned from Parliament earlier this year.

Daniel Béland, a political-science professor at McGill University, said the Liberal sweep showed Carney retaining strong support across regions, but called the Quebec result the most significant. He said the easy win in Chicoutimi-Le Fjord likely reflected, in part, the popularity in Quebec of Carney’s Aug. 21 decision “to pull the plug on trade negotiations with the White House.”

Béland said the Conservative collapse there was also bad news for leader Pierre Poilievre. The party won the riding with 34% of the vote last year but fell to about 13% and third place Monday. “These numbers do look bad,” he said.
Carney won Canada’s election last year, fueled by public anger over Trump’s annexation threats, and he has vowed to reduce Canada’s reliance on the U.S.

articles.title: GSIS returns ₱19 billion to 700,000 members through loan relief programs
articles.summary: State-run pension fund Government Service Insurance System (GSIS) has returned ₱19 billion to more than 700,000 members through its Balik Ginhawa loan relief programs as of end-August, freeing up…

blocks.text: State-run pension fund Government Service Insurance System (GSIS) has returned ₱19 billion to more than 700,000 members through its Balik Ginhawa loan relief programs as of end-August, freeing up funds that government workers can use for household expenses instead of loan payments.

In a statement on Tuesday, Sept. 1, GSIS said the refunds covered nearly 1.3 million loan contracts, with ₱8.9 billion credited under the first Balik Ginhawa program and another ₱10.1 billion through the enhanced Balik Ginhawa 2.

The programs provide qualified members with refunds corresponding to loan payments covered by a moratorium, allowing them to temporarily redirect money otherwise earmarked for amortizations toward expenses such as tuition, household bills, medical needs, groceries, and home repairs.
For instance, GSIS said a government employee paying ₱20,000 in monthly loan amortizations could free up as much as ₱120,000 in spending power over six months.

“Balik Ginhawa is about putting money back into the hands of our members and letting them decide where their families need it most. That can make a real difference in a family’s life,” GSIS President and General Manager (PGM) Wick Veloso said.

The first Balik Ginhawa program began on March 1, followed by Balik Ginhawa 2 on July 1. Unlike a new loan, the programs provide relief without requiring members to take on additional debt to obtain funds for immediate needs.
With two months remaining before the program closes on Oct. 31, GSIS said the total amount returned to members is nearing the ₱20-billion mark.
Veloso urged qualified members who have yet to avail themselves of Balik Ginhawa 2 to apply before the deadline.
“We want every qualified member to benefit. There is still time to apply for Balik Ginhawa 2, and we encourage our members not to wait until the last minute,” Veloso said.
GSIS said Balik Ginhawa forms part of its broader effort to translate the pension fund’s financial strength into benefits for its members.

“Our goal is not simply to build a stronger GSIS. Our goal is to make that strength felt by every member and every family we serve. Ang pondo ng GSIS ay para sa ginhawa ng ating mga miyembro,” Veloso said.

articles.title: UN spotlights nuclear weapon states' refusal to ratify test ban treaty at divisive time
articles.summary: UNITED NATIONS (AP) — With the U.S., Russia, China and other countries that have nuclear weapons refusing to ratify the treaty that bans atomic testing, the United Nations warned on Monday that any…

blocks.text: The UN flag flies on a stormy day at the United Nations during the United Nations General Assembly, Sept. 22, 2022. (AP Photo/Ted Shaffrey, File)

UNITED NATIONS (AP) — With the U.S., Russia, China and other countries that have nuclear weapons refusing to ratify the treaty that bans atomic testing, the United Nations warned on Monday that any new test could trigger another arms race.

U.N. disarmament chief Izumi Nakamitsu told the U.N. General Assembly that it was meeting to mark International Day against Nuclear Tests at a time of “deep geopolitical tension, growing division and diminishing trust,” as well as concern about the possible resumption of testing.

Late last year, the United States and Russia, which have the world’s largest nuclear arsenals, threatened to resume nuclear testing, setting off global alarm bells. President Donald Trump accused Russia and China of conducting tests, which they deny.

“Even contemplating such a course is dangerous,” Nakamitsu warned. “Any resumption would erode decades of restraint, deepen mistrust and risk triggering reciprocal tests and an arms race. This must never become reality.”
When the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty was adopted in 1996, it had a very high bar to enter into force. It had to be ratified by 44 specific countries, and nine of them have not yet done so.

The United States, China, Iran, Egypt and Israel have signed but not ratified the treaty. India, Pakistan and North Korea have neither signed nor ratified. Russia signed and ratified, but revoked its ratification in 2023.
Robert Floyd, head of the organization overseeing the treaty known as the CTBT, told the General Assembly that Tonga’s ratification last month brings the number of parties to the treaty to 179.

Since 1945, he said the planet has seen more than 2,000 nuclear test explosions, but in the past three decades fewer than 12. He cautioned, however, that “the international scene is tense, full of mistrust,” including about nuclear testing
If nuclear testing resumes, Floyd warned, the result would be new technologically advanced nuclear arsenals, soaring risks of nuclear miscalculation, and “devastation from nuclear `bad luck.’”

The International Day Against Nuclear Tests was established to commemorate the Aug. 29, 1991, shutdown of the former Soviet nuclear test site at Semipalatinsk, now in Kazakhstan, which saw 456 nuclear tests, Floyd said.
It also puts a spotlight on victims of the atomic era.

Tina Cordova described to the U.N. General Assembly how five generations of her family were exposed to radiation that began with the testing of the first atomic bomb on July 16, 1945, in New Mexico — and how every succeeding generation until today has suffered from cancer.

“We were never warned before or after of the danger, so we lived our lives off the land as we always did," said Cordova, who co-founded an organization called the Tularosa Basin Downwinders Consortium 21 years ago to spotlight the negative health effects of radiation suffered by the people of New Mexico.
She stressed that they were not alone.

Nuclear testing took place around the world, she said, and people living in Guam, Tahiti, Kazakhstan and Aboriginal areas of Australia as well as in Idaho, Utah, Arizona, Nevada, Colorado and Montana were also exposed — including uranium workers and their families.

“We’re the people that became the collateral damage to the development and testing of nuclear devices and were left to deal with the consequences on our own,” Cordova said. “It is why we fight for acknowledgment and assistance.”

articles.title: Eala set to draw big crowd at big stadium for US Open opener
articles.summary: Filipino fans are expected to troop to Louis Armstrong Stadium in New York on Tuesday evening, Sept. 1 (Wednesday morning, Sept. 2, Philippines time) as Alex Eala begins her US Open campaign against…

blocks.text: Filipino fans are expected to troop to Louis Armstrong Stadium in New York on Tuesday evening, Sept. 1 (Wednesday morning, Sept. 2, Philippines time) as Alex Eala begins her US Open campaign against American qualifier Mary Stoiana.

The match is slated not before 8:30 p.m. (8:30 a.m. Wednesday, Philippine time), immediately after the opening men’s singles clash between 2016 semifinalist Gael Monfils and Adolfo Vallejo, which is set for 7 p.m. (7 a.m. Wednesday, PH time).
Organizers are expecting the 14,000-capacity stadium to be packed for Eala’s highly anticipated appearance.

In an interview with Tennis Channel, tournament director Eric Butorac said organizers are embracing the growing fan support for Eala by putting her on the tournament’s second-largest stadium following the huge crowd that turned out for her exhibition match against Iva Jovic during Fan Week.
“I don’t know if you guys caught any of that match, but it was electric in there. I mean, unbelievable,” sai Butorac.

“We scheduled her first match at Louis Armstrong Stadium (because) we knew it had to be a major stadium. We thought that’s a great place to start. But I’ve already kind of monitored some of the secondary pricing, and that session is blowing up,” he added.

As of Monday, Aug. 31, ticket prices at Ticketmaster for the night session at Louis Armstrong Stadium are as low as US $279.60 (around P17,000) to as high as $1,747.50 (around P109,000) on a verified resale ticket.
“I can’t wait to have her out there late at night and see all the Filipino crowd behind her. It’s going to be really special,” Butorac said.

Eala, seeded 17th, is meeting Stoiana for the second time. They first faced each other at an W100 International Tennis Federation (ITF) tournament in Landisville, Pennsylvania where the 21-year-old Filipina won in straight sets.

On paper, Eala holds a big advantage against Stoiana. The Filipina enjoys a career-high ranking at No. 18 and is coming off a breakthrough WTA Tour title victory at the Mubadala DC Open in Washington DC a few weeks ago.
Eala is also on a mission of eclipsing her previous best Grand Slam finish of a fourth-round appearance at the Wimbledon a few months back.
A victory for Eala would arrange her a second-round meeting with the winner between Oleksandra Oliynykova of Ukraine and wildcard Reese Brantmeier of the United States.

articles.title: Otoc, Sanchez banner field as Digos jrs netfest unwraps
articles.summary: Julius Otoc and Cyrelmae Sanchez headline a strong field seeking top honors and ranking points as the MJFC Araw ng Digos Juniors Age Group Tennis Championships fires off Wednesday, Sept. 2, at the…

blocks.text: Julius Otoc and Cyrelmae Sanchez headline a strong field seeking top honors and ranking points as the MJFC Araw ng Digos Juniors Age Group Tennis Championships fires off Wednesday, Sept. 2, at the Digos City courts in Davao del Sur.

Otoc and Sanchez are seeded No. 1 in the boys’ and girls’ 18-and-under division, respectively, with both also seeing action in the 16-and-U category, albeit with lower seeding. The weeklong Group 2 tournament ushers in the Palawan Pawnshop Mindanao swing, which also features legs in Sultan Kudarat and Cotabato.

Seeking to spoil the top seeds’ bids for championship honors and valuable ranking points are Jhazz Fernando, Kurt Alcantara and Shaun Globasa in the boys’ 18-and-U division, and Aika Salahuddin, Marxian Sira and Dyan Placa in the girls’ side.
Cristiano Calingasan heads the boys’ 16-and-U cast, with Otoc seeded No. 2, followed by Kresthan Belacas, Kyle Ramos, Rein Hayana, Krisnel Batilo, Carlo Eduarte and Richlord Sira.
Multi-titled Francine Wong leads the girls’ 16-and-U field, which also includes Justine Gumbao, Sanchez, Teresinha Calingasan, Kyth Solis, Marxian Sira, Placa and Dominique Calingasan.

Belacas, another multi-winner in the nationwide junior circuit, tops the boys’ 14-and-under cast alongside Archie Roceta, Xian Sugsi and Andrei Domasing. Wong is likewise tipped to make a strong run in the girls’ 14-and-U division, which includes Gumbao and sisters Teresinha and Dominique Calingasan.
Domasing and Arissa Macapendeg headline the youngest 12-and-U division of the tournament, supported by ICON Golf & Sports and the Palawan Group of Companies.

The Mindanao swing is part of the nationwide junior tennis series put up by Palawan Pawnshop president and CEO Bobby Castro, whose program seeks to bring competitive junior tennis closer to the countryside, where a growing number of promising players are emerging but often lack opportunities to test themselves in high-level competition.
The tournament is hosted by Mayor Josef Fortich Cagas and sanctioned by Philta and Universal Tennis Rating.
Aside from the singles events, titles are also at stake in the boys’ and girls’ 14-and-U and 18-and-U doubles competitions.

Meanwhile, Sultan Kudarat will host the next leg on Sept. 10-15 for the Bagong Pilipinas age-group tournament, with the Capital Indoor and Outdoor courts in Isulan serving as venue. The circuit then winds up in Cotabato with the Kidapawan Juniors Championship on Sept. 16-22 at the Kidapawan City courts.

articles.title: Eruption of Sinabung volcano on Indonesia’s Sumatra island prompts higher alert
articles.summary: JAKARTA, Indonesia (AP) — Mount Sinabung on Indonesia erupted Monday, spewing a column of black ash and smoke 3,500 meters (11,482 feet) from the top of the mountain into the sky over Sumatra island.…

blocks.text: In this photo released by the Geological Agency (Badan Geologi) of Indonesia's Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources, Mount Sinabung releases volcanic materials into the air during an eruption in Karo, North Sumatra, Indonesia, Monday, Aug. 31, 2026. (Badan Geologi via AP)
JAKARTA, Indonesia (AP) — Mount Sinabung on Indonesia erupted Monday, spewing a column of black ash and smoke 3,500 meters (11,482 feet) from the top of the mountain into the sky over Sumatra island.

There were no immediate reports of casualties, evacuations or disruptions to flights in the region. But residents, visitors and tourists were advised to refrain from activities in nearby villages in Karo district in North Sumatra province and areas within 6 kilometers (3.7 miles) of the summit.
Roads, vehicles and buildings in several villages in Karo affected by the eruption were covered in gray ash. Local authorities distributed masks to residents to protect themselves.
Officials raised the volcano alert level to “Watch,” the second-highest level for volcanic activity, which expanded the safe zone around the 2,600-meter (8,530-foot) mountain.
“This eruption is considered an initial eruption, and it is possible that a larger eruption could occur,” Lana Saria, chief of Indonesia’s Geological Agency, said in a statement Monday.
The agency previously recorded visual evidence of Mount Sinabung's increased activity in mid-August including dozens of earthquakes and expanded the recommended radius for public activities.
About 30,000 people have been forced to leave their homes around Sinabung in the past few years because of volcanic activity.

Indonesia is an archipelago of more than 280 million people with frequent seismic activity and Sinabung is among more than 120 active volcanoes. The country is prone to seismic upheaval due to its location on the Pacific “Ring of Fire,” an arc of volcanoes and fault lines encircling the Pacific Basin.

articles.title: SINAG urges early water release from San Roque dam
articles.summary: PANGASINAN — San Roque Dam’s water elevation has climbed to 282.96 meters above sea level (masl) as of 5:00 a.m., Sept 1, prompting renewed calls for precautionary action as downstream communities…

blocks.text: In photo Engr . Rosendo So.chairman SINAG (Photo via Liezle Inigo)

PANGASINAN — San Roque Dam’s water elevation has climbed to 282.96 meters above sea level (masl) as of 5:00 a.m., Sept 1, prompting renewed calls for precautionary action as downstream communities remain vulnerable to flooding.
Samahang Industriya ng Agrikultura (SINAG) Chairman Engr. Rosendo So had earlier urged dam authorities to begin controlled water releases when the reservoir was still at around 278 meters.
“I ask San Roque Dam to release water at 278 level,” So said.

With the current level already at 282.96 masl, or nearly five meters higher than the level cited by So, the appeal underscores the urgency of closely monitoring the reservoir and managing releases carefully to reduce potential downstream flood risks.

The situation also recalls the massive flooding in 2009 following Typhoon Pepeng. On October 9, 2009, when San Roque Dam reached approximately 289.05 masl, all six spillway gates were reportedly opened, with discharge reaching about 5,072 cubic meters per second at one point.

In 2009, after Typhoon Pepeng, Rosendo So and affected parties pursued legal action against National Power Corporation (NPC) and San Roque Power Corporation (SRPC) over the massive flooding and alleged improper/sudden release of water from San Roque Dam.
With the dam now at 282.96 masl, authorities and downstream communities are urged to remain vigilant and closely monitor official dam and flood advisories.

articles.title: Easy Japanese in focus as way to deliver info to foreigners
articles.summary: TOKYO, Sept. 1 (Jiji Press) -- Easy Japanese is in the spotlight as a way to disseminate information to foreigners in Japan, especially at the time of disasters such as a recent powerful earthquake…

blocks.text: Information for foreign residents is provided in easy Japanese on a support website launched by information technology company WizTry for people affected by the July 28 powerful

TOKYO, Sept. 1 (Jiji Press) -- Easy Japanese is in the spotlight as a way to disseminate information to foreigners in Japan, especially at the time of disasters such as a recent powerful earthquake that hit the southwestern prefecture of Kumamoto.
According to a survey targeting foreigners living in Tokyo, 41.3 pct said they want to read information written in easy Japanese, higher than 35.9 pct seeking information in English.

"It's probably because the nationalities of foreigners living in Japan have diversified, and fewer people are from English-speaking countries and regions," said Nobuko Inoue of Tokyo Metropolitan Foundation Tsunagari, which conducted the survey and works to promote and raise awareness about easy Japanese.

The crux of giving out information in easy Japanese is to avoid using onomatopoeia, mimetic words, words adopted from foreign languages and ambiguous expressions, and to use short and clear sentences, according to the foundation.

For example, "kyanseru," which derives from the English word cancel, can be replaced with "yameru" in easy Japanese. "Moraeru," meaning "you can get," can be used for "teikyo-suru," which means to provide.
In Kumamoto, people from Southeast Asian countries, such as Vietnam and Indonesia, account for more than half of foreign residents.

"We have many people whose native languages are not English," an official of the Kumamoto prefectural government's international affairs division said. "We are trying to provide information in easy Japanese rather than in English."

On July 29, the day after the 7.1-magnitude earthquake, which measured up to 7, the highest level on Japan's seismic intensity scale, WizTry, an information technology company in Kumamoto, created a website (https://kumamoto-shien.jp/) to give affected people necessary information, which includes an easy Japanese page for foreign residents (https://kumamoto-shien.jp/yasashii).
The page for foreigners says, for example: "Mizu wo kubaru basho ga arimasu. Okane wa irimasen," which means there are places where you can get water and no money is needed.
WizTry President Kotaro Suematsu said he hopes the company's easy Japanese page will help foreigners who tend to be left out of information.

articles.title: Periods of rain can reduce air pollution levels amid haze from Indonesia --DENR-EMB
articles.summary: The Department of Environment and Natural Resources' Environmental Management Bureau (DENR-EMB) said that periods of rain can help reduce the air pollution amid the haze brought by the forest fires…

blocks.text: Published September 1, 2026 1:46pm

The Department of Environment and Natural Resources' Environmental Management Bureau (DENR-EMB) said that periods of rain can help reduce the air pollution amid the haze brought by the forest fires from Indonesia.
The department explained that the Southwest Monsoon or Habagat brings the smoke from Kalimtan to the country.

"From September 1 to September 3, haze may continue to affect parts of the Philippines because smoke from Kalimantan is still being transported by the prevailing southwest monsoon (Habagat) while fires remain active," said Jundy del Socorro, chief of the Environmental Quality Management Division of DENR-EMB, in a message to reporters.
"However, periods of rain can help reduce pollution levels by washing smoke particles and fine particulate matter (PM2.5) out of the atmosphere."

"In general, a wet Habagat is beneficial for air quality. As long as the monsoon continues to bring moisture and rainfall, it helps suppress haze by removing suspended particulate matter from the atmosphere and reducing the concentration of smoke particles in the air," he added.
Several areas in Metro Manila continue to record high concentration of PM 2.5, with 11 stations with "acutely unhealthy" air quality and four others with "very unhealthy" levels.
But the DENR-EMB said that air quality could improve between September 4 to 6.

"Between September 4 and September 6, air quality could gradually improve if rainfall remains widespread and wind patterns begin to shift. Rain is one of the most effective natural mechanisms for removing suspended particles from the air, which can lead to better visibility and lower haze concentrations," said Del Socorro.

"Beyond September 6, conditions will depend primarily on whether the fires in Kalimantan continue to generate smoke, whether new hotspots emerge, and whether winds continue to carry smoke toward the Philippines," he added.
The DENR-EMB added that it's been monitoring air quality as well in Central Luzon, Calabarzon, and Mimaropa.
The agency advised the public to limit prolonged outdoor activities, especially those sensitive to air pollution.
Local government units have also urged the residents to use face mask when going outside. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Tuesday briefing: Scotland has promised on violence against women – now it needs to deliver
articles.summary:
In today’s newsletter: First minister John Swinney has pledged to put an end to violence against women and girls. But can he turn ambitious laws into real change?

Good morning. Violence…

blocks.text: Good morning. Violence against women and girls, in all its myriad forms – physical and mental, blatant and insidious – is a global challenge. It reaches back through millennia and, lately, it has been turbo-charged by technology, which offers abusers new ways to shame, harass and monitor victims. What would it take to eradicate it?

Scotland’s first minister John Swinney wants to find out. Today, he will set out his programme for government (the Holyrood equivalent of the King’s speech), and Swinney surprised many when he pledged to put ending violence against women at the heart of his government’s ambitions for the coming year and beyond.

But haven’t we been here before? Scotland has produced a raft of radical strategies, as well as legislation hailed as the international gold standard on domestic violence. So what hasn’t changed? For today’s newsletter, I spoke to equalities campaigner Talat Yaqoob, who co-chaired the Scottish government’s National Advisory Council on Women and Girls after four years until last month. I asked her what government – and societal – action constitutes meaningful change, and what other countries can learn from Scotland. But first, the headlines.
Five big stories

items: Nepal-Tibet | Rescue teams are working to reach more than 900 missing hydropower workers, who are thought to be trapped in underground areas in Nepal, after the devastating flash floods.
Iran | The new US sanctions campaign is expected to push many Iranians into deeper poverty as food inflation soars.
UK | The British Museum privately hosted Palantir founder Peter Thiel in a private viewing of the Bayeux tapestry, the Guardian understands.
Slavery | Countries are legally obliged to consider reparations for the transatlantic slave tried, and address the legacy racial discrimination, a UN committee has said.

US news | A Las Vegas jury has found former South Side Compton Crips gang leader Duane Keith Davis guilty of the murder of Tupac Shakur, bringing the case to a close nearly 30 years after the famous rapper was gunned down.

blocks.text: In depth: Why Scotland’s pioneering laws aren’t enough

blocks.caption: The context for Swinney’s pledge is bleak. Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The Guardian

blocks.text: We’ll find out later today the detail of the measures John Swinney is proposing, but the SNP leader’s preliminary talk has been big: pledging his personal leadership, acknowledging that alongside resources to protect those most at risk of violence right now, his government needs to address underlying economic inequalities – and hinting at the need for focused prevention when he says that lasting change requires all of society to play our part.
The context for Swinney’s vow is bleak: a steady increase in misogyny and violence against women and girls across the world.

In Scotland, both domestic abuse and sexual crimes are on the rise – crimes recorded by Police Scotland including rape and attempted rape, sexual assault and communicating indecently were up 10% last year and are now at their highest level since 1971. Rape Crisis Scotland has pointed out that these figures reflect a significant rise in historic offences and that, despite the best efforts of Reform in Scotland to link them with immigration, the vast majority are perpetrated by people known to the victim.

Moreover, as Yaqoob tells me, technological advances have “enabled an entirely new field of violence against women and girls – deepfakes, ‘revenge porn’, online coercion and control of women through things like GPS tracking” – while the now-quotidian misogyny of the manosphere is saturating playgrounds and classrooms. A survey of Scottish secondary school boys last year found a third believed that girls who wear revealing clothing were “asking for trouble”, while a third of female teaching staff, in a separate study, reported sexist abuse from children as young as eight years old.

“We also know that when there is recession, when there is poverty, there is a rise of the far right, there’s a rise of anger, and women are often the victims of that anger,” Yaqoob says. The Guardian’s own research last year found that two out of every five people arrested after participating in the 2024 summer riots had been previously reported to the police for domestic abuse.

Recession hits funding too: many services are on their knees, according to campaigners, while the post-pandemic court backlog and ongoing crisis in the legal aid system continues to deny victims access to justice.
Haven’t we been here before?

When I returned to Scotland to report for the Guardian just over a decade ago, there was a new female first minister, Nicola Sturgeon, one of three women heading the main political parties at Holyrood, and you could taste the change in the air.

This visibility of women in top jobs – necessary, of course, but never sufficient – was accompanied by a raft of ambitious strategies and bills. Equally Safe, launched in 2014, was a plan across central and local governments to act together on tackling gender-based violence. The National Advisory Council on Women and Girls, established by Sturgeon in 2017, brought forward radical proposals to offer two months of paid paternity leave and establish a world-leading process for complainants of sexual violence.

In 2018, the Scottish parliament passed legislation to criminalise coercive control for the first time, hailed by international experts at the time as “the gold standard”, and three years later added further powers with domestic abuse prevention orders.

There’s been funding for sexual violence prevention programmes in schools and universities, and a national advocacy service to support victims as they navigate the justice system. And, in 2025, a landmark justice reform bill abolished the Scottish verdict of “not proven” – a global legal anomaly thought to be a key factor in the country’s significantly lower convictions rate for rape and sexual assault.

These offer a useful case study of what Yaqoob describes as “the implementation gap”. While the 2018 Act was undoubtedly radical, campaigners say it hasn’t achieved its full potential because the institutional change demanded of police and prosecutors – including the training of officers and shifting of mindset over charging decisions – hasn’t happened. Only 4% of domestic abuse crimes were prosecuted under the new legislation last year. Meanwhile, many of the 2021 powers are gathering dust because poor drafting has rendered them too difficult to implement.

“There is a theme here,” says Yaqoob. “There’s no shortage of inspiring rhetoric and in some cases good strategy and legislation. What there isn’t is the priority and resources when it leaves the desk of the Scottish government and that means a lack of tangible change in women’s lives.”
What needs to happen now?

blocks.caption: A demonstration outside New Scotland Yard, reflecting the number of Metropolitan police officers who have been, or are now, under investigation for allegations of domestic abuse or violence against women and girls. Photograph: Aaron Chown/PA

blocks.text: Removing this block between declaration and delivery doesn’t have to be onerous, Yaqood argues. Partly it’s about making gender equality a priority across the public sector. “Gender equality is always on the periphery of interventions. Until it’s at the centre, you can have as many big commitments as you want, but it will not make a difference enough to women and girls’ lives”.

And placing gender equality at the centre is the beginning of the systemic change demanded of the police and prosecution service, as well as resourcing the tailored, often grassroots, projects that can make a difference in schools and communities – especially those designed by and for men – like the Many Good Men project which takes the conversation into football clubs.
“We don’t have to reinvent the wheel,” says Yaqoob. “There are years of well-evidenced practice that we need to scale up.”

Credit where it’s due: Police Scotland has done some very decent work in recent years with Don’t Be That Guy – a campaign that has young men talking directly to their peers about problematic behaviour. But the force has struggled to take on misogyny and racism within its own ranks.

In recent years in Scotland, the discussion around violence against women has been dominated by arguments around women-only spaces – the UK’s most influential gender critical group, For Women Scotland, is based in Edinburgh – and unfounded claims that Scotland’s asylum population is responsible for an increase in sexual violence.

Yaqoob is clear: “Anyone who tries to position themselves as protectors of women and girls, but does not have an agenda that is focused on tackling poverty, putting money back into communities for women and girls, or the need for consent and sexuality education in schools, is selling you a lie.”
(For more, that broader agenda of tackling gender inequality in all its forms is the subject of a new book of essays, co-edited by Yaqoob.)
The solution is global – and also local
A global problem demands, in part at least, a global solution. As I’ve written in previous First Editions, change at street levels demands that all of us engage in small acts of solidarity.

Yaqoob puts it this way: “Whether you’re calling out misogynistic language in the pub or you’re the leader of a local council allocating resources, there are so many different facets of society where people need to take more responsibility for the space they occupy.”

So much of this conversation applies beyond Scotland, but back at Holyrood it’s fair to say that, while there’s a bit of eye-rolling as yet another male politician “discovers” violence against women and some head-scratching over precisely what reforms he intends to unveil, there’s also wary optimism to hear this focus at the beginning of the SNP government’s five year term.
after newsletter promotion
As one campaigner told me yesterday: “This is an opportunity to kick the door down for bigger changes”.
What else we’ve been enjoying

blocks.caption: ‘The US is being sold for parts, or just handed over to the oligarchy,’ writes Rebecca Solnit, of Trump’s plan to sell off parts of Yosemite. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images

items: Rebecca Solnit is on form in this column lambasting Donald Trump’s plan to “sell off” chunks of Yosemite national park. “The US is being sold for parts or just handed over to the oligarchy,” she writes. Charlie Lindlar, newsletters team

The story of how Jackson Pollock’s masterwork Blue Poles became Australia’s most controversial painting takes in Gough Whitlam, the Shah of Iran and Paul Hogan – and Guardian Australia’s political editor, Tom McIlroy, tells it brilliantly in this Full Story podcast. Libby

Our Laura Snapes’s music coverage is indispensable, yet not even her Taylor Swift opus can compete with this vital piece against the term “picky bits”. “It’s the Boaty McBoatface of dinner time,” she correctly argues, “exposing our once-repressed nation’s surprisingly twee core and total disregard for shame”. Charlie

Football | Bukayo Saka scored the only goal of the game as Arsenal held off a much-improved Aston Villa to make it two wins from two in the Premier League.
The front pages

blocks.caption: Photograph: The Guardian

blocks.text: “Public control of utilities is key to growth – Burnham”, is the Guardian’s front page today. The Times leads with “Healey: I’ll prove I’m no hypocrite on defence”, the Telegraph writes “SAS chief: Army witch hunts put UK at risk”, and the Mail has “Kemi gets Tories battle ready with ruthless reshuffle”.
The i Paper’s splash is “Killer kitchen dust: victims’ loved one to receive higher compensation”, the FT says “Crunch warning for consultants as clients harness AI to cut IT spending”.

The Express has “Million OAPs hit with top-rate tax bills”, and the Sun’s headline is “Prem’s £10m crypto cash frozen”. The Mirror leads with “Maxwell to beg Trump for freedom”, and Metro’s front page is “Dad’s gift of life”.
Today in Focus

blocks.text: War of words: my language lessons in Ukraine

For Charlotte Higgins, the Guardian’s chief culture writer, visiting Ukraine and meeting the artists, novelists and poets under fire changed her life. “It was even before I went home that I decided I needed to learn some Ukrainian,” she tells Helen Pidd. She talks about why she was inspired to learn Ukrainian and what it taught her about its people.
Cartoon of the day | Ben Jennings

blocks.text: The Upside
A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

blocks.caption: ‘On a trip with no podcast diversions, my mind flooded with ideas, plans and insights’ … Rachel Aroesti on a train. Photograph: Alicia Canter/The Guardian

blocks.text: Rachel Aroesti has always loved podcasts, especially the kind that can be described as ‘Two Men Talking (In Excessive Detail About Their Lives)“. Initially drawn to them for their humour, she began to find them hugely comforting – sometimes falling asleep listening to Adam and Joe’s BBC 6 Music show. But, as her consumption increased, she became aware that she used podcasts as a psychological crutch, to prevent being alone with her thoughts.

After a silent, tech-free train ride across the East Anglian countryside, Aroesti felt she was undergoing a mental reboot. Her mind flooded with ideas, plans, insights and reflections at a speed and intensity she had not experienced for years. Nowadays, she savors silence and boredom, and has successfully reduced her listening by at least 80%. “I’ve given my mind permission to wander – both productively and pointlessly – again,” she writes.

articles.title: PCG recovers body of Agana Bridge victim in Dagupan; search for 3 others continues
articles.summary: DAGUPAN CITY, Pangasinan — The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) recovered on Monday, Aug. 31, the body of one of the five people who went missing after their vehicle plunged into the Tarlac River…

blocks.text: Body of Agana Bridge victim recovered off Barangay Pugaro, Dagupan City Monday .(PCG via Liezle Inigo)

DAGUPAN CITY, Pangasinan — The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) recovered on Monday, Aug. 31, the body of one of the five people who went missing after their vehicle plunged into the Tarlac River following the partial collapse of Agana Bridge in Tarlac City.
The body was recovered in the waters off Barangay Pugaro , Dagupan City after a motorbanca operator reported seeing a floating cadaver at around noon.
Coast Guard Station Dagupan immediately deployed a response team and conduct retrieval operations.
Responders confirmed the sighting and recovered the body, which was brought to Barangay Poblacion Oeste and turned over to Dagupan City Police Station 5 for proper disposition.
Tarlac City Mayor Susan Yap later confirmed that the recovered body was that of one of the victims of the Agana Bridge incident.
The vehicle, carrying five occupants, plunged into the Tarlac River on Aug. 29 when the bridge partially collapsed.
The incident triggered a search operation along the river and downstream areas.
The PCG continues to search for the three other missing individuals, with teams scouring the Tarlac River and downstream areas in coordination with other government agencies.

articles.summary: Senator-Judge Vicente “Tito” Sotto III on Tuesday clarified that an alias may be used as a pseudonym for entertainment purposes, but if there is no actual person behind the name, it could be…

blocks.text: Published September 1, 2026 1:44pm

Senator-Judge Vicente “Tito” Sotto III on Tuesday clarified that an alias may be used as a pseudonym for entertainment purposes, but if there is no actual person behind the name, it could be considered a “fictitious name” or “fake name.”
On the 20th day of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, Sotto cited Republic Act No. 6085, which regulates the use of aliases.

“It’s only allowed in the Philippines for pseudonyms, solely for literary, cinema, television and other entertainment purposes. Therefore, if there is a person behind the alias, then it is an alias,” he said.
“If there is no person behind the name, it is a fictitious name or a fake name. Just for the record, Mr. President,” he added.
Section 1 of RA 6085 states:

Except as a pseudonym solely for literary, cinema, television, radio or other entertainment purposes and in athletic events where the use of pseudonym is a normally accepted practice, no person shall use any name different from the one with which he was registered at birth in the office of the local civil registry, or with which he was baptized for the first time, or, in case of an alien, with which he was registered in the Bureau of Immigration upon entry; or such substitute name as may have been authorized by a competent court.

Sotto made the manifestation in response to an exchange between Senator-Judge Robin Padilla and private prosecutor Mae Divinagracia on Wednesday, August 26, regarding the use of aliases in confidential activities.

During the hearing, Padilla pointed out that Philippine heroes and revolutionaries also used aliases during the Spanish colonial period, citing names such as Dimasalang, the alias of José Rizal; Siling Labuyo, used by Marcelo H. del Pilar; Taga-Ilog, used by Antonio Luna; Magdalo, used by Emilio Aguinaldo; and Lakambini, used by Lope K. Santos, among others.
Divinagracia, however, argued that the circumstances under which the aliases were used back then were different because there was a war and the Philippines was under Spanish rule.
On Tuesday, before the trial journal was approved, Sotto also refuted a report that Divinagracia was supposedly not allowed to answer and was cut off several times during Padilla’s interpellation.

“I browsed through the journal and she was able to, Atty. Divinagracia, I believe, she was able to answer most of the questions. There was one or two instances where she was cut off, but I think she was pertaining to, so just for the record, to complete it, she was pertaining to Republic Act 6085, and I think the court allowed her to answer this but probably she was not able to elaborate more,” he said.
Senate impeachment court Presiding Officer Francis Escudero took note of Sotto’s manifestation and confirmed that Divinagracia was able to answer Padilla’s query.
“Although she was not able to give that much detail that the good senator-judge made,” Escudero said.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Agri technician dies in San Carlos flooding; 2 rescued, 60-year-old man missing
articles.summary: SAN CARLOS CITY, Pangasinan — A 28-year-old agricultural technician died after being pulled into extremely deep floodwaters while traversing a submerged road with three companions in Sitio Gulisan,…

blocks.text: Rescuers evacuated flood-affected residents in Brgys. Tamayo, Salinap, and Guelew, San Carlos City, Pangasinan. (Photo courtesy of San Carlos City PNP via Liezle Inigo)

SAN CARLOS CITY, Pangasinan — A 28-year-old agricultural technician died after being pulled into extremely deep floodwaters while traversing a submerged road with three companions in Sitio Gulisan, Barangay Mabalbalino, this city, on August 31.
Police said the incident occurred at around 3:50 p.m. as the group was making its way home along a concrete road submerged by floodwaters.

Initial investigation showed that one of them accidentally stepped toward the edge of the road where the water was deeper, causing the group to lose their balance and pull one another into the deeper portion of the flooded area.
The victim was subsequently retrieved by personnel of the City Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (CDRRMO) and rushed to Virgen Milagrosa Medical Center.
Despite efforts by medical personnel to revive him, the physician declared the victim dead.
Meanwhile, a 27-year-old woman and a minor who were part of the group were rescued by concerned residents in the area.
Search and rescue operations are continuing for another companion, a 60-year-old vendor, who remains missing as of the latest report.
Authorities reminded residents to avoid crossing flooded roads.

articles.title: Relief as Australian missing in Nepal-Tibet floods found alive
articles.summary: One of 43 unaccounted for Australians has been located in Tibet, Dfat says

blocks.text: An Australian believed to be missing after floods ravaged the Nepal-Tibet border last week has been found alive.
The person made contact with officials from the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (Dfat) on Tuesday from Tibet.
They are receiving support from Australian consular officers and has spoken with their family.
This brings down the number of Australians missing in the flash floods from 43 to 42 and comes after another Australian, 25-year-old Cara Severino, was safely located on the weekend.
“We’re incredibly thankful another Australian, who had been unaccounted for, has now been found,” the foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, said.
“It’s hard to imagine the sense of relief their loved ones must be feeling after what will have been an incredibly harrowing few days.”
Due to privacy obligations Dfat was unable to provide further details about the individual.
The death toll from the ⁠unprecedented deluge of ice, rock, mud ​and debris on Wednesday last week has risen to 939 people, with 16 more dead reported in Tibet.
More than 4,400 are missing on the two sides of the border.
Wong said the government needed to “remain realistic” about the days ahead.
“Communications remain difficult, infrastructure has been destroyed and many areas are still difficult to reach,” she said.
“As each day passes, our grave concerns for those still unaccounted for inevitably grow.”
“Our thoughts remain firmly with all those waiting for news of family and friends, and with the search and rescue teams working in extraordinarily difficult circumstances.”
Australia has sent a $8m assistance package for affected communities on the Nepal-China border.
Nepal has deployed nearly 20,000 security personnel to support search and rescue, and Chinese state media has reported that 2,141 emergency personnel have been deployed.
