articles.title: DepEd: Nationwide school safety drill to push through Sept. 3
articles.summary: The National Simultaneous School Safety Drill will push through on Sept. 3 to strengthen schools’ preparedness for active threats, the Department of Education (DepEd) said on Tuesday, Sept. 1. In a…

blocks.text: (MB FILE PHOTO)
The National Simultaneous School Safety Drill will push through on Sept. 3 to strengthen schools’ preparedness for active threats, the Department of Education (DepEd) said on Tuesday, Sept. 1.

In a statement, DepEd said the drill was rescheduled following consultations with the Philippine Psychiatric Association (PPA), Philippine Society for Child and Adolescent Psychiatry (PSCAP), and Philippine Pediatric Society (PPS) to ensure that safety protocols comply with child-centered, trauma-informed standards under its “Do No Harm” directive.
According to DepEd Secretary Juan Edgardo “Sonny” Angara, efforts to ensure school safety must address both physical security and the mental well-being of learners.
"Safety is not just about physical security; it is equally about protecting our children's peace of mind,” he said.
Angara said DepEd is working closely with medical experts and psychiatric societies to keep children’s overall well-being at the center of the drill’s implementation.

“Our goal for September 3 is to build calm operational confidence and muscle memory through proper orientation, not fear. Preparedness saves lives, and trauma-informed execution protects our learners," he added.

DepEd said participating schools will prepare for the drill through teacher capacity-building, school readiness assessments, age-appropriate learner orientations, advance notices to learners, parents, and staff, and the securing of informed written parental consent and learner assent.

“To build psychological readiness and eliminate surprise, school heads and teachers must provide advance notices to learners, parents, and staff. Schools are also required to secure informed written parental consent and learner assent before participation,” the agency said.
“Learners identified as needing additional safeguards or whose parents request accommodations will be provided safe alternative activities without penalty or stigmatization,” it added.

The education department said classes will conduct step-by-step walkthroughs of key protective measures, including securing entry points, remaining silent and out of sight of windows, and reviewing evacuation routes.
Accommodations will be provided for learners with special needs, disabilities, or sensory sensitivities, it added.

DepEd stressed that the drill will exclude all fear-inducing or graphic elements, including threat simulations, active aggressor role-players, weapon props, pyrotechnics, simulated gunfire, and artificial casualties, in accordance with existing disaster risk reduction guidelines.

“Instead, a distinct signal separate from earthquake or fire alarms will initiate the activity. Schools will focus exclusively on building procedural muscle memory without generating distress,” it said.
Angara said safety measures must be tailored to the varying levels of resilience and understanding among learners, as a one-size-fits-all approach would not address their individual needs.
“When we prepare our learners and train our teachers with empathy, age-appropriate guidance, and proper care, we give our school communities confidence and reassurance instead of anxiety,” he said.
“At the end of the day, our schools must remain sanctuaries where learners feel safe, supported, and protected at all times.”
Per DepEd, designated guidance personnel and school health officers will provide psychological first aid (PFA) and conduct post-drill debriefings to maintain a supportive environment.

“Schools will also establish clear referral arrangements with DepEd Schools Division Offices (SDOs), local government units (LGUs), and health facilities for learners needing specialized mental health care,” the agency said.

As such, the education department said coordination with the Philippine National Police (PNP) will be limited to external perimeter security, emergency notification systems, dispatch response-time testing, and post-incident learner tracking.

“Learners will also practice a compliance posture of raising hands high, empty and visible, upon encountering first responders during evacuation. Police officers are strictly prohibited from exposing learners to tactical disarming drills or aggressive uniform displays,” it stated.
On Aug. 24, DepEd postponed the nationwide active attack simulation originally scheduled for Aug. 25 following concerns raised by the PPA and PSCAP.
The groups cited insufficient evidence that such exercises reduce casualties and studies indicating that they could cause lasting psychological harm to learners.

articles.title: Marcos to PCG: Always remember who you serve
articles.summary: President Marcos has reminded newly promoted flag officers of the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) to honor their oath and always remember who they serve. "Serve in a way that honors the oath that you…

blocks.text: President Marcos has reminded newly promoted flag officers of the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) to honor their oath and always remember who they serve.
"Serve in a way that honors the oath that you took today. Lead with courage and integrity. Always remember who you serve," Marcos said in his speech.
The President administered the oath of office to the newly promoted flag officers during a ceremony at Malacañan Palace on Tuesday, Sept. 1.
He also urged them to lead by example and uphold the highest standard of integrity while preparing the next generation of Coast Guard leaders.

"So to our newly promoted flag officers, lead by example, uphold the highest standards of integrity, prepare the next generation of Coast Guard leaders, embrace innovation and modernization, strengthen the partnerships that allow us to address challenges that no institution can tackle alone," he said.
The Chief Executive underscored that the responsibility of the PCG is among the most crucial in government.

"This past year alone has reminded us of that. Our Coast Guard has been out on the water patrolling the West Philippine Sea, escorting and supporting our re-provisioning missions there, and standing beside our fisherfolk in times of distress," Marcos said.
The Coast Guard, Marcos further said, has also been keeping ports and travelers safe by inspecting vessels and looking after millions of passengers moving through the ports.

It has protected the seas by conducting environmental inspections nationwide and the first responders when it comes to enforcing laws, such as going after illegal fishing, smuggling, and other threats.

"Yesterday, we celebrated National Heroes Day. If there is one thing that this day reminds us, it is that courage is built long before the moment that it is tested. It is built through training, discipline, preparation, and the readiness to act when service calls for it," Marcos said.

"This heroism is shown in the willingness to put the needs of others above your own, even when duty requires great personal risk. This is the courage that we see in the men and women of the Philippine Coast Guard. This is the standard that I ask you to carry into your command," Marcos added.
The President also recognized the Coast Guard as it has always been present, rescuing families, and reaching communities that need help.
"These are difficult, sometimes dangerous tasks. For these, we are all grateful for your sacrifice," he said.

articles.title: SIM cards linked to most cybercrimes despite registration law – PNP
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Despite the SIM Card Registration Act, almost all cybercrime in the country involve SIM cards, according to the Philippine National Police-Anti-Cybercrime Group (PNP-ACG).…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Despite the SIM Card Registration Act, almost all cybercrime in the country involve SIM cards, according to the Philippine National Police-Anti-Cybercrime Group (PNP-ACG).

PNP-ACG Director Police Major General Wilson Casil Asueta revealed this in a press conference on Tuesday after reporting that authorities arrested a 26-year-old man in Obando, Bulacan, on Aug. 24, for allegedly illegally selling registered SIM cards.
He said around 400 SIM cards were confiscated during the entrapment operation.
Asueta said that crimes involving SIM cards include scamming, online gambling, and identity exploitation.
He pointed out that the SIM Card Registration Act was “not effectively implemented” and must be amended.

“Ang ating SIM Card Registration Act ay hindi effective ang ating implementation. Kailangan po ng bagong mga provision dito sa SIM Card Registration Act. So we are appealing to our legislators for the immediate passage of amended laws for this purpose,” Asueta said.

(Our SIM Card Registration Act is not being implemented effectively. We need new provisions here in the SIM Card Registration Act. So we are appealing to our legislators for the immediate passage of amended laws for this purpose.)

“Talaga masasabi ko, almost all the cyber cases, mga cybercrimes committed, nagsisimula po sa SIM card. Ito po ang problema natin, ang hirap po nating mamonitor because marami pong pagkukulang at hindi na naaayon ang ating existing laws, itong SIM Card Registration Act,” he pointed out.

(I can honestly say that almost all the cyber cases, cybercrimes committed, start with the SIM card. This is our problem, it is difficult to monitor because there are many shortcomings and our existing laws, this SIM Card Registration Act, are no longer effective.)
Among the PNP-ACG’s proposed amendments to the law are identity authentications and the activation of SIM cards only after successful authentication and registration.
“Kung pwede po, isang ID lang ang gamitin, itong ating national ID. So meron po tayong national ID na meron kaakibat na biometrics details. So ito na lang po ang gamitin natin,” Asueta said.
(If possible, we should only use one ID, our national ID. So we have a national ID that has biometric details attached to it. So this is the only ID we should use.)
The PNP-ACG official likewise suggested limiting SIM card ownership to a maximum of five per person and monitoring the distribution and redistribution of the SIMs.
In 2022, President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. signed the SIM Card Registration Act or Republic Act No. 11934.
The law is aimed at providing “accountability in the use of SIM cards and aid law enforcers to track perpetrators of crimes committed through phones.”

articles.title: PNP okay to hold training with DepEd to detect red-flag behaviors
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Tuesday expressed its readiness to conduct training sessions in schools to identify red-flag behaviors and help adults properly respond…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Tuesday expressed its readiness to conduct training sessions in schools to identify red-flag behaviors and help adults properly respond to warning signs involving children.

According to the PNP, its local police offices and units are prepared to work with the Department of Education (DepEd) to conduct training sessions to help parents and teachers recognize violent acts, criminal activities, and behavioral red flags among children.
“Protecting students and teachers in schools requires efforts from various stakeholders,” PNP chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez said in a statement.

“And we in the PNP are ready to extend assistance and impart knowledge through training sessions that will educate parents and teachers in the interest of the safety and welfare of learners,” he added.
The PNP made the pronouncement after DepEd recently began expanding its Kaagapay Program aimed to train parents in helping them identify red flags in their children’s behavior.
The police are also offering protection sessions focused on addressing bullying, online sexual abuse and violent extremism.

The PNP Anti-Cybercrime Group and the Women and Children Protection Center also extended its assistance in these sessions to strengthen the parents’ and teachers’ capacity to address concerns related to violence and other criminal activities.
—Martina Nieyandra Calica, INQUIRER.net trainee

articles.title: Local leaders surrender 44 loose firearms in Maguindanao Norte town
articles.summary: COTABATO CITY – In their bid to help the campaign against loose firearms and establish peaceful communities in Datu Odin Sinsuat, Maguindanao del Norte, local officials and residents in 25 of 34…

blocks.text: COTABATO CITY – In their bid to help the campaign against loose firearms and establish peaceful communities in Datu Odin Sinsuat, Maguindanao del Norte, local officials and residents in 25 of 34 villages voluntarily surrendered 44 unlicensed guns to the military on Monday.

The assorted loose firearms were presented to authorities during a turnover program in Barangay Bitu as part of efforts to curb violence and the proliferation of unregistered weapons ahead of the Sept. 14 Bangsamoro parliamentary elections.
Village officials collected the weapons from their constituents, including those in the hands of barangay leaders.

The turnover was held at the evacuation center in Barangay Bitu, which is the same village where the convoy of Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) Interim Chief Minister Abdulraof Macacua was ambushed on Aug. 15.

Military authorities said the incident served as a serious reminder of the continuing threat of violence and the need for stronger collective action against loose firearms, particularly with the elections fast approaching.
The initiative brought together government agencies, security forces, local leaders, and residents to help prevent further violence and maintain peace and order in Datu Odin Sinsuat.

Lt. Col. William G. Sabado, commanding officer of the 1st Mechanized Infantry Battalion, led the program. Also present were Datu Odin Sinsuat Mayor Abdulmain Abas Sr.; Lt. Col. Sahibun Mamantal, Maguindanao Norte police deputy provincial director; Lt. Col. Brian A. Balite, Datu Odin Sinsuat municipal police chief; and officials from 25 barangays in Datu Odin Sinsuat.

The surrendered weapons included four 7.62mm sniper rifles, 11 fabricated 12-gauge shotguns, 12 fabricated .38-caliber revolvers, three fabricated 9mm submachine guns, three .45-caliber pistols, three grenade launchers, and other firearms.
Sabado said the surrender of the weapons is an important step toward reducing potential security threats and preventing their possible use in violence.
“The voluntary surrender of firearms was more than just a turnover. It demonstrated the communities’ trust and cooperation in the pursuit of peace,” Sabado said.
“Every firearm voluntarily surrendered represented a potential threat removed and a step toward safer communities,” he added.

Sabado noted the turnover of 44 loose firearms reflected Datu Odin Sinsuat’s collective resolve against violence and underscored how unity and concerted action can help strengthen and protect peace in the community.
Maj. Gen. Ronel R. Manalo, commander of the Philippine Army’s Armor Division, expressed the division’s full support for initiatives to reduce threats to peace and strengthen community security.
He called for continued cooperation among local governments, security forces, and residents to preserve peace and ensure a safe, orderly, peaceful election./coa

articles.title: WATCH: No DepEd funds went to 2023 youth summit, says AFP witness
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – Armed Forces of the Philippiines Col. Manaros Boransing II testifies before the impeachment court that no confidential or general funds from the Office of the Vice President…

articles.title: Hungary drained its waters for generations. Now drought is exposing the cost
articles.summary: GÁRDONY, Hungary (AP) — A fisherman disembarked from his boat in a small harbor on Lake Velence in Hungary last week, trudging up the dock plank that had become extremely steep as the water receded…

blocks.text: GÁRDONY, Hungary (AP) — A fisherman disembarked from his boat in a small harbor on Lake Velence in Hungary last week, trudging up the dock plank that had become extremely steep as the water receded to record lows.

blocks.caption: People walk on sandbanks exposed by record-low water levels in the Danube River after drought and extreme heat near Nagymaros, Hungary, Tuesday, on Aug. 18, 2026. (AP Photo/Bela Szandelszky)

blocks.text: People walk on sandbanks exposed by record-low water levels in the Danube River after drought and extreme heat near Nagymaros, Hungary, Tuesday, on Aug. 18, 2026. (AP Photo/Bela Szandelszky)

Árpád Selmeci said that navigating even a small fishing boat on Hungary's third-largest lake is becoming increasingly difficult as the water level has ebbed to around 20 centimeters (8 inches), well below the 150 centimeters (5 feet) optimal for August. Swimming beaches across the lake, once popular with tourists, have been closed.
Lake Velence’s decline is part of a broader water crisis confronting Hungary as increasingly prolonged droughts and climate change-driven heat waves have pummeled Europe.
“I've lived on Lake Velence since I was a child, and I've never seen the water so low," said Selmeci, 58. "It's terrible. My heart aches every single moment.”

This summer, wildfires scorched the continent from the United Kingdom to Greece, while in Hungary, drought has damaged crop yields, led to drinking water shortages and threatened to shut down the country's only nuclear power plant.

Yet the lack of rainfall linked to human-driven climate change is only part of Hungary's water problem. Experts say the country's long-standing practice of channeling water away from its landscape and draining natural wetlands has left it especially vulnerable as droughts become more frequent and severe.
A legacy of draining away water

Around 99% of Hungary’s lands are currently under severe or extreme drought conditions, according to the national meteorological service, and desertification, a process where vegetation recedes because of high heat and low rainfall, threatens much of the Great Hungarian Plain.

blocks.caption: Boats lie on cracked soil at a dried-out marina on Lake Velence, Hungary, on Aug. 13. 2026. (AP Photo/Bela Szandelszky)

blocks.text: Boats lie on cracked soil at a dried-out marina on Lake Velence, Hungary, on Aug. 13. 2026. (AP Photo/Bela Szandelszky)

Yet more than a quarter of Hungary consists of low-lying land that naturally retains precipitation, and in past centuries its many rivers and streams made it rich in freshwater resources. However, a 2023 study published in the journal Nature estimated Hungary’s historical wetland loss at more than 80%.

Zsuzsanna Ujj, a biodiversity policy specialist and project coordinator with environmental group Friends of the Earth Hungary, said the country “has not been a good steward of its waters in the last 200 years.”

A major contributor is Hungary's network of more than 40,000 kilometers (25,000 miles) of drainage canals — a length that exceeds the circumference of the Earth — which drain accumulated precipitation from fields, wetlands and the soil to make room for agriculture and other enterprises.

The priority on draining land rather than allowing natural flooding cycles to occur has contributed to a consistent drop in the water table and the drying out of wetlands and topsoil. With less water available to evaporate, the air dries out, further reducing the chances of localized precipitation.

Ujj said that Hungary — which is among the most drought-exposed countries in Europe and ranks 16th globally, according to a report by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development — “needs to realign its water management practices, shifting from a drainage-based approach to one focused on water retention.”
Disappearing lakes

The drying out of Hungary isn't limited to streams and wetlands. Lake Garancsi, a small recreational lake around 20 kilometers (12 miles) northwest of Budapest, was once a popular destination for fishing, swimming and ice skating, and was the setting of the 2001 cult Hungarian comedy “Üvegtigris” (“Glass Tiger").

The bed of Lake Garancsi is exposed as the popular tourist destination near Budapest after the lake died out following an extended drought period near Tinnye, Hungary, on Aug. 8, 2026. (AP Photo/Bela Szandelszky)

But the lake, present since the Middle Ages, has shrunk so dramatically in recent years that none of the previous recreational activities are permitted, and most of the former lake bed is now exposed, cracked and dry.
What remains of the water is so shallow and warm that all of the fish and most of the other wildlife have disappeared, and authorities have predicted no water will be left by the end of summer.

Zoltán Mettner, who runs the Glass Tiger bar on the shores of the lake, said conditions have gotten worse every year. After spending years beside the lake, he said looking at it now is “terrible, there’s no other way to put it.”
“It’s sad enough that we’ve let things get this far, and that we couldn’t have taken gradual steps to prevent this lake from being completely destroyed,” he said.
Hungary's government plans a change of course
Hungary's new government has promised to begin taking those steps.

In late June, on the same day the country set a high temperature record of 42 Celsius (107.6 Fahrenheit), Prime Minister Péter Magyar told lawmakers that his government would put water management policies “on new footing,” and launch a comprehensive water conservation program to mitigate the effects of drought.
"Many have said year after year that water shortage will be one of Hungary’s problems and one of the most important strategic issues to be solved. They were right,” Magyar said.

In addition to poor water retention practices, Magyar said that aging water utility infrastructure causes 20-25% of the country’s drinking water to leak out through damaged pipes, costing some 17 billion forints ($54.4 million) annually.
“For years, even the existence of the problem was denied and relativized,” Magyar said. Now, he added, “water retention will be the basic principle of Hungarian water management.”
Danube River at historic lows
Yet implementing such sweeping changes will be time consuming and costly, while Hungary's current water crisis threatens its ability to produce adequate energy.

The Danube, the European Union's longest river which runs through 10 countries from southwestern Germany to the Black Sea, has set successive records this summer for low water levels, threatening to shut down Hungary's only nuclear power plant, which uses water from the river to cool its reactors, for the first time in its 44-year history.

Hungary's government has taken emergency interventions to raise the water level at the Paks plant, including sinking two 80-meter (262-foot) barges just upriver and beginning to install a riverbed sill designed to divert more water toward the plant's pumps.

blocks.caption: People walk on sandbanks exposed by record-low water levels in the Danube River after drought and extreme heat near Nagymaros, Hungary, on Aug. 18, 2026. (AP Photo/Bela Szandelszky)

blocks.text: People walk on sandbanks exposed by record-low water levels in the Danube River after drought and extreme heat near Nagymaros, Hungary, on Aug. 18, 2026. (AP Photo/Bela Szandelszky)
In such drought conditions, wetlands near rivers like the Danube normally act as a “natural reservoir” for retaining water when weather gets dry, said Ujj, the biodiversity specialist.

The extremely low level of the Danube — as well as the increased chances for more frequent and intense floods — are effects of human-driven climate change that can be partially mitigated through appropriate land use and restoration of wetlands and other natural habitats, she added.

“We do indeed expect water levels to fluctuate more, and we also expect precipitation patterns to become more extreme with drier summers,” she said. "However, restoring wetlands and increasing evaporation in certain areas could help boost precipitation during the summer months.”

articles.title: Price rises gather pace in UK shops amid higher energy costs
articles.summary:
In-store inflation rises to an annual 1.5% in August, according to a survey for the British Retail Consortium

The pace of price rises in UK shops rose to its highest level in two years in…

blocks.text: The pace of price rises in UK shops rose to its highest level in two years in August, a trade body index shows, with higher energy costs pushing up the price of food and AI chip demand making technology more expensive.

In-store inflation stepped up to 1.5% year on year in August, up from 0.9% in July, led by prices for tinned and packaged food which increased by 2.5% against 1.1% in the prior month, according to data from the research company NIQ for the British Retail Consortium.

Inflation for fresh produce remained high at 3%, amid pressure on growers from the hot dry summer plus hefty fuel and energy costs. However, that marked a slight easing off from the 3.1% recorded in July,

Helen Dickinson, the chief executive of the consortium, said: “The impact of higher energy, input and commodity costs is beginning to filter through into prices, particularly for ambient foods which are typically imported and processed.

“In non-food, electrical prices rose amid the ongoing AI boom, which is forcing up the price of memory chips and storage. Meanwhile, retailers kept clothing prices low to offer value for families getting ready for the new school year.
“The months ahead look challenging for households, with rising bills putting further pressure on budgets.”

Mike Watkins, head of retailer insight at NIQ, said he expected price competition between retailers to intensify in the autumn months as businesses competed to attract families concerned about potentially higher energy bills.

However, Dickinson said companies were facing “persistently high operating costs” that limited their ability to absorb price rises. She added: “If the government is serious about supporting growth while keeping the cost of living in check, it must address the cost of doing business, including by tackling the growing burden of business rates, packaging and employment taxes.”
The evidence of higher shop prices comes after the boss of Asda said he was seeing inflation on some fresh food begin to rise after a hot dry summer that affected crop yields.

Cereals including wheat and barley were hit particularly badly, according to the Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board. Its first harvest report of 2026 said the hot weather had resulted in the earliest harvest since records began in 2006.
after newsletter promotion
The rise in shop price inflation adds to the challenge for Andy Burnham’s government in achieving its aim of granting “breathing space” to hard-pressed households

Wider consumer price inflation across the UK rose to 2.9% in July with the Iran war affecting energy prices, according to the latest figures from the Office for National Statistics. The agency said inflation rose from a 15-month low of 2.6% in June, driven by more costly gas and electricity.
Despite government measures to ease electricity costs, households in Great Britain face the sharpest summer increase in energy bills in four years.

articles.title: Burnham warned running prison capacity near limit is ‘big risk’
articles.summary:
U-turn on early release scheme will create ‘stresses and strains’ on prison system, says former justice secretary

Andy Burnham is taking a “big risk” by seeking to continue running prison…

blocks.text: Andy Burnham is taking a “big risk” by seeking to continue running prison capacity to the limit, according to the former justice secretary appointed by Keir Starmer to oversee a review of sentencing.

As parliament resumes on Tuesday, the government will confirm its U-turn on its early release scheme, which would have seen thousands of prisoners released early as part of a plan to ease prison overcrowding.
About 5,000 prisoners had been due to be released early from October under the plans, down from 6,000 after ministers intervened to exempt rapists and “serious” child sexual abuse offenders.

However, David Gauke, the former Conservative minister who led Starmer’s independent review of sentences, warned of the “stresses and strains” from choosing to run prison capacity at a “red hot” level, even as he recognised options available to Burnham were limited.
“He is in a bind. I have some sympathy for any government that is wrestling with this, but that is why we came forward with the recommendations we came forward with,” Gauke told the Guardian.
“I am going to see what Alex Norris [the justice secretary] says in parliament, but my concern – and I hope this isn’t the case – is that they are essentially taking a big risk on prison capacity.”
Gauke said that Burnham’s political strategy was in contrast to his predecessor in that the new prime minister was “very sensitive to public opinion”.

blocks.caption: David Gauke, a former justice secretary, expressed concern the government was ‘essentially taking a big risk on prison capacity’.  Photograph: Anna Gordon/The Guardian

blocks.text: He also said it would be “irresponsible” to release prisoners serving indefinite jail terms, which Burnham has pledged to abolish. The government is pinning some hope of increasing capacity on reducing the number of prisoners serving Imprisonment for Public Protection (IPP) sentences, and deporting more foreign prisoners more swiftly.

“In terms of public protection, releasing IPPs comes with much higher risks than the categories excluded from the early release scheme,” said Gauke, who examined them when he was justice secretary in Theresa May’s government but said it was clear from prison disciplinary records why such prisoners had not been released.
The intervention came as the government said on Monday night that the largest prison-building programme since the Victorian era would be accelerated through a £110m investment.

The funding will go towards speeding up the construction of hundreds of prison places with plans to add 14,000 extra spaces by 2031, and cells being created from existing space within prisons including unused offices, laundry rooms and other areas.
The Ministry of Justice also said on Monday there would be investment to buy new land to secure potential sites for future prisons.
“This government is serious about fixing the broken prison system we inherited, which is why we’ve already delivered more than 3,200 prison places in just two years,” said Norris.

blocks.caption: The government plans to add 14,000 extra prison spaces by 2031 in the largest prison-building programme since the Victorian era.  Photograph: PA Images/Alamy

blocks.text: However, the Conservatives sought to keep up political pressure over the early release scheme, saying that it left at least 23 categories of serious violent and sexual offences eligible for automatic early release, including trafficking, strangulation and assault by penetration.

“Labour’s plan to stop the release of dangerous criminals is to release a whole new group of dangerous criminals,” said the shadow justice secretary, Nick Timothy, who called for a delay to the scheme and emergency primary legislation to exclude the worst offenders.
The victims minister, Alex Davies-Jones, insisted during interviews on Monday that “release does not mean freedom” for those let out under the early release scheme.
“When these offenders come out of prison, the presumption will be that they will all be placed on a GPS monitoring tag,” she said.

In terms of capacity, she told the BBC’s Today programme: “We will have capacity in the system with those numbers but we will run it very tight, which is why we have been tasked to look at what more we can do.”
A leading police chief, meanwhile, warned that tracking people let out of prison under the early release scheme would be an additional challenge on the strained resources of police officers.

Jason Hogg, the chief constable of Thames Valley police, told LBC on Monday: “The police haven’t received any additional funding for this additional work, so I’m going to be having to move resources away from one area of business to another to seek out, arrest and bring before the court individuals who don’t follow the restrictions that they will be set.”

articles.title: Dry weather sewage discharges soar as water companies face scrutiny
articles.summary:
Exclusive: 7,280 suspected illegal spills in rivers and sea recorded in first five months of 2026

The number of suspected illegal discharges of raw sewage into rivers and seas by water…

blocks.text: The number of suspected illegal discharges of raw sewage into rivers and seas by water companies during dry weather increased significantly during the first five months of 2026.

Dumping raw sewage into waterways during dry spells via overflows amounts to pollution. It is considered a breach of the permits given to water companies and is illegal. Discharging during dry weather increases the toxicity of the sewage pollution entering waterways. Rivers have less flow and volume, and there is no rainwater to dilute the sewage pollution entering the waterway.

Last year, in what regulators said was tougher action on sewage pollution, water companies in England were for the first time required to report to the Environment Agency the number of times they discharged raw sewage from combined sewer overflows during dry weather. A dry day spill is flagged when an overflow operates despite little to no rainfall that day and the previous day.

In 2025, water companies in England and Wales reported 8,576 dry spill pollution discharges. But according to freedom of information requests submitted by Environment Agency whistleblower Robert Forrester, the pollution is getting worse, not better, despite the regulator’s promise of tougher action.

Between January and May this year alone, water companies discharged raw sewage into rivers and seas during dry weather 7,280 times. The data is comparable as it is based on the same instruction and taken from the same data recording system.
The water industry said the figures were as yet unverified and it was too early to describe them as dry spills.
Forrester, an Environment Agency officer for more than 20 years, revealed failures by the agency to take on water companies’ illegal practices before leaving his job.
“Dry day spills will almost always be deliberate and illegal, otherwise there would be non-stop raw sewage spilling from pipes,” said Forrester.

“The huge increase in a much drier year appears to show that water companies have quotas of sewage to dump and will do whatever the weather, and whatever the risk to the public and the environment. Making money is the primary focus.” He said the regulator was no deterrent to the actions of the water companies.
“This level of criminality shows that water companies do not believe they, or the government, will ever do anything meaningful to stop them.”

Combined sewer overflows are an emergency system designed to be used in extreme weather to relieve pressure in the sewage system. But decades of underinvestment by the privatised water industry have led to the outflows being used regularly to discharge sewage.

In the first five months of 2026, South West Water, which operates across Devon, Cornwall and parts of Dorset and Somerset, discharged raw sewage on dry days 1,299 times. This compares with 2,451 times during the whole of 2025.

Water companies are facing outrage across the country for discharging raw sewage via storm outflows in August following the first moderate spell of rain after more than six weeks of drought. Public mapped data revealed water companies including Southern Water and South West Water discharging raw sewage from storm overflows within hours of the first significant rain.
In the south-west, after weeks of drought, the company’s own data suggested it discharged sewage into rivers and the sea for a combined total of almost 300 hours in the third week of August.
Ed Tyldesley, a Liberal Democrat county councillor in north Devon, said the company’s own figures showed 664 separate spills across 184 sites despite just 16.5mm of rain across the south-west.
“They are using a storm system when there are no storms. It is unbelievable. The worrying thing is that this all seems to be getting worse,” he said.

Tyldesley said he had been told by the water company that its live monitoring data could sometimes contain false readings. “That leaves two possibilities. Either the South West Water data is correct and sewage was discharged into our rivers and seas for 299 hours in a single week, or their legally mandated monitoring system is so unreliable that hundreds of apparent sewage spills are being reported to the public, which may not actually have happened.”

A spokesperson for Water UK, the trade association for the water industry, said: “These are unverified figures, and it is too early to describe them as dry day spills. Nonetheless, no spill is ever acceptable. Water companies are working to end them as fast as possible by tripling investment. Companies are investing £12bn to halve spills from storm overflows by 2030, including relining and sealing sewers to prevent groundwater infiltration – one of the main causes of dry day spills.”
South West Water has said the company publishes near real-time monitoring data, which has to be validated before being used for regulatory reporting.
“Storm overflow activations can happen for a range of reasons and aren’t determined by rainfall figures alone.

“We continue to invest in our monitoring and are spending record amounts to reduce storm overflow use across the region. We’re reviewing the locations raised by the councillor so we can provide a full response.”
A Defra spokesperson said: “It is totally unacceptable that some water companies are failing to deliver value for money for customers and polluting our rivers, lakes and seas.

“After years of failure, we have taken immediate action to make water companies more accountable, and, for the first time ever, they are now required to report dry day spills as pollution incidents, providing the government with the evidence to go after water companies where performance falls short.”

articles.title: 'I've never been to Afghanistan': Six million deportees forced to start over under the Taliban
articles.summary: As of August, the number forced to return this year from Pakistan and Iran had reached another million.

blocks.text: Watch: BBC's Lyse Doucet reports on the biggest cross-border movement of people
ByLyse Doucet
Chief international correspondentReporting fromTorkham crossing and Kabul
The elderly grimace, hobbling on crutches, and wide-eyed children stare, cradling chickens carried from homes they were forced to leave behind.
"It feels good to be in my own country," 35-year-old Nazia says, just minutes after she crosses from Pakistan, where she was born, into Afghanistan.
The Torkham crossing, known as "Zero Point", is where one hard life ends and another begins.

"But I've never been to Afghanistan before and many people here don't even have enough bread to eat," Nazia sighs as she heads, two of her children in tow, toward registration counters festooned with white and black Taliban flags.
Nearly her entire family, eight sisters and their offspring, were deported to Afghanistan this year from Pakistan or Iran.
They are part of the biggest cross-border movement of people anywhere in the world.

Millions of Afghans have fled across the borders to Pakistan and Iran for decades – seeking refuge or employment - and the number escaping Afghanistan has continued to rise since the Taliban takeover in August 2021.

Most are now being forced to return as these two neighbours crack down on undocumented migrants. Nazia and her family were undocumented but the UN and human rights groups say the security sweep is reaching far beyond that group to include registered Afghans too. Even Pakistan now publicly says that Afghans with Proof of Registration cards are not exempt.
The expulsions show no sign of stopping.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Trucks carrying returnees parked along the highway near the border

blocks.text: Image source, AFP
Trucks carrying returnees parked along the highway near the border
The number forced to return this year from Pakistan and Iran has already reached another million, according to the UN's Refugee Agency, the UNHCR.

"In a little under three years, we've seen six million people, a population that is itself the size of a small country, come back to Afghanistan," observes Charlie Goodlake, spokesperson for the UNHCR in Afghanistan.
"We've never seen in recent history a return movement on this scale," he underlines, standing in the baking heat in the tented village close to the border.

It's a desolate landscape of tarpaulin and plastic shelters, many now tattered and torn, erected by the UN and other aid agencies to provide refuge for a few nights for a people arriving with nowhere to go.
Many returnees have not set foot in Afghanistan for decades; many like Nazia have never been here at all.

"I left 45 years ago during the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan and most of my brothers were born in Pakistan," explains Sarwar, who arrived a few days earlier with seven brothers and their families in a convoy of 40 people and the jumble of their worldly goods packed into a lumbering Pakistani lorry.
"We spent a long time there, so of course I felt heartbroken when they forced us out of our home," he says.
"But, despite all that pain, I am also happy because I am finally free of harassment by Pakistan's police."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Afghan returnees deported from Pakistan arriving at the Torkham crossing

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
Afghan returnees deported from Pakistan arriving at the Torkham crossing
Every family we met told us they had experienced prejudice and harassment by authorities in Pakistan.

The Pakistan government has not responded to the BBC's questions, but a foreign ministry spokesman told a briefing in Islamabad on Sunday that "the Government of Pakistan undertakes the necessary measures to prevent any instance of harassment or maltreatment of Afghan nationals in Pakistan. If such incidents have taken place, they are sporadic and are dealt with fully in accordance with the law".
Both Pakistan and Iran say it's past time for Afghans to go home, accusing some of posing a security risk, and others of being a financial burden.

The expulsions from Pakistan and alleged abuse intensified after a major escalation in fighting between Pakistan and Afghanistan last October. In February, Human Rights Watch highlighted "door-to-door raids, late-night home searches and arrests without warrants".
In Iran, which claimed last year to host more than four million undocumented Afghans, the mass deportations were accelerated after its 12-day war with Israel and the US in June 2025.

The New York based Centre for Human Rights in Iran accused the authorities of using the post-war climate to "cast suspicion on Afghan migrants - accusing them of espionage and branding them as potential spies for Israel".
The UN's refugee agency continues to underscore the humanitarian principle that any return should be "voluntary, safe and dignified".
But in Torkham, Sarwar's sister-in-law Zarina laments the precarious future they face: "We have no resources to start a business or earn a living, and we don't even own a tent to live in".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Zarina, 40, is among the million Afghan who have returned this year alone

blocks.text: Zarina, 40, is among the million Afghan who have returned this year alone
Inside the barren transit tent, which provides little escape from scorching 41C heat, Zarina sits alongside an anxious huddle of women and their children.
Are they worried about the future for women and girls in a country where the Taliban has barred women from much of public life, including secondary school and university?
Forty-year-old Zarina turns to make a sweeping gesture with her arm: "Look at them, they're all girls. Of course I'm worried."
Some returnees are not just worried; they're terrified.
"I don't leave this house," a former Afghan security guard, first deported from Iran and then Pakistan, nervously tells us when we meet him far from the border in what he hopes is a safe house.
"We are all living in fear including my wife and children who are also afraid to go outside."

He dismisses the Taliban government's amnesty, announced days after their return to power which declared that former government officials, security personnel and civil servants would not face retaliation and were encouraged to return to work.
"I have no trust in their amnesty because many of my colleagues have been killed." He says his case had been registered with the UN but was deported before he could be transferred to a safer country.
Financial hardship magnifies the pain. The steep cuts in foreign aid worldwide are especially sharp in Afghanistan where the Taliban are still stuck in sanctions linked to terrorism and human rights.
Pakistan confirmed on Sunday that 16,000 vulnerable Afghans have now been granted, on humanitarian grounds, a temporary exemption from being deported – a decision welcomed by the UN.
But sources estimate that the number of Afghans in Pakistan at risk of serious harm, including women and girls who would be denied education, could be as high as 250,000.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Zarina says she is worried about the future of the girls who cannot attend school in Taliban-run Afghanistan

blocks.text: Zarina says she is worried about the future of the girls who cannot attend school in Taliban-run Afghanistan
At the graceful foreign ministry compound in Kabul, Taliban Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi tries to put on a brave face.
"There's no doubt that we need some help," he admits. "There is pressure due to their return but in the long run, it will benefit them as well as Afghanistan."
In the first years after the Taliban swept to power in 2021, some of their ministers made light of humanitarian issues, saying God would provide.

The UN now estimates that 21.9 million people, nearly half the country, need assistance this year to survive. The UN's children agency, UNICEF, said last week that one million children faced "life-threatening" malnutrition.
"No country in the world could handle this kind of crisis on its own," UNHCR spokesperson Goodlake assesses, while acknowledging Taliban government efforts to help returnees as they arrive.
But, he adds, "We also know that many of the restrictions and edicts they put in place, particularly on women and girls, don't help us elicit international support".
Muttaqi reiterates his government's line that matters like girl's education are "internal issues" for Afghans to resolve.

The severe restrictions on the lives of girls and women is one of the major issues in the Taliban's international relationships and that has cost them. Five years on, only one country, Russia, has formally recognised their rule.
But when asked about this, Muttaqi points to the deepening diplomatic and economic ties with neighbours such as China and India, as well as Central Asian states.
As for Kabul's relative isolation from western nations, he asks, "those who didn't have relationships with us over the past five years, what have they achieved?"
He answers his own question: "Nothing."
We heard that word - "nothing" - from every family we met at Zero Point, but in a much different sense.
All were embarking on the hardest of homecomings, beginning all over again - with almost nothing.

articles.title: Who is Col. Manaros Boransing II, the AFP witness in Sara Duterte impeachment trial?
articles.summary: Philippine Army (PA) official Col. Manaros Boransing II took the witness stand on Tuesday after the Senate impeachment court ordered him to testify in Vice President Sara Duterte"s trial.

blocks.text: Published September 1, 2026 12:58pm
Philippine Army (PA) official Col. Manaros Boransing II took the witness stand on Tuesday after the Senate impeachment court ordered him to testify in Vice President Sara Duterte’s trial.
But who is Boransing, and why is he a witness?
The Senate impeachment court is not the first time Boransing has been asked about Duterte’s confidential funds.
A retired military official, Boransing previously appeared before the House committee on good government and public accountability during its inquiry into Duterte’s confidential funds in 2024.

According to Batangas Rep. Gerville Luistro, Boransing was called to testify during the panel’s hearing on the Commission on Audit’s (COA) disallowance of P15.54 million out of the Department of Education’s (DepEd) P112.5 million in confidential expenses in 2023 due to a lack of supporting documents.
The P15.54 million was part of the P75 million initially flagged by COA for lack of documentation.
To justify the P15.54 million in expenses to COA, DepEd presented certification letters from the military stating that the funds had been used for the Youth Leadership Summit (YLS).
The YLS is an ongoing Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) program that engages young people in various training activities aimed at developing leadership skills.
Boransing was among the Army officials who provided the certificates. However, he said he was unaware that the certificates would be used to justify DepEd’s expenses before COA.
Then-DepEd spokesperson Michael Poa told the House panel that he had asked DepEd Undersecretary and retired Major General Nolasco Mempin to request the certificates from the military.
Poa stressed that there was no malice involved, saying he assumed there had already been coordination between the two agencies.

Mempin later testified that he was unaware of the purpose of the certifications. He said Boransing and the other military officials from whom he requested certificates were his classmates at the Philippine Military Academy.
Boransing, however, said the military would not have issued the certificates if there had been no actual participation by a representative in the YLS. — MCG, GMA News
