articles.title: Shein shares slide in long-awaited stock market debut
articles.summary: The firm's Hong Kong listing on Tuesday comes after a years-long quest to sell shares in New York and London.

blocks.text: Shares in fast-fashion giant Shein fell sharply in their highly anticipated stock market debut on Tuesday as the firm listed in Hong Kong after a long quest to go public.
It comes after failed attempts to list in the US and UK, as concerns were raised over issues including Shein's labour practices and its environmental impact.
Once estimated to be worth nearly $100bn (£74bn), Shein is now valued at around a quarter of that figure, as the firm faces other challenges like heated competition and trade tensions.
Shein became hugely popular, especially among younger people, due to its ability to source the very latest fashions at ultra-low prices through a vast network of factories in China.

At a ceremony to celebrate the listing, chief financial officer Leigh Gui said the company's model of selling large numbers of small orders with rapid payment options now reaches about 160 markets worldwide.
"Let global consumers enjoy the sound of fashion," he said.
On Monday, Shein priced its shares at HK$48.56 each, raising ‌13.6 billion Hong Kong dollars ($1.7bn; £1.3bn) from the listing.
That gave the company a stock market valuation of $26.3bn.
Shein's shares were trading 8.7% lower at 44.4 Hong Kong dollars each on Tuesday morning.
The disappointing debut suggests the market is not convinced that Shein's growth can make a "comeback", said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at investment bank Saxo.
Shein has more than 273 million active customers who placed a total of more than a billion orders in the year to the end of March 2026, the firm said in a filing ahead of the listing.
But Shein now faces higher costs, regulatory scrutiny and more competition, while investors are increasingly drawn towards technology companies, Chanana said.
For customers, the slump in Shein's shares is a sign that the firm's cheap prices are "becoming harder to sustain", which may lead to higher prices, she added.
Shein was founded in China in 2008 and is now headquartered in Singapore.
The firm's long road to the stock market highlights the geopolitical pressures and regulatory scrutiny faced by Chinese companies with global ambitions.
The company once looked set for one of the largest stock market debuts ever by a Chinese firm, with Wall Street in its sights.
Its business had surged during the Covid-19 pandemic as people, stuck at home, turned to online retailers.
Shoppers shared clips of themselves trying on large numbers of its garments, a trend called Shein Hauls, boosting the company's online presence.
An initial public offering (IPO) in the US - by far Shein's largest market - would have offered it a chance to further increase its global profile and tap into Western financing.

But the firm faced resistance from US lawmakers, who objected to the planned listing over concerns of forced labour in Shein's factories. In response to such allegations, the company has said it takes a "zero-tolerance policy for forced labour".
It has also been accused of copying other designers' ideas. Shein has said "it takes all claims of infringement seriously" and that it respects the rights of all designers.
Shein also explored the possibility of making its stock market debut in London but faced similar opposition.
The BBC has contacted Shein for further comment.
Its rivals are feeling the pressure too. In August, Temu-owner PDD reported lower-than-expected quarterly revenue.
Shein is also being investigated by US and European regulators over its business practices.

The company also needs to find ways to stand out from its rivals, that are now also using predictive technology to make their websites more appealing to shoppers, said Jason Hsu from Rayliant Global Advisors.
"Shein is not longer a unique player," Hsu said.
Despite these challenges some analysts still see strong potential for Shein.
Investors will be scrutinising whether the company can navigate these issues, such as shifting logistics out of China to avoid the US and EU's import fees, Deglise-Favre said.
The slump in the firm's valuation shows "genuine deterioration", but it is still backed by a "formidable supply chain" and a global reach, she added.
People are still buying the company's goods, but costs have weighed on its business and have shown that its business model does not generate profits in the way it once did, said Dudarenok.
As a listed company, Shein will need to "prove its margins still work in a world of tighter regulation, tariffs and more expensive customer acquisition," she added.

articles.title: Pilandok intensifies into tropical storm Tuesday morning
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Tropical depression Pilandok intensified into a tropical storm (international name: Krovanh) on Tuesday morning, according to the state weather bureau. In its latest tropical…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Tropical depression Pilandok intensified into a tropical storm on Tuesday morning, according to the state weather bureau.

In its latest tropical cyclone formation outlook update issued at 10 a.m., the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (Pagasa) said that Pilandok developed into a tropical storm as of 8 a.m. inside the Philippine area of responsibility (PAR).
Pilandok slightly gained strength with a maximum wind speed of 65 kilometers per hour (kph) and gustiness of up to 80 kph.
It was last located 1,060 kilometers east of extreme Northern Luzon as of 8 a.m.
3 weather disturbances
Meanwhile, three other weather disturbances are being monitored outside the PAR.
Tropical Storm Saudel was last spotted some 900 kilometers west of extreme Northern Luzon with a maximum wind speed of 65 kph and gustiness of up to 90 kph.
Pagasa also said that another tropical depression weakened into a low pressure area (LPA) and is unlikely to redevelop into a tropical cyclone within the next 24 hours.
Meantime, an LPA outside the country has a medium chance of developing into a tropical depression within the next 24 hours. /gsg

articles.title: Marcos to PCG flag officers: Lead by example, uphold integrity
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Tuesday urged newly promoted Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) flag officers to lead by example and uphold the highest standards of integrity in…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Tuesday urged newly promoted Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) flag officers to lead by example and uphold the highest standards of integrity in their service.

In his speech during the oath-taking ceremony of 21 newly promoted officers, including one vice admiral, two rear admirals, and 18 commodores, Marcos commended them for protecting the country’s maritime interests in the West Philippine Sea (WPS) and responding to emergencies and disasters.
“These are difficult, sometimes dangerous tasks. For these, we are all grateful for your sacrifice,” he said.

“So, to our newly promoted flag officers, lead by example. Uphold the highest standards of integrity. Prepare the next generation of Coast Guard leaders. Embrace innovation and modernization. Strengthen the partnerships that allow us to address challenges that no institution can tackle alone,” the President added.
Marcos said the PCG’s responsibilities are among the most crucial in government, noting its role in patrolling the WPS and escorting and supporting maritime resupply missions.
“The Coast Guard has also been keeping our ports and travelers safe. They inspect vessels and look after millions of passengers moving through our ports,” he said.

“They have protected our seas by conducting environmental inspections nationwide. And when it comes to enforcing our laws, such as going after illegal fishing, smuggling, and other threats, the Philippine Coast Guard is always among the first to respond,” the President said.
He also highlighted the courage of PCG personnel, which he said is built through “training, discipline, preparation, and the readiness to act when service calls for it.”
“This heroism is shown in the willingness to put the needs of others above your own, even when duty requires great personal risks,” he said.
Marcos reminded the newly promoted officers to always remember whom they serve.
“Serve in a way that honors the oath that you took today. Lead with courage and integrity. Always remember whom you serve,” he said.
“Ang bawat paglalayag at bawat pagbabantay ay para sa sambayanang Pilipino,” the President added.
(Every voyage and every watch is for the Filipino people.) /jpv

articles.title: Sara Duterte impeachment trial: Who is lawyer Reynaldo Robles?
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Atty. Reynaldo Robles is among the private lawyers assisting the House prosecution panel in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte. Robles, who will lead the…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Atty. Reynaldo Robles is among the private lawyers assisting the House prosecution panel in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

Robles, who will lead the examination of the prosecution’s witness for the 20th day of the impeachment trial, is a veteran litigation lawyer with experience handling civil, criminal, labor, and commercial cases at all levels of the Philippine judiciary.
Robles is the founding and managing partner of the Law Firm of Chan Robles & Associates, where he served since 1993.
He earned his Bachelor of Science in Business Management, major in Economics, from the University of the Philippines in 1986, where he was President and Dean’s lister.
He later earned his Bachelor of Laws degree from Far Eastern University in 1990, graduating cum laude and as class valedictorian. He also placed 10th in the 1990 Philippine Bar Examinations.

Moreover, Robles is also president and chief executive officer of ChanRobles LawNet Inc. and Chan Robles Professional Review, Inc., and serves as trustee and legal counsel of Blas F. Ople Policy Center & Training Institute, Inc.
He has also served as legal counsel and legislative consultant to national and local government officials and legislators.

Robles has chaired technical working groups that assisted the Senate Committee on Civil Service, Government Reorganization and Professional Regulations, and the Senate Committee on National Defense and Security in drafting committee reports and versions of more than 50 bills.
Robles likewise previously served as a professor of law at the Far Eastern University Institute of Law, teaching criminal, administrative and election law, and special proceedings. /jpv

articles.title: PNP ramps up response after motorists stranded due to flooding
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines—The Philippine National Police (PNP) intensified its deployment and monitoring of roads and expressways to help stranded motorists amid flooding and traffic congestion. “Motorists…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines—The Philippine National Police (PNP) intensified its deployment and monitoring of roads and expressways to help stranded motorists amid flooding and traffic congestion.
“Motorists are usually left on their own in dealing with flooded roads. We do not want that to happen,” said PNP chief Gen. Melencio Nartatez Jr. in a statement on Tuesday

“There should be police presence in areas where they are needed, and that includes this kind of situation in cases of emergencies and other forms of assistance that the PNP is capable of,” Nartatez added.
Nartatez said police vehicles must be strategically deployed and prepositioned in flood-prone areas for quick response to emergencies.
He said the deployment is particularly important amid severe traffic congestion, such as the recent situation along the San Simon portion of the North Luzon Expressway (NLEx).
Flooding along the San Simon section of NLEx, which began Friday and worsened over the weekend, left motorists stranded for hours.
On Tuesday morning, heavy traffic was still observed at Tulaoc, San Simon Interchange along NLEx amid rising water levels in the Pampanga River.
The northbound traffic tail-end extended to Candaba and covered more than seven kilometers.
Meanwhile, the southbound queue reached about five to six kilometers.
Traffic management measures were implemented in the area, with Class 1 vehicles directed to the innermost lane.
Trucks and buses were then allowed to use the second lane.
Nartatez said flooded roads should be included in regular ground monitoring and considered in the deployment of police personnel and resources for public safety.
Police units were instructed to maintain visibility, assist stranded motorists, and facilitate the passage of emergency vehicles.
“We urge motorists to avoid unnecessary travel through the affected area,” said Nartatez.
“Those who need to travel should exercise caution, follow traffic advisories, and cooperate with police and highway authorities on the ground,” he added.
Police units were also urged to coordinate with local government units and expressway operators for a unified response. /gsg

articles.title: In disaster aftermath, Nepal battles a flood of misinformation
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — Hours after the Bhotekoshi floods swept away settlements in Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts on Wednesday morning, social media platforms were inundated with dramatic clips purporting…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — Hours after the Bhotekoshi floods swept away settlements in Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts on Wednesday morning, social media platforms were inundated with dramatic clips purporting to show the destruction.
Some depicted genuine disasters, but from other countries or earlier events. Others were digitally manipulated. Several appeared to have been created entirely by artificial intelligence.

The scale and speed of misinformation has complicated an already chaotic information environment at a time when families are desperately searching for missing relatives and authorities are struggling to establish the full extent of the disaster.
For social media users chasing views and virality, the flood has also become lucrative content.
At 7:26 am on Saturday, a Facebook page called Dudhauli FM posted a 20-second video claiming to show Home Minister Sudan Gurung inside a tunnel at the disaster site.
“Home Minister Gurung’s unique style: He reaches inside the tunnel at the incident site to join the rescue,” the caption said, praising what it described as the minister’s proactive involvement.
The page later amended the caption.
The video quickly spread across Facebook, TikTok and X.
But it was not from Nepal.

Fact-checkers established that the footage showed a tunnel rescue operation in Uttarakhand, India. The uniforms worn by the rescuers and the surroundings matched those seen in the original footage, which had been posted by the Fire Service Uttarakhand Police’s Facebook page on August 14.
The false attribution was only one example of misleading content circulating after the disaster.

As rescuers race against time to reach people trapped in tunnels and communities cut off by the devastating flash flood, a torrent of fabricated videos, recycled footage, artificial intelligence-generated imagery and cruel online commentary has bewildered a wider populace.
On August 27, at 7:54 am, an X account named Prakash Kunwar posted a 10-second video showing what appeared to be a catastrophic flood.
“No one imagined this would happen… What can anyone do when nature goes mad! May all those caught in the disaster be rescued safely,” the caption said.
The video had received more than seven million views, over 4,100 reposts and around 15,000 reactions at the time of reporting.
Yet the dramatic scene was not real.

When analysed using Hive Moderation, an AI detection tool, the video was assessed as 97.2 percent likely to have been generated by artificial intelligence. X’s community notes also flagged the clip as artificial, while BBC Verify independently debunked it.

Another viral video posted later that day showed a bridge apparently collapsing amid a raging flood. The user who shared it wrote: “If this video of the Nepal-Tibet flood is true, I have never seen anything like this in my lifetime…”
The clip, analysed through Hive Moderation, was assessed as entirely AI-generated.
International fact-checkers have also joined efforts to trace misleading visuals linked to the disaster.

Nepali fact-checking website Nepal Fact Check recently debunked a video that purported to show a glacial lake outburst flood, or GLOF, in Rasuwa. The clip showed a violent torrent of water and carried the English text: “This is a GLOF.”
The footage had no connection to Nepal.
Fact-checkers traced it to a glacial outburst flood at Columbia Glacier in Alaska, United States.

blocks.caption: Nepali and foreign factcheckers have been regularly debunking misinformation and disinformation circulating in the aftermath of the August 26 Bhotekoshi flooding. Photo: Courtesy of NepalFactcheck.org

blocks.text: Similarly, a pair of “before and after” photographs claiming to show a picturesque settlement destroyed by the Rasuwa flood went viral on social media. Both images were fabricated, according to an independent verification by the Australian Associated Press fact-checking unit.
The false videos and manipulated images are only one part of the digital disorder surrounding the disaster.
Graphic footage of bodies, injuries and devastated communities has also spread widely, often shared by personal social media accounts without warnings or consideration for victims and their families.

The Nepal Press Council, the country’s media regulatory body, says it has been monitoring online content related to the disaster. Over the past four days, it has instructed 72 social media users to remove inappropriate content, most of it posted through personal accounts.
The council has also opened a dedicated portal, titled “Special Complaints on the Bhotekoshi Incident”, through which members of the public can report misinformation and graphic material.
By 5 pm on Saturday, the portal had received 101 complaints, according to Umesh Shrestha, chairman of the Press Council.
“It was found that 67 personal accounts had posted gruesome scenes. Similarly, complaints have been lodged against some online news portals and their social media pages,” Shrestha said.
He said mainstream media organisations had largely avoided publishing misleading information and excessively graphic visuals.
“This is a positive takeaway,” he said.
For fact-checkers, the Rasuwa disaster illustrates how artificial intelligence has made an old problem more difficult to contain.
Chetana Kunwar, assistant editor at Nepal Fact Check, said misleading visuals connected to the Bhotekoshi flood were increasingly being created with AI.

“AI-generated content and manipulated ‘before and after’ visuals make it significantly easier to create false impressions, which can be extremely difficult for the general public to detect,” she said. “At the same time, videos from disasters in other countries are deliberately being circulated as if they were from Nepal.”

The spread of false information during disasters is not new. Old photographs and videos have long been recycled after earthquakes, floods and other major emergencies. But generative AI has added another layer to the problem, allowing convincing images and videos to be created from scratch within minutes.
The result is an information ecosystem in which even genuine footage can become difficult to verify.
The information vacuum
Why does misinformation spread so rapidly during disasters? Shrestha, a former editor of Nepal Fact Check, points to the intense competition for attention that follows major emergencies.

“Some people post such material for views, while others are driven by the desire to go viral,” he said. “During a crisis, public attention is heavily concentrated on one event, creating a strong emotional response. People begin liking, commenting on and sharing posts without verifying them.”
Deepak Adhikari, an investigative journalist and editor of Nepal Check, says an “information vacuum” often emerges immediately after a major disaster.
When verified information from the ground is delayed, incomplete or contradictory, social media users begin filling the gaps themselves.
“People start crowdsourcing photographs and videos and sharing them without verification, which makes the problem worse,” Adhikari told the Post.
At the same time, he said, social media influencers and content creators face constant pressure to publish material that attracts attention.
“As a result, they share visually striking graphics and videos without properly verifying where they were recorded,” he said.

The dynamic is particularly dangerous during a fast-moving disaster, when official information can take time to emerge and the public is searching urgently for news about relatives, roads, rescue operations and possible further threats.
Kunwar said people were particularly vulnerable to misinformation during such periods.
“When there is an information vacuum, people often do not stop to assess what is right or wrong. They tend to believe whatever information reaches them first,” she said.
Social media algorithms can amplify the problem, she added. Once users engage with disaster-related content, platforms often recommend more of the same, regardless of whether it is accurate.
The consequences can extend beyond confusion.

Shrestha warned that circulating old or fabricated footage as current events could create unnecessary fear and panic, not only among the public but also among rescue and relief workers operating in difficult conditions.
Adhikari said misinformation could directly interfere with emergency operations.
“Someone may already have been rescued and moved to a safe place, but people might continue sharing an old video showing that person trapped somewhere,” he said.
“The primary focus should be rescue and relief, but many people appear more concerned about promoting themselves and posting photographs and videos.”
For survivors and families of the missing, false information can repeatedly reopen trauma.
Rumours suggesting another flood is imminent, or that the disaster is about to repeat, can further frighten people who have already lost homes, relatives or livelihoods, Kunwar said.

Government agencies are now attempting to respond. The government’s Social Media Regulation and Management Committee, which has been tasked with addressing graphic content, AI-generated misinformation, fake QR codes and other forms of online deception, has begun discussions with social media platforms.
But controlling misinformation after it has gone viral remains a formidable challenge.
A crisis of empathy
The information crisis surrounding the Rasuwa flood has also revealed something more troubling: a striking absence of empathy.
A video showing a woman tearfully appealing to the government to speed up the search for her husband, who is missing inside a tunnel, has drawn a stream of cruel and abusive comments.

The woman, visibly distressed, pleads for authorities to rescue her husband. Instead of offering sympathy, some users mocked her grief. Others criticised her for speaking only about her husband or attacked her for blaming the government.
The cruelty was often casual and anonymous, delivered from behind screens to someone facing the possibility of losing a loved one.
Comments questioning why her husband had taken the job and suggesting that she was secretly happy about his disappearance turned an expression of grief into another spectacle for online consumption.

Such reactions have become an unsettling feature of Nepal’s social media culture during the disaster, where genuine suffering is sometimes treated as entertainment, political ammunition or an opportunity for engagement.
For journalists and fact-checkers, the combination of misinformation and insensitivity presents a broader challenge than simply identifying fake videos.
Disasters create an extraordinary demand for information. They also create a market for attention.

The faster the information circulates, the less time users may spend asking whether it is authentic. And when a video provokes fear, outrage or shock, the incentive to share can overwhelm the instinct to verify.
That is why responsibility cannot rest solely with authorities, technology companies or fact-checkers, Kunwar said. /dl

articles.title: It was Ortonio’s piercing, not an earpiece, in viral VP trial photos
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – Office of the Vice President (OVP) Assistant Chief of Staff Lemuel Ortonio was not wearing an earpiece when he testified during Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial,…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – Office of the Vice President (OVP) Assistant Chief of Staff Lemuel Ortonio was not wearing an earpiece when he testified during Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial, Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero said on Tuesday.
Rather, it was his ear piercing that appeared in viral photos manipulated to look like an earpiece, the presiding officer said.
After Ortonio’s testimony as a prosecution witness ended on August 26, several photos of his ear decorated with a piece of small metal were spread online. The metal was speculated to be an earpiece.

“After Mr. Ortonio testified before this court, an image of him allegedly wearing an earpiece was widely circulated on the internet… It was an AI generated image and simply false… What he had was an ear piercing at the front fold helix of his ear. Not an earpiece,” Escudero told the court.
Still, Escudero reminded that witnesses’ testimonies must be free of influence.
“Every witness must testify, nevertheless, solely from his or her own knowledge, free from coaching or influence from counsel or any other person,” he said.

Escudero cited the case of a ruling by the United States Supreme Court which barred witnesses testifying from having access to earpieces, headset, mobile phone, smart watch, smart glasses, and any other gadget where information could be transmitted.
The same ruling also prohibits any form of signalling or suggestion to the witness while inside or outside of the courts.
He also cited the ruling of a court in Texas wherein no parties are allowed to influence the witness through a script by any interested. /jpv

articles.title: Nepal floods: A pilgrimage cut short, loved ones swept away
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — When the sacred festival of Janai Purnima approached, the residents of Majhtar in ward 5 of Palungtar Municipality in Gorkha decided to embark on a holy pilgrimage to Gosainkunda in…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — When the sacred festival of Janai Purnima approached, the residents of Majhtar in ward 5 of Palungtar Municipality in Gorkha decided to embark on a holy pilgrimage to Gosainkunda in Rasuwa. Early on Wednesday morning, 36 people boarded a chartered bus, their hearts filled with devotion. Hours later, as the vehicle reached Bhainse in Nuwakot, a sudden, violent flood on the Bhotekoshi river swept the vehicle away.

Five days after the disaster, the bus with the registration number Ga 2 Kha 1152 remains missing. Authorities have recovered two bodies, six passengers survived by jumping off the moving vehicle, and 28 remain missing. Among the survivors are Badri Prasad Devkota and his cousin Tularam Devkota, who returned home to Palungtar on Friday bearing deep bodily injuries and agonising grief. Both men survived, but their wives and neighbours remain missing along with the bus.
Back in their quiet village, Badri Prasad breaks down whenever he speaks of his wife Samjhana, while Tularam is inconsolable over his missing wife Tej Kumari.

“I was sitting right behind the driver when a passenger in another seat asked him to stop so he could relieve himself,” Badri Prasad recalled. “The driver did not stop because we were travelling at speed. But as we reached the bend at Bhainse, the driver froze upon seeing the floodwaters ahead. The passenger who needed to step out immediately jumped off. Tularam moved forward to see why he had jumped.”

Badri Prasad looked out the window and saw a wall of murky water rushing towards them. “I saw a dark plume of water that looked as if it would cover the entire sky,” he said. “Thinking that I had to leap whether I lived or died, I stood up. My wife grabbed my hand and pleaded, ‘Do not jump.’ I told her, ‘We will die here,’ broke free from her grip, stepped over a bag in the aisle, and threw myself out the door.”

Moments after Badri Prasad landed, the bus engine stopped. He scrambled to run, but a violent wave crashing against the vehicle knocked him into a roadside drainage ditch. “Even as the heavy mud struck me, I did not lose consciousness. Then a second wave surged over us. I looked up and saw my brother Tularam clinging to a bush on the hillside,” he said. “I grabbed onto a shrub and looked back just in time to see the bus submerged completely. It never surfaced again.”

Perched on the steep hillside just two cubits above the roadside drain, the survivors watched helplessly as the torrent swallowed their loved ones. “Covered in thick mud, we looked like wooden logs,” said Badri Prasad. “My wife was inside that bus. My neighbours were inside. I immediately felt immense regret for leaping out. My family was gone. I screamed at the top of my lungs, but there was no one to hear us.”

Clinging to bushes, Badri Prasad and Tularam dragged themselves up the cliffside, scanning the Trishuli river in vain hopes of spotting survivors. “After climbing about 20 metres, we reached a small patch of grass and stayed there for two hours,” said Badri Prasad. “Looking down at the site where the bus vanished, we saw people stranded on rooftops crying for help, while others had only their hands protruding from the mud. When the immediate torrent subsided, a helicopter finally arrived. Realising an immediate rescue was unlikely, we climbed higher to Hilekharka village.”

In Hilekharka, compassionate locals provided them with tea and biscuits before assisting them to Suryagadhi Rural Municipality for basic first aid. Driven by desperate hope, the survivors returned to Bhainse the following day to search for their families. Finding no trace, they travelled back to Gorkha on Friday via Kulekhani in Hetauda.

Tularam’s anguish matches his cousin’s. “When we planned the pilgrimage, neighbours sent their wives, daughters, and daughters-in-law, believing they would be safe with us,” said Tularam. “I am consumed by regret that I could not bring them back.” Before returning home, Tularam visited the disaster site twice, searching in vain.

He believes early warnings could have averted the catastrophe. “If the government had issued timely alerts to downstream areas as soon as the flood began upstream, human losses would have been significantly lower,” said Tularam. “We only realised the danger when the water hit the road and touched our vehicle. Effective communication along the Trishuli corridor could have prevented this immense tragedy.”

Tularam noted that the disaster has devastated the entire village in Gorkha. “There is no one left to unlock the doors of many homes. Some children have been left behind while both their parents are missing,” he said.

Silence now hangs over Naukhor settlement in Palungtar. Search parties have scattered across riverbanks from Nuwakot to Nawalpur. Those offering condolences to grieving families invariably pass the silent home of Dil Bahadur Khatri and his wife, Murari.

At Dil Bahadur Khatri’s house, corn remains spread out in the courtyard, untouched for five days. The front porch light, switched on before the couple departed early Wednesday morning, remains lit. “There were only the two elderly occupants in this house, and both went missing during the pilgrimage,” said neighbour Ram Chandra Khatri. “The doors remain locked, and we have deliberately chosen not to break the lock. We come in the morning and evening, look at the house, and return.”

Dil Bahadur’s two daughters live abroad—the eldest in the United Kingdom and the youngest in the United States. “It was easy for the elderly couple to travel because they had no livestock to tend to,” said Ram Chandra. “We decided not to break the lock because their eldest daughter is currently preparing to fly back to Nepal from the UK.”

For the grieving families of Palungtar, the lack of timely warnings has transformed a holy pilgrimage into an enduring nightmare, leaving an entire community searching for answers along the muddy banks of the Trishuli. /dl

articles.title: Kākāpō rising: 90 chicks swell population of the world’s heaviest parrot
articles.summary:
Critically endangered New Zealand bird enjoys record breeding season triggered by mass fruiting of native tree, pushing its numbers to 325

The population of the world’s heaviest parrot,

blocks.text: The population of the world’s heaviest parrot, the kākāpō, has surpassed 300 birds for the first time in 75 years, after a record breeding season triggered by the mass fruiting of a native New Zealand tree.
Ninety chicks were officially added to the population of the critically endangered birds on 1 September, pushing the total to 325 – a record high since recovery efforts began.
“The last time the population is thought to have exceeded 300 birds may have been as long as 75 years ago,” said Deidre Vercoe, the conservation department’s kākāpō recovery operations manager.
“We had a four-year gap between breeding seasons, so it’s fantastic to finally see the population increase after all that time.”

blocks.caption: Kākāpō population tops 300 for first time in 75 years, after record breeding season Photograph: Department of Conservation

blocks.text: Kākāpō, the world’s only nocturnal and flightless parrot, were once abundant across New Zealand. But their population plummeted after the introduction of predators such as cats and stoats. By the 1900s, they were nearly extinct.

A recovery programme was established in 1995 with a population of just 51 birds and has battled challenges with genetic diversity, infertility and poor chick hatching rates. There are three kākāpō breeding populations, all based on predator-free islands off the South Island.

Kākāpō breed only every two to four years when the native rimu trees produce large numbers of berries, so repopulation is slow. This year, after a four-year wait, a bountiful harvest of rimu berries prompted the birds to breed and produce a record number of chicks.
“In the early years of recovery, it took 16 years to produce that many chicks,” Vercoe said.

Kākāpō are thought to live between 60 and 80 years, can weigh up to 4kg and are famously entertaining. More than 100,000 people tuned in to watch a live stream of a kākāpō sleeping, eating and attending to her nest and chicks during breeding season.

The parrots have unusual mating rituals. Male birds gather in a “lek” to produce a distinctive booming sound, emitted from air sacs in their chests while sitting in a dugout bowl in the ground. The deep boom, which can travel up to 5km, sounds similar to a softly plucked cello string.
After choosing a partner and mating, females typically lay one to four eggs. The females become solely responsible for their eggs and hatched chicks for roughly six months.

At 150 days of age, the chicks are fledged and considered independent enough to be added to the total population. The youngest chick of the 2026 breeding season was female Awarua-A3, who hatched on 30 March.
Modelling indicated the next breeding season could occur as soon as 2028, Vercoe said.
“So, while we’ll take a moment to stop and reflect on this remarkable year, we’re already looking ahead to 2028 and preparing for what could come next.”

articles.title: Senate impeachment court calls out fake, 'AI' photos of witness Ortonio wearing earpiece
articles.summary: The Senate impeachment court said Tuesday the pictures circulating on social media supposedly showing hostile witness Lemuel Ortonio wearing an earpiece was generated with artificial intelligence…

blocks.text: Published September 1, 2026 10:55am

The Senate impeachment court said Tuesday the pictures circulating on social media supposedly showing hostile witness Lemuel Ortonio wearing an earpiece was generated with artificial intelligence (AI).

"Hindi totoo 'yung lumalabas na mga letrato na hindi umano mayroong earpiece si Mr. Ortonio. 'Yun po ay AI," the tribunal's presiding officer Francis "Chiz" Escudero said at the beginning of Day 20 of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.
(The photos circulating that supposedly show Mr. Ortonio without an earpiece are fake. They were AI-generated.)
"What he had was… an ear piercing in the front fold helix of his ear. Not an earpiece," he added.
Ortonio, Office of the Vice President (OVP) Assistant Secretary and Assistant Chief of Staff, took the stand last week as a hostile witness on Duterte's alleged misuse of confidential funds.
Escudero, meanwhile, reminded the parties that every witness "must testify solely from his or her own knowledge, free from coaching or influence from counsel or any other person."

"No witness, while testifying, shall possess, have access to or use any earpiece, headset, cellphone, smartwatch, smart glasses, or any other similar device capable of transmitting or receiving information or communication," he said.

"Witnesses are also prohibited from receiving or attempting to receive any communication, suggestion, answer, signal, message or prompt for any person whether inside or outside of this court," he added.
The presiding officer said the use of any necessary medical accessibility or device shall be subject to the court's approval.

Escudero directed the clerk to inform witnesses of the rules prior to testifying, secure all prohibited communication devices in the witness' possession before he or she is sworn in, and obtain the witness' confirmation on the record that he or she understands and shall comply with the directive.
He said any violation will be dealt with accordingly under the court's disciplinary powers. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Archaeological dig challenges story of 1903 battle in Lanao del Sur
articles.summary: The findings prompt a reevaluation of the accepted narrative surrounding the Battle of Kota Kalawi, raising questions about the historical accuracy of the events attributed to the US military…

blocks.text: University of the Philippines-School of Archaeology's Leee Anthony Neri presents the archological report on Kota Kalawi in Lanao del Sur.
Mike Banos/Rappler

The findings prompt a reevaluation of the accepted narrative surrounding the Battle of Kota Kalawi, raising questions about the historical accuracy of the events attributed to the US military campaign in Mindanao

items: An archaeological excavation in Lanao del Sur challenges the historical account of the Battle of Kota Kalawi, suggesting it may be a 'historical hoax' fabricated by American forces.
The excavation, led by Leee Anthony Neri from the University of the Philippines, found minimal evidence, including only one bullet, contradicting the intense battle described in American accounts.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

CAGAYAN DE ORO, Philippines – For decades, the Battle of Kota Kalawi has stood in the historical record as a bloody encounter between American forces and Meranaw defenders along the shores of Lake Lanao. Now, an archaeological excavation is challenging that account, raising questions about one of the most consequential episodes attributed to the US military campaign in Mindanao.

At the presentation and turnover of the Kota Kalawi Archaeological and Historical Project on August 24 at the Lanao del Sur Provincial Capitol, project team leader Leee Anthony Neri, dean of the University of the Philippines’ School of Archaeology (UPSA), delivered this assessment: the battle was a “historical hoax” written by Americans in the 20th century.

Neri said the archaeological dig, commissioned by the Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage (BCPCH) and conducted by a team from UPSA from July 29 to August 19, 2024, showed no evidence that the purported Battle of Kalawi ever took place.

This was the first formal archaeological excavation in Lanao del Sur. The project was a collaboration among the UP School of Archaeology (UPSA), Mindanao State University-main campus and Mindanao State University-Iligan Institute of Technology (MSU-IIT), organized by the BCPCH.

blocks.caption: ILLUSTRATE. A reconstruction of Kota Kalawi in Lanao del Sur. courtesy of Leee Anthony Neri

blocks.text: “Of the six trenches we dug on the Kota Kalawi site, we found only a single bullet and no evidence of bullet penetration on the North Wall from the purported machine gun fire or mortar fire,” Neri noted. “There’s also simply no space within the kota (earthen/stone forts) to accommodate a hundred defenders.”
“Archeologically, this does not support the historical narrative,” Neri stressed.
Iligan historian Ricardo Jorge Caluen said the excavation was the first formal archaeological re-examination of the accepted narrative surrounding the Battle of Kota Kalawi.

“Neri’s assertion is therefore a bold challenge to the traditionally-accepted events of the battle that could alter its historiography,” Caluen said. “It is difficult to challenge findings of archaeology that are based solely on material evidence.”

The American account dated June 30, 1903 was written by American Brigadier General Samuel S. Sumner, commander of the Department of Mindanao, and included as Appendix II in the Annual Report of Major General George W. Davis, United States Army commanding Division of the Philippines from October 1, 1902 to July 26, 1903.

According to Sumner’s report, the Battle of Kota Kalawi – often referenced alongside the Battle of Bacolod Grande – was a violent clash that took place at Bacolod Grande from April 6 to 8, 1903, and at Kalawi on April 9, along the shores of Lake Lanao. Kalawi is also spelled Calahui in the American account.

At the time of the battle, then-captain John J. Pershing, who later commanded the American Expeditionary Forces (AEF) on the Western Front during World War I, was newly promoted as commander of Camp Vicars, overseeing the early American pacification campaigns in the Meranaw and Iranun areas surrounding Lake Lanao.

The defensive fortifications, or kota, served as vital strongholds during local resistance against foreign invaders around Lake Lanao. Built strategically on plateaus and along the shores of the lake to control movement and trade, they were constructed with heavy timber, stone, earth and bamboo, and often bristled with sharp bamboo spike pits (surung) and high walls. Defenders used indigenous blades such as the kris and kampilan, along with swivel cannons called lantakas.

Sumner described Kota o Panondiongan as “the strongest fort in Mindanao.” Based on his account, the Americans’ superior firepower, including machine guns, mountain artillery and mortars, gave US forces a decisive advantage over traditional Meranaw defenses.

The American field expedition was led on the ground by Pershing, commanding roughly 700 soldiers composed of four companies from the 27th Infantry, three troops of the 15th Cavalry, and two mountain artillery batteries.

Sumner recounted that American forces surrounded the earthen walls of Kota o Panondiongan, with initial bombardments from Vickers-Maxim mountain guns countered by traditional Meranaw lantakas (brass cannons). He wrote that the US tightened the siege using 3.6-inch mortars, dropping shells directly into the fort. Despite a water-filled moat and heavy fire from hidden loopholes, Meranaw defenders repeatedly drove back infantry advances and rejected all offers of surrender.

Relentless artillery fire, based on the account, breached the front wall, allowing US forces to overrun Kota o Panondiongan. Supposedly, a quick body count taken in the still-burning fort showed 30 Moro warriors dead on the top floor, with one American killed and 14 wounded.

The following day, April 9, 1903, the Americans supposedly bombarded Kota Kalawi with mortars and Maxim-Vickers machine guns. Sumner claimed the Meranaw defenders abandoned their positions after suffering 23 casualties.

blocks.caption: TEAM. Members of the Kota Kalawi archeological project team in Lanao del Sur. courtesy of Leee Anthony Neri

blocks.text: For over a century, the American account has shaped the history of Kota Kalawi. But the archaeological findings merely showed a single bullet, and no physical evidence of the intense exchange of gunfire and artillery described in Sumner’s report.

The findings have raised questions about what really happened at Kota Kalawi in 1903 and prompted a closer examination of the account that for generations was seen as established history. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Death toll from Luis, Maymay, Neneng, Habagat rises to 34 --OCD
articles.summary: Death toll from Luis, Maymay, Neneng, Habagat rises to 34 --OCD

blocks.text: Published September 1, 2026 10:41am
Death toll from the combined effects of Tropical Cyclones Luis, Maymay, and Neneng, as well as the Southwest Monsoon or Habagat has risen to 34, the Office of Civil Defense (OCD) said Tuesday.
In an update as of 6 a.m., the OCD said the fatalities were recorded across several areas, with Benguet accounting for the highest number at 15.
Of the 15 deaths in Benguet, 10 were recorded in Baguio City, three in Atok, and two in La Trinidad. All were due to landslides. Rizal and Batangas, meanwhile, had four deaths each.
In Rizal, two people died due to a rockslide in Rodriguez, while one each died due to a fallen tree in Antipolo and drowning in Binangonan.
In Batangas, one person each died due to drowning in Batangas City and Mabini, electrocution in Lipa, and a landslide in Santa Teresita.
Caloocan also recorded three deaths, all due to drowning.
Quezon recorded two deaths, both due to drowning in Candelaria and Sariaya, while Occidental Mindoro also recorded two deaths in Rizal town due to electrocution and drowning.
La Union, Pangasinan, Oriental Mindoro, and Negros Occidental each recorded one fatality.
Injured/ missing
The OCD said 19 people were injured and three others were missing due to the bad weather.

A total of 9.1 million individuals or 2.6 million families were affected by the weather disturbances in Ilocos Region, Cagayan Valley, Central Luzon, Bicol, Western Visayas, Zamboanga Peninsula, Calabarzon, Cordillera Administrative Region, Metro Manila and Mimaropa.
Of the affected population, 135,905 people or 39,386 families were staying in 1,255 evacuation centers.
Around 3,700 houses were damaged — 3,300 partially and 458 totally.
Infrastructure damage was estimated at ₱6.27 billion, while agricultural damage reached ₱2.32 billion.
A total of 678 areas were flooded.
The government has so far provided ₱1.79 billion worth of assistance to affected communities. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: UP study: Resort visitors willing to pay P75 to conserve Mt. Makiling
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Visitors to resorts in Calamba City and Los Baños, Laguna, said they were willing to pay about P75 per visit for improved conservation of Mt. Makiling’s groundwater, a…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Visitors to resorts in Calamba City and Los Baños, Laguna, said they were willing to pay about P75 per visit for improved conservation of Mt. Makiling’s groundwater, a University of the Philippines Los Baños (UPLB) study found.

If captured through a proposed water user fee, the amount could generate an estimated P159.52 million a year for groundwater conservation, resort water conservation measures and the management of Mt. Makiling, according to the study.

The estimate was based on an online survey of 492 resort visitors, who were asked how much they would be willing to pay under a hypothetical program that required resorts to recycle and treat pool water and support groundwater conservation. The researchers used a contingent valuation method and interval regression to estimate the visitors’ willingness to pay.

The study, “Potential Contribution of Tourism for Groundwater Conservation in Mt. Makiling, the Philippines,” was written by Margaret M. Calderon, Analyn L. Codilan, Jan Joseph V. Dida, Vanessa M. Palma-Torres, Angela Marie S. Alducente and Canesio D. Predo of the UPLB Institute of Renewable Natural Resources, College of Forestry and Natural Resources. It was published in the Philippine Journal of Science, Volume 154, No. 2, in April 2025.
The researchers stressed that P75 is an estimated willingness to pay under a hypothetical scenario, not an existing fee or money currently being collected from resort visitors.
Resort boom puts pressure on groundwater

Mt. Makiling is a dormant volcano and a vital watershed that supplies water for domestic, agricultural and industrial uses. Its hot springs and groundwater have also supported the growth of the resort industry in Calamba and Los Baños.

The study cited an earlier inventory that counted 1,043 resorts in the two areas as of 2020 — 871 in Calamba and 172 in Los Baños. The number of resorts in Calamba alone increased from 193 in 1998 to 466 in 2014, according to earlier research cited in the paper.

blocks.caption: mt. makiling

blocks.text: Graphics by Ed Lustan/Inquirer.net
“The growing number of resorts has naturally led to a surge in tourism,” the researchers wrote.

The expansion of the resort industry has also meant greater use of groundwater. The researchers said many resorts had shifted from naturally flowing hot springs to pumping groundwater for their pools and other uses.
They noted that resorts predominantly use pumped groundwater because it is cheaper than metered water from local water districts, which charge based on the volume consumed.

The paper also cited an earlier survey that found resort pools had an average size of 80 cubic meters, with water temperatures ranging from above 30 C to 50 C. The researchers said drained pool water eventually reaches Laguna de Bay and pointed to the need to regulate and monitor its disposal.
Many visitors did not know where the water came from
Despite using resort pools supplied by groundwater or hot springs, many respondents were unsure about the source of the water.

Of the 492 respondents, 52.6% said they knew the source of the resort’s water. Among those who identified a source, 26.2% said hot springs, 14.8% identified Mt. Makiling and only 7.3% identified groundwater.
The researchers also found that 40.7% correctly identified pumping as the way pools were filled, while 34.1% believed the water flowed naturally.
“A notable finding was that while 40.7% of respondents correctly identified pumping as the method for filling the pools, 34.1% mistakenly believed the water flowed naturally,” they wrote.
The paper said this was significant because resorts in the area have increasingly relied on pumped groundwater rather than naturally flowing hot springs.

blocks.caption: mt. makiling

blocks.text: Awareness was stronger when it came to the role of forests in maintaining groundwater. Some 98.4% of respondents agreed that good forest cover was important to securing groundwater supply, while 66.7% knew that groundwater was not unlimited.
Still, 33% believed groundwater was unlimited regardless of how much water was used, the researchers found.
The researchers described this as “disturbing,” noting that the findings “may imply a need to improve citizens’ understanding of water scarcity.”
Relaxation draws visitors to resorts

For most respondents, resort visits were primarily for recreation. The most common reason was relaxation or enjoyment, followed by the accessibility of resorts for family and friends and their affordability.

“The main reasons of the respondents for visiting the resorts in Los Baños or Calamba are for relaxation (53%), to be with family and friends (39.6%), and because of the resorts’ accessibility (40%) and affordability (37.2%),” the researchers said.

“About a fourth of the respondents went because they heard positive reviews either of a specific resort (28.3%) or the resorts in Los Baños and Calamba in general (27.4%) and for therapeutic or health reasons because of the perceived therapeutic properties of the hot water common in the pools (25%),” they added.

blocks.caption: mt. makiling

blocks.text: PROTECTING MT. MAKILING’S GROUNDWATER Mt. Makiling’s forests and groundwater help sustain the resort industry in Calamba and Los Baños, Laguna. A University of the Philippines Los Baños study found that resort visitors were willing to pay an estimated P75 per visit for improved groundwater conservation, potentially generating P159.52 million a year if captured through a proposed water user fee. —PHOTO COURTESY OF MAKILING CENTER FOR MOUNTAIN ECOSYSTEMS

The study also found that 81.7% of respondents were repeat visitors, having visited resorts in the area at least twice. Social media and recommendations from family and friends were among the main ways they learned about resorts.

The researchers said the findings showed that the resort industry was not simply providing recreational services but was also drawing visitors who depended on the natural water resources associated with Mt. Makiling.
Willingness to pay P75 fee

The researchers used contingent valuation, a survey method that estimates how much people are willing to pay for an environmental resource or improvement that does not have a conventional market price.

In the hypothetical scenario presented to respondents, local governments would require resorts to reuse and treat pool water rather than routinely replace it. An additional water user fee would be added to existing resort entrance fees.
Under the proposed arrangement, half of the fee would be used to maintain pool water quality, while the other half would go toward the conservation of Mt. Makiling.
Respondents were presented with payment amounts ranging from zero to more than P200 per visit.

blocks.caption: mt. makiling

blocks.text: Of the 492 respondents, 488 selected an amount greater than zero. The most common choices were P50, selected by 25%, and P100, selected by 25.81%. Another 11.2% chose P20, while 8.1% selected P200.
Only four respondents, or 0.81%, indicated zero willingness to pay.
“The mean [willingness to pay] estimated using the payment card format was P75 [per] visit,” the researchers wrote.

The P75 figure was calculated using interval regression based on the payment amounts selected by respondents. The researchers cautioned that the result represents stated preference rather than actual behavior or a guaranteed amount of revenue.

“Stated preference techniques may be used when it is not possible to infer or observe people’s [willingness to pay] from markets or when markets are absent, as in the case of the groundwater resource of Mt. Makiling,” the study noted.
Conservation was the main reason to pay
The researchers found that the strongest motivation for willingness to pay was concern about Mt. Makiling’s groundwater.
Among respondents who were willing to pay, 82.2% said they wanted to contribute to groundwater conservation on Mt. Makiling, while 52.3% cited the belief that groundwater is a finite resource.
The researchers said only 28.2% cited the perception that current resort water use was wasteful as a reason for their willingness to pay.

“Most respondents were willing to pay, primarily because they wanted to support the conservation of Mt. Makiling’s groundwater resources and recognized its limited availability,” the researchers wrote.
The survey also found broad support for the conservation measures presented in the hypothetical scenario.

blocks.caption: mt. makiling

blocks.text: About 84% agreed or completely agreed that conserving Mt. Makiling would enhance groundwater supply, while 78% agreed or completely agreed that recycling pool water would help conserve groundwater.
About 75% agreed or completely agreed that the proposed groundwater conservation program was plausible.
“For all three questions, there were more respondents who completely agreed than only agreed,” the researchers observed.

The four respondents who indicated zero willingness to pay gave different reasons. Two did not believe groundwater was limited, one cited affordability, and another said visitors “should not be responsible for paying for pool water recycling.”
The researchers said these responses showed that willingness to pay was influenced not only by environmental concerns but also by how visitors viewed the proposed fee and its affordability.
Potential P159.5 million a year
To estimate how much could potentially be raised, the researchers multiplied the P75 mean willingness to pay by average annual resort visitor numbers in the two cities.

For Calamba, they used an average of 2,015,124 resort visitors a year, based on visitor figures from 2013, 2014 and 2018. For Los Baños, they used an average of 111,821 visitors annually, based on available figures from 2013, 2015, 2016, 2017, 2018 and 2019.
This produced an estimated P151.13 million in annual potential revenue for Calamba and P8.39 million for Los Baños, or P159.52 million combined.

blocks.caption: mt. makiling

blocks.text: The researchers estimated that, assuming the annual benefits remained constant, the amount would have a present value of P1.358 billion over 20 years at a 10% discount rate.
“This present value can be used to decide policy options that will contribute to the conservation of Mt. Makiling’s groundwater resource,” the researchers said.

Under the hypothetical fee arrangement used in the survey, half of the estimated annual revenue — or P79.76 million — could be allocated to improved management of Mt. Makiling, while the same amount could support water conservation practices among resorts.

“These funds could support the enhanced management of Mt. Makiling and help resorts implement water conservation measures while maintaining pool water quality at international standards, reducing unnecessary and excessive water disposal,” the researchers stressed.
Visitors favored frequent water replacement
The survey also asked respondents how often they believed resort pools should be emptied and refilled.

Among visitors to public resorts, 45.5% believed pool water was changed daily, while 38.4% thought it was changed weekly. Among private-resort visitors, 42.5% believed water was changed daily and 19.3% thought it was changed every 12 hours.

When asked how frequently water should ideally be replaced, 27% of public-resort visitors preferred replacement before every group’s use, while 39% preferred daily replacement. Among private-resort visitors, 46.5% preferred changing water before each group and 23% preferred daily replacement.

blocks.caption: mt. makiling

blocks.text: The study also found a gap in visitors’ knowledge about pool water treatment.
Only 23.4% knew that properly maintained and monitored pool water could remain in use for years without annual replacement, while 76.6% did not know this.
At the same time, 67.9% said they would be less satisfied if they learned that pool water had not been changed for two years, even if it had been properly treated and maintained.
“This points to the need for information dissemination about safe pool water standards,” the study noted.
Age, water-saving habits also mattered
The study also examined factors associated with respondents’ willingness to pay.
Its model found that age and water-conserving behavior were significant predictors. The researchers estimated that willingness to pay decreased by P0.802 for every additional year of age.

blocks.caption: mt. makiling

blocks.text: Meanwhile, respondents who consistently practiced water conservation also had an estimated P27.23 lower willingness to pay than those who did not consistently practice water conservation.

“Interestingly, respondents who do not consistently practice water conservation demonstrated a higher WTP. Conversely, those who already engage in water-conserving behaviors showed a lower WTP, possibly reflecting costs they have already absorbed for their current practices,” the researchers stated.
Researchers urge policy, public education

The researchers recommended that local governments consider policies that would capture visitors’ stated willingness to pay and use the resulting funds for Mt. Makiling management and resort water conservation measures.

The researchers also called for stronger information and education efforts among resort owners, visitors, the public, and local and national government officials to raise awareness of growing groundwater scarcity in Mt. Makiling and other parts of the country.
“Additionally, resort owners should be informed about the importance of proper pool maintenance to minimize frequent and unnecessary water replacement,” the study noted.
“In contrast, resort visitors should be educated on how pool water can meet international quality standards without excessive water use,” it added.

articles.title: Sandiganbayan defers Tarlac solon’s arraignment until Oct. 7
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Sandiganbayan Fifth Division on Tuesday moved the arraignment of Tarlac Rep. Noel Rivera to October 7 in light of his motion to consolidate the cases against him. Rivera,…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Sandiganbayan Fifth Division on Tuesday moved the arraignment of Tarlac Rep. Noel Rivera to October 7 in light of his motion to consolidate the cases against him.

Rivera, who represents the third district of Tarlac province, faces nine counts of violating Republic Act No. 3019 or the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act before the Sandiganbayan, two of which were raffled to the court’s Fifth Division.

At the hearing on Tuesday, Sandiganbayan Fifth Division Chairperson Associate Justice Zaldy Trespeses noted the motions for consolidation and to quash the information filed by Rivera through his legal counsel on August 11 and 24, respectively.
“The arraignment is deferred, considering [the] pendency of the motion for consolidation and the motion to quash filed by the accused in both cases,” Trespeses said.
He also acknowledged the omnibus consolidated comment-opposition filed by state prosecutors on August 28 in response to Rivera’s motions.
“The same are now submitted for resolution,” Trespeses noted.

The charges against Rivera stem from his and his wife’s alleged shareholdings in Tarlac 3-G Construction and Development Corporation, which obtained nine government infrastructure contracts during his term in office from 2022 to 2025.

State prosecutors indicted Rivera for violating Section 3(h) of RA No. 3019, which prohibits “directly or indirectly having financing or pecuniary interest in any business, contract or transaction in connection with which he intervenes or takes part in his official capacity, or in which he is prohibited by the Constitution or by any law from having any interest.”
Last Thursday, the Sandiganbayan Sixth Division, which also handles two of Rivera’s cases, denied his move to consolidate the nine counts of graft to a single court division.
The Sixth Division agreed with the prosecution’s argument that consolidating the cases “will only result in the muddling of facts and issues, which may cause confusion and delay.” /jpv

articles.title: Indonesia fire-linked haze affects Metro Manila air quality
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Some cities in Metro Manila reached “very unhealthy” to “acutely unhealthy” levels of air quality on Tuesday morning due to haze possibly linked to ongoing fires in Kalimantan,…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Some cities in Metro Manila reached “very unhealthy” to “acutely unhealthy” levels of air quality on Tuesday morning due to haze possibly linked to ongoing fires in Kalimantan, Indonesia, according to the Department of Environment and Natural Resources – Environmental Management Bureau (DENR-EMB).

In its data as of 6 a.m., the DENR-EMB in the National Capital Region (NCR) said several areas recorded high PM2.5 levels. PM2.5 refers to fine particulate matter measuring 2.5 micrometers or less in diameter.

The DENR-EMB in the NCR said that the following areas logged acutely unhealthy air quality index (AQI). Under this level, the bureau said that the AQI ranges from 201 to 300 where everyone may be noticeably affected and outdoor activities must be restricted:
