articles.title: Head of Viktor Orbán’s favourite thinktank quits over unpaid wages
articles.summary:
Frank Furedi announces resignation from MCC Brussels after organisation’s staff ‘not paid in July or August’

The head of Viktor Orbán’s favourite Brussels thinktank has quit, citing unpaid…

blocks.text: The head of Viktor Orbán’s favourite Brussels thinktank has quit, citing unpaid wages since the change of government in Hungary.

The sociology professor Frank Furedi said he was resigning as the executive director of MCC Brussels with “immediate effect” on Monday over “persistent failure to provide the contractually agreed funds”.
A spokesperson for MCC Brussels confirmed Furedi’s resignation and said no one working for the organisation in the EU capital had been paid in July or August.

MCC Brussels launched in late 2022 with a self-styled mission to shake up political debate in the EU capital, although critics said it defended Orbán’s illiberal rule in Hungary while using a well-funded position to attack civil society groups.

It was an ostensibly independent offshoot of the Mathias Corvinus Collegium Foundation in Budapest, a training ground for Orbán’s Fidesz party that was lavishly funded by his rightwing nationalist government.

The future of MCC Brussels was thrown into doubt when Péter Magyar won a landslide election victory in April pledging to crack down on corruption in Hungary, which numerous independent organisations said had proliferated during Orbán’s 16 years in power. Soon after his victory, Magyar promised to end state financing for MCC Budapest and to investigate a large transfer of state assets to the organisation, which he described as a crime.
Furedi has previously dismissed Magyar’s claims of a criminal transfer of assets to MCC Budapest as “bullshit”, while MCC Brussels said it condemned corruption by all politicians.
after newsletter promotion

In a letter to the senior leadership of MCC Budapest seen by the Guardian, Furedi wrote: “Without the contractually agreed resources, our colleagues cannot function and are facing serious economic hardship. We have been placed in a situation where our individual reputations and the integrity of our intellectual mission are systematically undermined.”
The failure to provide funds, Furedi said, meant MCC Brussels had effectively ceased operations and was unable to pay suppliers or meet conditions under Belgian insolvency law.

Furedi said he intended to ensure, “along with like-minded individuals, the work and intellectual legacy of our institution will continue to flourish in another form”, without elaborating on future plans.
The letter was first reported by Politico. MCC Budapest did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

MCC Budapest has also seen change at the top following the election of the new government. The MCC board was previously led by Viktor Orbán’s chief of staff, Balázs Orbán, who is no relation to the former prime minister. Balázs Orbán, now an MP for the Fidesz party, announced he was standing down as chair in June.

The MCC Brussels spokesperson said after Furedi’s resignation and a round of lay-offs in June and July, MCC Brussels was down to 12 staff and three research fellows. Before the cuts it had employed 25 people and was one of the best-funded thinktanks in Brussels.

articles.title: US singer D4vd's celebrity lawyers withdraw from murder case
articles.summary: The singer, 21, will be now represented by a public defender in the murder trial of 14-year-old Celeste Rivas Hernandez. He has pleaded not guilty.

blocks.text: The celebrity lawyers hired to represent US musician D4vd in his upcoming murder trial have withdrawn from his case.

The star, whose legal name is David Anthony Burke, has been appointed a public defender to mount his defence for the murder of Celeste Rivas Hernandez, 14, whose remains were found in September 2025 in a Tesla registered to his address.
Burke, 21, pleaded not guilty to the murder charges in Los Angeles court on Monday.
A judge determined last month that he will stand trial for murder. Prosecutors have alleged he stabbed the teen after years of sexual abuse, before dismembering her body.
A pretrial hearing is set for 19 October.

Lawyers Blair Berk, Marilyn Bednarski and Regina Peter said in a statement to BBC that the court granted their request to withdraw from the case and has appointed the Los Angeles County Public Defender's to represent the singer.
The statement said that it D4vd "qualified for appointed counsel".

"We continue to support David and his defense against these serious charges," they said. "We are grateful that the Los Angeles County Public Defender's Office has taken over the representation and that David has a highly capable and committed team of attorneys and investigators behind him."
Berk, who led the defence team, has previously represented US actor Mel Gibson and film mogul Harvey Weinstein, as well as singer Britney Spears and actress Lindsay Lohan.
In a statement, deputy public defender Walid Kandeel said Burke "is entitled to a defense that takes his circumstances seriously and carefully examines the evidence".
"We are committed to providing him with that defense," he said.

articles.title: The Canadian suspected of spying on NATO was denied bail. Here’s what comes next
articles.byline: Aloysius Wong, Albert Leung, Idil Mussa

image.caption: 33-year-old computer scientist Biwei Zhang lost an appeal for release from pretrial detention in Belgium amid allegations of spying on NATO's military headquarters, where she was working as an intern. (Reuters, Catina Zhang/Facebook)

blocks.text: The Canadian suspected of spying on the NATO military headquarters in Belgium is expected to remain in detention until her trial, which could be a year or more away.
Biwei Zhang, 33, will remain in custody after a Belgian judge on Monday denied the former NATO intern’s appeal for release.
"Today, the Chamber of Indictments decided to extend the suspect’s pretrial detention by one month," the federal prosecutor’s office said in a statement.
Zhang must appear before a judge at regular intervals — once a month for the first three months and every two months thereafter — to determine whether pretrial detention remains appropriate.
Because of the seriousness of the allegations and the risk that the suspect may abscond, it is "rather unlikely" that Zhang will be released before the trial, one Belgian legal expert told CBC News.

"If they have a serious case with lots of indications that she might have committed an offence, then it will be hard to be released before the trial," said Frank Verbruggen, a criminal law professor at KU Leuven, a Catholic research university in Leuven, Belgium.
The trial likely won’t begin until sometime next year "at the earliest," he said.
Unlike in Canada, Belgian courts do not name criminal defendants until trial.

However, CBC News was first to identify the suspect as Biwei Zhang — also known by the names Claire and Catina — an intern at NATO's Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe (SHAPE) with a background in computer science and economics.

The Canadian woman was arrested on July 24, a day after her home and workplace were searched, and was subsequently charged by Belgian authorities with "spying on behalf of a third country and of being a member of a criminal organization."
CBC News identifies Canadian intern accused of spying on NATO
Sources have told Reuters and other media that the suspected third country is China.
The Chinese embassy in Canada told CBC it firmly opposes the "baseless speculations and smears against China."
The allegations have not been tested in court.
Neither Zhang nor her lawyer responded to CBC News requests for comment.
Espionage 'test case'

Verbruggen says the criminal organization charge is one Belgian prosecutors charge "very often," as it is defined broadly as an association of more than two people working together to commit certain offences.
"That has the advantage that the number of investigative methods, for instance, like infiltration or covert observation and so on, are quite easy to justify," he said.

But Verbruggen says the spying charges against Zhang will likely be a "test case" for Belgian courts, as definitions of espionage were updated in 2024 to account for modern techniques of intelligence gathering.
Why prosecuting spy cases makes it harder to keep information secret
He says espionage cases are "very rare," as criminal prosecution of spies is often considered a last resort, with authorities more likely to remove or monitor them instead.
"There is a kind of understanding that it's better to know who's spying on you and tolerate them and keep an eye on them than to expel them and then get new ones."
The case has also raised questions about the efficacy of Canada’s security screening, which was responsible for clearing Zhang for her NATO position.
Prime Minister Mark Carney said earlier this month that although he is limited in what he can disclose amid the active investigation, "Canadian officials have been involved from the start."
Canada involved 'from the start' in investigation of NATO intern accused of spying: Carney

The House of Commons standing committee on public safety and national security is set to convene to review Canada’s screening processes after opposition parties called for an emergency meeting following the spying allegations.

Former CSIS intelligence officer Dan Stanton, who has no direct knowledge of the case, speculates it’s possible Zhang was identified "quite some time ago" and that "there could be a very complicated counterintelligence operation in the background."

items: Ottawa will look into screening processes amid NATO intern spying allegations
Conservatives, Bloc want probe into Canadian NATO intern spying allegations

blocks.text: Suspect may have 'crossed the line' later
Prior to moving to Europe, Zhang worked as a public servant at multiple federal government agencies in Canada.

This included data scientist jobs at both Employment and Social Development Canada and Statistics Canada, and later work as a systems engineer for the Canadian Space Agency, according to her LinkedIn profile as well as her CV, which was included in a federal court case.

None of the three agencies would confirm details about the suspect but told CBC they will continue to collaborate with domestic and international partners "to protect national security and preserve the integrity of the investigative process."

Stanton, now the director of the national security program at the University of Ottawa's Professional Development Institute, said if Zhang was indeed spying for a foreign power, another possibility is that she was recruited more recently.
"They may have, on paper in terms of initial vetting, been fine, but at some point maybe they were cultivated and recruited by a hostile intelligence service."

The federal court documents also included a report from the Public Service Commission of Canada, which concluded that Zhang had committed fraud by applying for the same government job under two names and emails.

items: CBC identifies Canadian woman accused of spying at NATO military HQ
Canadian intern at NATO military headquarters in Belgium faces spying charges

blocks.text: In an apology letter to an investigator included in court filings, Zhang described herself as a young professional "passionate about using the power of data to drive public policy with an ambitious, innovative mind."
Stanton says it's "quite possible" this is a case where a Canadian decided to spy after having a negative experience working for the government.
"There may be some revenge-seeking here with this individual, and then they crossed the line and became an insider threat," he said.
NATO spy suspect possibly recruited after she was vetted, says ex-CSIS officer
Zhang had been working in SHAPE’s IT department, according to Reuters.

European media have reported that Zhang allegedly exhibited suspicious behaviour that triggered the investigation, such as asking questions about SHAPE’s security and entering off-limits areas. After her apartment was searched, Zhang’s home was reportedly broken into by suspected accomplices.

It is unclear whether Zhang will be prosecuted under Belgium’s old criminal code or its new one, which goes into force in September. Each code contains several spying offences with different maximum penalties.

Depending on whether there are any alleged aggravating factors, Verbruggen expects Zhang could face up to a decade in prison if convicted of espionage or three years' imprisonment for working with a criminal organization.
Given the sensitivity of what the suspect might have accessed, Verbruggen says prosecutors may want to avoid a public trial or pivot to other offences like hacking to keep more information secret.
"Many people are involved in a criminal trial. The fear of leaks or the risk that information is leaked is always there."

articles.title: Lingayen placed under state of calamity
articles.summary: The capital of Pangasinan was placed under a state of calamity yesterday as the enhanced southwest monsoon and tropical cyclones Luis, Maymay and Neneng caused widespread flooding and damage to the…

blocks.text: September 1, 2026 | 12:00am
Emergency responders use a rubber boat to evacuate residents of Barangay Basing in Lingayen, Pangasinan as monsoon rains inundate low-lying and near-river communities on August 29, 2026.
Cesar Ramirez

MANILA, Philippines — The capital of Pangasinan was placed under a state of calamity yesterday as the enhanced southwest monsoon and tropical cyclones Luis, Maymay and Neneng caused widespread flooding and damage to the province.
Headed by Vice Gov. Mark Ronald Lambino, the Sangguniang Panlalawigan (SP) approved Provincial Resolution 985-2026 during a special online session declaring Lingayen under a state of calamity.

The resolution said the weather disturbances “brought torrential rains and widespread flooding in low-lying areas of Pangasinan, resulting in severe flooding and widespread impacts on communities, infrastructure, agriculture, private properties and livelihoods.”
More than 1.2 million people have been affected, according to reports from the Department of Social Welfare and Development.
Eight local government units have also declared their own states of calamity, with the number of affected families and damage expected to rise as assessment and response operations continue.
As of Aug. 30, the monsoon and the three cyclones had caused P232.5 million in infrastructure damage, more than P649 million in agricultural damage and more than P2.1 million in livestock damage.

According to the SP, the declaration will allow the automatic price freeze on basic necessities and prime commodities under Republic Act 7581, or the Price Act, to prevent overpricing, hoarding and profiteering during the emergency period.
Aside from Lingayen, other provinces nearby also sustained significant damage due to recent weather disturbances.
At least 10 houses were damaged after a strong whirlwind tore through two villages in Burgos, Ilocos Sur on Sunday evening amid heavy rains brought by the southwest monsoon.

Ilocos Sur Provincial Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Officer Rhon Arquelada said the incident occurred around 6 p.m. in Barangays Manaboc and Bangbangar. Several roofs and garages were damaged while trees were uprooted by strong winds.
No injuries were reported as police and disaster response teams immediately rushed to the affected areas after barangay officials alerted authorities through handheld radios.
Pampanga Gov. Lilia Pineda, meanwhile, appealed yesterday to the private sector to help in implementing projects that could address widespread flooding in their province.
“We need the participation of the private sector because the DPWH already has a lot on its plate,” she said in an interview with “Storycon” on One News.

“This is the first time that even towns that previously did not experience flooding have been submerged. The volume of water was different this time… We did not expect it. Before, we could still cope…but this time, it has really been difficult,” she added. — With Mark Ernest Villeza, Rainier Allan Ronda, Artemio Dumlao, Bella Cariaso

articles.title: Congressman hits OVP execs
articles.summary: A leader in the House of Representatives has pointed to a possible staffing problem and accountability failure inside the Office of the Vice President as issues surrounding its use of confidential…

blocks.text: September 1, 2026 | 12:00am
Gina Acosta and Lemuel Ortonio
STAR / File

MANILA, Philippines — A leader in the House of Representatives has pointed to a possible staffing problem and accountability failure inside the Office of the Vice President (OVP) as issues surrounding its use of confidential funds continue to unravel before the Senate impeachment court.
Deputy Speaker Paolo Ortega V cited the repeated claims by OVP officials that they could not remember or did not know crucial details of the confidential funds used by the office.
“Maybe they had problem with HR because they seemed to have forgotten everything. They knew nothing,” he said.

Former OVP special disbursing officer Gina Acosta and OVP Assistant Secretary and assistant chief of staff Lemuel Ortonio were both declared hostile prosecution witnesses as the impeachment court examined how confidential funds were requested, released, implemented and liquidated under Duterte.

They both testified that they did not know how the confidential funds were used and that they put their trust in Vice President Sara Duterte and her security chief Col. Raymund Dante Lachica, whom she had tasked to handle the funds.
Ortega said government personnel entrusted with public funds are expected to perform their assigned responsibilities regardless of how much trust they place in their superiors.
“It means they’re blind followers. They just release funds, unmindful of where they would end up,” Ortega said.

Acosta testified that she turned over the funds to Lachica, the former head of the Vice Presidential Security and Protection Group, per Duterte’s instruction, while Ortonio testified on documents and processes involving the funds but repeatedly qualified the extent of his personal knowledge.

For Ortega, the recurring inability of officials directly involved in the transactions to explain what happened after the money left their hands raises questions about whether basic staff work was performed at all.

articles.title: NOAH head: Philippines ignored 1941 flood control master plan
articles.summary: The massive flooding being experienced in Metro Manila and various areas in the country is the result of decades of failure to follow the 1941 master plan, according to a University of the…

blocks.text: September 1, 2026 | 12:00am
Residents wade through floodwaters along Zapote Junction in Las Piñas on Saturday morning, Aug. 28, 2026 as the flooded road remains closed to vehicles.
The STAR / Edd Gumban

MANILA, Philippines — The massive flooding being experienced in Metro Manila and various areas in the country is the result of decades of failure to follow the 1941 master plan, according to a University of the Philippines expert.

UP Resilience Institute (UPRI) executive director and Project NOAH (Nationwide Operational Assessment of Hazards) head Mahar Lagmay warned Monday that flooding would continue to worsen if the country fails to implement science-based solutions.

“Our problem today is the accumulation of decades because the master plan was drafted in 1941. This is not different from the master plan of Cebu, which was the development plan of 1939 but it was not followed. The master plan would have been good, if we had followed that,” Lagmay said over radio dzBB.
“It’s all too late, the plan is to propose solutions other than just dikes, so not just one but many, let’s not call it flood control, but flood management instead,” he added.

Lagmay said concerned government agencies such as the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) and Metropolitan Manila Development Authority (MMDA) are now consulting Project NOAH (Nationwide Operational Assessment of Hazards) before undertaking flood-related projects.

“We have simulations that are very, very high, high-resolution. Simulations that are being done, which are constantly being passed by the DPWH, the MMDA, the designs, particularly DPWH, so that before we invest in the project, we have already seen on the computer how high the flood has been lowered, which ones will no longer be flooded…which ones would be flooded, how effective is the investment before we spend money on an area,” Lagmay said.
Since 2012, Lagmay said Project NOAH has helped reduce the number of deaths caused by floods and storms to about 250 to 300 per year.
Lagmay stressed that there is no overnight solution to the country’s flooding problem, saying authorities must begin implementing long-term measures as Metro Manila’s population continues to grow.

“This has been going on for a long time. I said 1941, that’s a few decades. We’ve been neglecting it for more than half a century, let’s not expect a magic bullet that will solve it immediately, it won’t happen tomorrow,” he said. “But it’s important to start this so that it doesn’t get worse.” — Ramon Efren Lazaro

articles.title: Study: 2 of 5 Pinoys age 10 face parental violence
articles.summary: A study by the Philippine Institute for Development Studies found that nearly two in five Filipino children aged 10 reported physical or emotional violence from a parent.

blocks.text: September 1, 2026 | 12:00am
MANILA, Philippines — A study by the Philippine Institute for Development Studies found that nearly two in five Filipino children aged 10 reported physical or emotional violence from a parent.

“Home Should Be Safe: How Parental Violence Affects Children’s Education in the Philippines,” authored by Aaron Carlos Manuel, Lyle Daryll Casas and Valerie Gilbert Ulep, said by age 14, children exposed to parental violence were significantly less likely to be enrolled in school, particularly girls.
The authors added that exposure to parental violence at age 10 was associated with lower odds of school enrolment at age 14 among both boys and girls.
The study said the association was stronger among girls when the results were stratified by gender.
The authors said parental violence was also associated with poorer academic performance, although this relationship was not statistically significant.

Among the recommendations of the study is to sustain and scale up multisectoral early intervention programs nationwide that integrate parenting education, school-based violence prevention and community advocacy, with gender-responsive approaches tailored to the distinct needs of boys and girls.
The study was done with support from the Australian government and the United Nations Population Fund.
It noted that the burden is particularly pronounced in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where legal protections and enforcement mechanisms are often weaker.
The authors noted that despite the magnitude of the problem, policy responses in many LMICs remain inadequate.
The study said this is frequently attributed to competing resource demands and a lack of context-specific evidence on effective prevention strategies and mitigation of long-term impacts.
It added that the failure to address this issue carries substantial costs.
According to the authors, worldwide, violence against children imposes a significant economic burden due to losses in health, education and productivity.
The authors said the Philippines confronts particularly acute challenges, citing data where about eight in 10 Filipino children have experienced some form of violence.
The study said more recent data indicate six in 10 children are subjected to violent discipline at home.

The authors added that violence also extends beyond the household, saying nearly three in 10 Filipino learners reported being bullied, citing results from the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development’s “Program for International Student Assessment 2022,” contributing to the country’s continued characterization as the “bullying capital of the world.”
Families are first line of defense

Education Secretary Sonny Angara yesterday said families are the first line of defense against school threats and violence, as he asked parents to be active partners in learner protection, values formation and anti-bullying efforts.
“We cannot solve violence in schools if we only act within the classroom. Home is our first defense,” Angara said.
He said families should take an active role in daily learner life and maintain close communication with school authorities.

“Let’s talk to our children every day, let’s listen to what they are going through and let’s communicate with their teachers and schools. We need to learn to notice red flags and changes in a child’s behavior before it even reaches the point of harm or bullying. Let’s make them feel that they are not alone,” Angara added.

The Department of Education issued DepEd Memorandum 002, s. 2026, or the Kaagapay Program, alongside with the Parent Effectiveness Service (PES) Program under Republic Act 11908 amid increase in school violence.

Angara said the Kaagapay Program equips parent communities with practical tools through capacity-building sessions to identify red flags, manage behavioral issues and directly coordinate with school Child Protection Committees and guidance personnel.

He said DepEd is collaborating with the Department of Social Welfare and Development to harmonize the PES modules with the Kaagapay Program, targeting full-scale implementation to tackle root causes of violence, including mental health struggles and online safety risks.

DepEd said it will roll out its program on Strengthening Collaboration of Parents and Teachers on Learner Protection across regions, including the Cordillera Administrative Region, Metro Manila, Region 2, Region 3, Region 4-A, Region 4-B and Region 5.

It said the initiative utilizes session guides developed by the DepEd Bureau of Learner Support Services-Learner Rights and Protection Division in partnership with ChildFund Philippines, Stairway Foundation Inc. and Meta Philippines.

articles.title: John Galliano exhibition at New York Met cancelled after backlash
articles.summary: The exhibition faced criticism over the British fashion designer's conviction for making antisemitic remarks in 2011.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
John Galliano said he realised "an exhibition honouring my work would be painful for some"
ByIan Youngs
Culture reporter
John Galliano has cancelled an upcoming major exhibition celebrating his work as a fashion designer after it prompted criticism due to his previous conviction for making antisemitic remarks.
The Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York had announced an exhibition titled John Galliano: Horizons that was due to open in May 2027.

But Galliano said on Monday: "After much reflection and discussion with the Met and all those involved, I have decided, with great sadness, that it is best for the exhibition not to take place at this time."
The British designer was sacked as creative director of Dior in 2011 and found guilty of abusing a Jewish curator in a restaurant in Paris.
A court also heard that he hurled racist insults at her friend, who is of South Asian origin, and in a separate incident declared a love for Hitler.
'I remain deeply sorry'
At the time, he apologised for his behaviour and his lawyer blamed it on "work-related stress and multiple addictions".

Galliano said in his statement on Monday: "I remain fully accountable for the pain caused by my words in the past, particularly the hurt I caused to the Jewish and Asian communities, and I remain deeply sorry for it.
"I understand that meaningful atonement is not achieved through an exhibition, institutional recognition or a single public gesture.
"It is a continuing responsibility, demonstrated through listening, learning and one's conduct over time."

Galliano added that he did not want "to distract from the remarkable work" of the Met's Costume Institute and said he recognised and respected that "an exhibition honouring my work would be painful for some".
Galliano's new statement noted his "15 years of sobriety and recovery from alcoholism and addiction".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Anna Wintour, pictured with Galliano in January, said he retained her "full support"

blocks.text: Anna Wintour, pictured with Galliano in January, said he retained her "full support"
As well as being the focus of the exhibition, Galliano and his work in fashion would have provided the theme for the next Met Gala.
The star-studded event is due to take place on 3 May, coinciding with Yom HaShoah (Holocaust and Heroism Remembrance Day).
Vogue global editorial director Anna Wintour, a trustee of the Met and co-chair of the Met Gala, gave her support to Galliano on Monday.
"John's decision that the exhibition devoted to his work should not take place at this time is very courageous and a measure of the man he is," she said.
"I believe this is the right decision, and both he and the Museum have my full support."
'Misguided'
Others had previously voiced their opposition to the Met's plan to commemorate Galliano.
Julie Menin, speaker of New York City Council, said, external: "After my numerous and lengthy meetings and conversations with the Met, I am pleased that they have agreed to not honour John Galliano.
"From the beginning, I have told them that I strongly disagreed with this decision, and at this rising time of antisemitism, it had served as a gut punch to the Jewish community.
"This is the correct decision, as the harm and pain this was causing was simply unacceptable."

Meanwhile, Jonathan Greenblatt, chief executive of the Anti-Defamation League, which aims to counter antisemitism, said that with antisemitism at "crisis levels", honouring Galliano would be "misguided".
"Even Galliano ultimately recognised what the Met should have done from the start," he added. "This was the wrong move at the wrong moment. Timing matters."
Galliano is regarded by some as one of the greatest fashion designers and returned to the fashion industry following his conviction, serving as creative director of Margiela for a decade until 2024.

articles.title: Lionel Messi announces retirement from international football
articles.summary: The Argentine legend announced that he will not play for the national team again, ending an illustrious international career.

image.caption: Lionel Messi won the World Cup with Argentina in 2022, but his side lost to Spain in the 2026 final [FILE: July 2026]Image: Brett Davis/IMAGN Images/REUTERS

blocks.text: Argentina legend Lionel Messi announced his international retirement on Monday.
The 39-year-old, widely considered the greatest football player of all time, won the 2022 World Cup in Qatar with Argentina, bringing the title back to the country for the first time since 1986.
The 2026 World Cup, Messi's last appearance in the world's most well-known footballing competition, ended in disappointment for Argentina after defeat to Spain in the final.
Despite being past his prime, the Argentina captain was the second most prolific goalscorer of the 2026 World Cup with eight goals, only being edged out by France's Kylian Mbappe with ten.

Messi is also second in the World Cup's all-time goalscorer list, where he is one goal behind Mbappe, with both overtaking Germany striker Miroslav Klose's 16 goals during the tournament in the US, Canada and Mexico.
Retirement comes at 'right time'

"It was a decision that hurt and still hurts deep in my soul," Messi posted on his Instagram account, adding that he wrote his international retirement message two days after the World Cup final defeat to Spain.
"But I understand that it is the right time," he added.
Messi said he "always gave everything, not just in the last few years," and that he wanted to bring Argentina fans joy ​and make them "feel proud to be ​Argentine through football."
"I leave with the peace of mind and pride of having given you — alongside my teammates — moments we once only dreamed of," he wrote, before concluding with "Vamos, Argentina!"
"I leave with the peace ​of mind ⁠and pride of having given you — alongside my ⁠teammates — ​moments we once only dreamed of," he added.
Miami contract until 2028
Messi is his country's most capped player with 207 appearances, in which he scored 125 goals, another all-time record.
With Messi as captain, Argentina also won the Copa America in 2021 and 2024.

His club career will continue at current club Inter Miami, where he has a contract until the end of the 2028 MLS season, although he did voice "serious doubts" about continuing to play football for "much longer" following the death of his father Jorge in August.

The attacker moved to the US side in 2023 from Paris Saint-Germain and after a 15-year career with Spanish giants Barcelona, with whom he won the UEFA Champions League four times and the Spanish title ten times.

Messi wanted to stay at Barcelona, but the club could not afford to keep him due to financial restrictions. This resulted in his move to Qatar-backed PSG, where he spent two years winning two league titles before moving to Miami.

articles.title: Trump pushes Apple to change 'Lake Ontario' to 'Lake America' on its maps
articles.summary: The request comes after Google made the switch for US-based users over the weekend. MapQuest, another US map provider, said it will not change the name.

blocks.text: Trump signed the executive order on Thursday seeking to change the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America, following the collapse of trade negotiations between Canada and the US.
The order directs Burgum to "take all appropriate actions" to rename the lake, including updating the Geographic Names Information System (GNIS), the official US government map database.
Google said in a statement on Saturday that its maps will display the Lake America name for US users to comply with GNIS.
It added that those in Canada will continue to see Lake Ontario displayed. In the rest of the world, users will see the name displayed as: Lake Ontario (Lake America).
Not all map providers are changing the name. MapQuest, an American free web mapping service that was launched in 1996, said "we're not changing it" in a short Facebook post on Friday.
The platform also unveiled a tool that allows users to change the lake to any name they choose and share their creations.
After its announcement that it will not be changing the name of Lake Ontario, MapQuest rose to the top of the most-downloaded free applications as of Monday morning on the Apple App Store in Canada.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford unveiled a large sign by the lakeshore on Saturday that read "Lake Ontario Now and Always" in both English and French, Canada's official languages.
"No one's going to call it Lake of America," Ford told American TV host George Stephanopoulos on Sunday. "It's been Lake Ontario for hundreds of years. It's going to continue being Lake Ontario."

articles.title: Met Gala honouring John Galliano cancelled following backlash
articles.summary: The Metropolitan Museum of Art is cancelling its planned exhibit honouring British designer John Galliano, which had led to severe backlash in the Jewish community and beyond because of the…

image.caption: Fashion designer John Galliano, shown here in Paris in 2010, will no longer be honoured at an upcoming Met Gala, according to the Metroplitan Museum of Art, following weeks of backlash over his prior antisemitic and racist statements. (Jacques Brinon/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

The Metropolitan Museum of Art is cancelling its planned exhibit honouring British designer John Galliano, which had led to severe backlash in the Jewish community and beyond because of the designer's past antisemitic and racist statements.
Fashion designer says he remains 'deeply sorry' for prior antisemitic, racist remarks

The New York museum said Monday that the exhibit, which had been planned as the May 2027 spring Costume Institute show launching the annual Met Gala, will be replaced by another show to be announced later.
"Following thoughtful discussions with John Galliano, we have together decided not to proceed with the exhibition," Max Hollein, director and CEO of the museum, announced in a statement.

The designer joined in the statement, saying: "After much reflection and discussion with The Met and all those involved, I have decided, with great sadness, that it is best for the exhibition not to take place at this time. I remain fully accountable for the pain caused by my words in the past, particularly the hurt I caused to the Jewish and Asian communities, and I remain deeply sorry for it."

Galliano, long recognized as one of the fashion world's biggest talents for his flamboyant designs, was at the pinnacle of that world for years as creative director of Christian Dior. He was fired from the post when a series of racist and antisemitic comments from 2010 and 2011 surfaced and went viral, leading to his conviction in an antisemitism trial in France.

Dropped by Dior, Galliano spent several years involved in public and private efforts to rehabilitate. He made a comeback in 2014 when he was hired by Paris fashion house Maison Margiela, where he remained for a decade.
He was to become only the third living designer to be the subject of a solo show at the Met's Costume Institute.

The spring season is launched by the annual Met Gala, the most visible event on the fashion calendar. The gala is overseen by Anna Wintour, Vogue's global editorial director and one of the most influential figures in fashion. Wintour has been a longtime friend and supporter of Galliano.

The museum had held discussions with Jewish community leaders before announcing the show, hoping to ward off anticipated backlash. But the anger only increased. One of the key critics of the planned show was New York City Council Speaker Julie Menin, who issued a statement Monday praising the decision to cancel.

"After my numerous and lengthy meetings and conversations with The Met, I am pleased that they have agreed to not honor John Galliano," Menin said. "From the beginning, I have told them that I strongly disagreed with this decision, and at this rising time of antisemitism, it had served as a gut punch to the Jewish community. This is the correct decision, as the harm and pain this was causing was simply unacceptable."

articles.title: Court says India must uphold Pakistan water treaty
articles.summary: An international tribunal has ordered India to "observe its obligations" under a water-treaty with Pakistan.

image.caption: The court said India's construction of hydroelectric projects on the Indus and associated rivers had to conform to the treaty [FILE: May 2025]Image: Nasir Kachroo/picture alliance/NurPhoto

blocks.text: The Permanent Court of Arbitration (PCA) in The Hague has ordered India to uphold a water-sharing treaty with Pakistan which has led to a recent increase in tensions between the two neighbors.
The PCA said New Delhi must "observe its obligations" under the treaty with on the sharing of the Indus and other rivers, which the Indian government this year sought to suspend.
In a statement, the court found unanimously found that "none of the grounds" put forward by India were justified and "concluded that the Treaty [...] remains fully in force."
The court noted that India "remains bound by the obligations incumbent upon it," particularly regarding the design and operation of "hydroelectric projects on the western rivers."
It said India's construction of hydroelectric projects on the Indus and associated rivers had to conform to the treaty.
A Pakistani government spokesman said Islamabad "welcomed" the PCA order.

articles.title: Nepal principal evacuates 900 students before floods sweep away school
articles.summary: BIDUR, Nepal — Rajendra Dawadi was inside his classroom when a colleague rushed in with a warning: Floodwaters were racing through Nepal’s Trishuli Valley, tearing apart homes, bridges and entire…

blocks.text: BIDUR, Nepal — Rajendra Dawadi was inside his classroom when a colleague rushed in with a warning: Floodwaters were racing through Nepal’s Trishuli Valley, tearing apart homes, bridges and entire villages.

Then a teacher received another warning by phone. Moments later, a parent arrived to take her child home. The danger had not yet been confirmed, but Dawadi, the principal, had little time to act. He rang the school bell and ordered his students and staff out of the building and toward higher ground.
“I immediately decided to stop … school” and get the children out, he told The Associated Press.

As he followed them to a nearby hill, the floodwaters rose behind him. From the safety of the hillside, he turned to watch the school where he had once been a student — and where he had spent years teaching — disappear beneath a torrent of water, mud, boulders and debris. Two staff members could not make it and remain missing.

Dawadi’s decision to evacuate the school saved at least 900 students from last week’s devastating flash floods in Nepal, unleashed after a glacial collapse in the Himalayas. The disaster killed over 900 people across Nepal and China, while more than 4,700 remain missing.
As Nepal grapples with the catastrophic natural disaster, Dawadi’s story has emerged as a striking example of foresight and courage.

The Tribhuvan Trishuli Secondary School had 1,643 students. At least 900 were on campus that morning, while some students were still making their way to school. Dawadi ordered those already there to leave and called bus drivers to tell them not to come.

One bus, packed with students, had already reached the school when Dawadi told the driver to turn back, he said. The bus crossed a newly constructed bridge and, moments later, the old bridge beside it collapsed.
For Dawadi, the scale of the destruction has become personal, as the school had been both his workplace and a large part of his life.
“I have no words. I got education from that school. And I gave education at that school,” he said.
The destruction of Dawadi’s school was not an isolated loss.

Across northern Nepal, the floods have left thousands of children without classrooms, disrupted their education and raised fears that the disaster could cost them months of schooling. Charity group Save the Children said in a statement that at least 69 schools in northern Nepal have been completely destroyed, putting the education of nearly 19,000 students at risk.

Dawadi’s quick thinking and swift response during the disaster have been hailed as an act of heroism. When he returned to the site of the school days later, parents embraced him as they thanked him for saving their children.
“Their parents hugged me, they cried with me,” he said. “They were emotional.”
Student Suvina Tamang, 14, said the building was swept away shortly after the students had been evacuated. “I will thank him when I see him” for saving my life, she said.

But Dawadi is reluctant to accept the role of hero. For him, rescuing his students was his responsibility. Now he says, students will need psychological counseling. Then, lessons must begin again, even if the school must temporarily relocate.
His appeal to the Nepalese government is simple: rebuild the schools and get children back to classes. /jpv

articles.title: How China buried Tibet flood images after Nepal disaster
articles.summary: A flood has devastated communities along the China-Nepal border, but in Tibet the disaster was followed by a digital crackdown. Censors erased viral footage while state media flooded platforms with…

image.caption: China's state-backed information control apparatus swung into action to shape the public narrative and bury inconvenient truthsImage: REUTERS

blocks.text: When a catastrophic flash flood swept through the rugged China-Nepal border on August 26, the physical devastation was immediate.
In Nepal, a black torrent of mud and rock tore through communities, leaving hundreds dead and thousands more missing along the borderlands.

But across the frontier in Tibet, an autonomous region of China, the physical disaster was almost instantly mirrored by a digital one: the rapid, high-tech erasure of the catastrophe's visual evidence.

As survivors tried to upload raw footage of the deluge, China's state-backed information control apparatus swung into action, executing a sophisticated, precision operation to shape the public narrative and bury inconvenient truths.
The contrasting realities — a tragic humanitarian crisis in Nepal and a tightly sanitized, triumphant rescue narrative in China — reveal the evolving mechanics of Beijing's modern censorship machine.

Rather than imposing a blunt, blanket blackout, authorities deployed advanced image-recognition technology and "saturated information" tactics to drown out domestic scrutiny while deflecting diplomatic friction abroad.
The fall of the 'National Gate'
In the immediate aftermath of the flood-triggered mudslide, local residents captured dramatic footage of the torrent engulfing Gyirong Port, a critical overland trade hub between China and Nepal.
The most striking video showed a black wall of water and debris crashing into and destroying the border crossing's massive "National Gate."

In an article titled "An Unrecorded Mudslide Rushes into Gyirong Port" on WeChat, a universal app that combines messaging with payment options and social media functions, local blogger "Matou Qingnian" described the chaotic scene.

"The most terrifying moment happened at the Gyirong Port," the author wrote, describing video footage of crowds, including children, fleeing in panic before a pitch-black torrent swallowed the camera's view.
Within hours, both the article and the raw video footage vanished from Chinese social media.

According to China Digital Times (CDT), an independent watchdog that tracks Chinese internet censorship, the video of the collapsing "National Gate" was systematically blocked from being shared on WeChat, even in private messages.

"The footage itself contained no graphic violence, no protests, and no political slogans," explained Mira, a CDT editor who specializes in tracking sensitive keywords and media. "The target of the censorship was the symbol itself: the National Gate."

Digital analysts note that this censorship highlights a significant upgrade in China's internet policing tools. Instead of merely filtering text-based keywords, platforms now rely heavily on video fingerprinting, image hashing, and machine-learning models to recognize specific visual scenes.
Once a visual sequence is blacklisted, it is intercepted before it can ever be posted.
Satiety as a shield: the art of 'saturated' censorship
The suppression of the Gyirong Port disaster reflects a broader shift in Beijing's strategy: from mass deletion to "precision surgery" and narrative flooding.
A search for "Tibet mudslide" on Xiaohongshu — China's popular lifestyle and search platform — reveals the mechanics of this "saturated information environment."
Rather than showing an empty search page, the platform's algorithm feeds users a carefully curated stream of state-media reports from China's state broadcaster CCTV and news agency Xinhua.

The visual landscape is dominated by high-resolution, sterile graphics: "before-and-after" comparisons, maps of high-altitude glacial collapses — the official scientific cause of the disaster — and state-approved aerial drone footage.
The raw, chaotic cellphone videos recorded by eyewitnesses at the border are entirely absent.

By filling the digital space with a high volume of "safe" and visually appealing official content, the state satisfies the public's immediate curiosity while preemptively suffocating independent reporting or organic discussions, ananysts note.

blocks.caption: Rescuers carry out search and rescue operations at the mudslide-hit Gyirong PortImage: Lhasa Fire and Rescue Mobile Detachment/Handout/Xinhua/picture alliance

blocks.text: On Weibo, China's microblogging giant, the narrative arc was similarly managed. While "Tibet mudslide" briefly trended on August 26, the domestic casualty figures were quickly frozen the next morning at three dead and 558 missing.
Almost immediately, the platform's trending topics were redirected toward the government's swift response.

Two heavily publicized, lengthy official reports dominated the news cycle: Chinese President Xi Jinping convening a Central Politburo meeting to coordinate rescue and relief efforts, and Premier Li Qiang arriving in Gyirong to personally direct operations on the ground.
These headlines effectively turned a major human tragedy into a highly orchestrated exhibition of state competence.
The dangerous 'half-year' question
Beneath the veneer of efficient state rescue efforts lies a deeper, systemic vulnerability that Beijing was desperate to hide: a history of structural negligence.

On August 27, a hashtag briefly slipped through the censors and trended on Weibo: "Gyirong Port Reopened Only Half a Year Ago." It amassed over 347,000 views in less than an hour before it was abruptly deleted. The hashtag pointed to a damning timeline of infrastructure failures.

In July 2025, Gyirong Port was completely shut down after being devastated by another severe flash flood. It took nearly six months to rebuild and reopen the port on January 1, 2026. Eight months later, the port has been destroyed again.

As the deleted "Matou Qingnian" article noted, Gyirong Port has now suffered mudslides during the flood seasons of 2024, 2025, and now 2026. In 2025, several Chinese personnel went missing or were killed.
By erasing the "half-year" trend, censors blocked an inevitable and dangerous train of public inquiry.

If the state-of-the-art border facility was destroyed twice in 14 months, it raises critical questions about site selection, shoddy infrastructure construction, and the complete failure of glacial lake monitoring and early-warning systems in Tibet.

These questions are especially sensitive in Tibet, a region under intense security and political control since the 1950s. Foreign journalists are strictly barred from entering the region outside of highly choreographed government-led tours.
According to human rights groups, local Tibetans who attempt to speak with foreign journalists or share independent accounts online face immediate detention or arrest.
High-altitude friction
The informational firewall does not stop at China's borders; it has also created a diplomatic rift with neighboring Nepal, which has borne the brunt of the disaster's human toll.
In Nepal, families cling to hope as thousands still missing
Parshuram Kaphle, a prominent Nepalese foreign policy journalist, publicly accused Beijing on X (formerly Twitter) of failing to share critical trans-boundary data.

"Nepal has been addressing the legitimate security concerns of our neighbors," Kaphle wrote in a post that has since been deleted. "However, it must be said with sadness that our northern neighbor has significantly undermined us. By failing to provide early warning of such a massive disaster, we suffered immense loss of human life."

He further wrote, "We have continually faced crises originating from their territory, while we continue to address all their concerns, necessary or unnecessary. Why must Nepal alone pay the price of one-sided love?"

The Chinese government has rejected any accountability. On August 27, the Chinese Embassy in Nepal issued a statement on Facebook, dismissing accusations of failing to issue warnings or causing the disaster through upstream dam failures as "fake news."
"Accusation helps nothing," the embassy statement read. "Cooperation saves lives."
But for families searching for more than 3,000 missing loved ones along the muddy banks of the Himalayan border, cooperation remains as obscured as the truth behind the digital firewall.
This article was originally published in Chinese.

articles.title: Germany poised to identify suspect in Leipzig drone attack on Ukrainian plane
articles.summary:
Berlin expected to outline response to incident this month widely speculated to have been coordinated by Russia

The German government is imminently expected to announce who it believes was…

blocks.text: The German government is imminently expected to announce who it believes was behind a suspected drone attack on a Ukrainian cargo plane earlier this month and to outline its response to the incident in coordination with its European and Nato partners.

The chancellor, Friedrich Merz, told the public broadcaster ARD in an interview on Sunday evening: “We are in the process of concluding the investigations; we have reached a broad agreement within the federal government on how we will respond, and we will make this clear in the coming days. It won’t take much longer.”

The government has so far declined to say officially who it thinks was behind the attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle airport on 4 August. There has been widespread speculation that it was coordinated by Moscow.

A drone containing explosives was discovered near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo aircraft used to transport military supplies. The drone was apparently intended to land on the wings of the aircraft, which was filled with kerosene, but the explosive device did not detonate, according to a report last week referencing the investigation.
About 20 minutes after the discovery of the first drone, a second drone possibly collided with a DHL cargo plane, which had to abort its landing manoeuvre and was diverted.

Days later, a third drone was found in a field in a municipality that directly borders the western edge of Leipzig airport. Forensic technicians from the federal criminal police office found residues of a substance that initial assessments indicated could have been the highly explosive substance hexogen.

This explosive also failed to detonate but according to media reports, the investigators’ report stated: “The perpetrators may have had a far larger attack in mind than previously known to the public.”
Moscow has denied involvement.
Merz indicated that the information the government was due to release was being closely communicated with Berlin’s partners, and any response would also be carried out in cooperation with them.
“It will be a response from Germany, but our partners in the European Union and Nato will not be taken by surprise,” he said.
It has been speculated in Berlin that meetings this week of EU defence and foreign affairs ministers in Wicklow, Ireland, could be used to make the announcement.

Last week Merz stopped short of naming a suspect but said: “They will pay for this.” He underscored the necessity for a decisive response due to the lengths he said those behind the Leipzig plot and other acts of sabotage had been prepared to go.
“Attackers are increasingly ruthlessly accepting even serious property damage, and even injuries and deaths,” he said.

The daily Die Welt and the news website Politico have reported, citing sources, that the government will blame Russia for the attack and that its retaliatory measures are likely to include a new, extensive package of sanctions coordinated with Brussels to hinder it financially, as well as more forceful measures against Russia’s shadow fleet, the Russian ships illegally transporting oil.

The closure of Russian House, an institution representing Russia’s cultural interests that has a large presence in the centre of Berlin, is also said to be on the cards. In return, Russia would be expected to close Germany’s cultural body in Russia, the Goethe Institute.

The political dimensions of the government’s response are potentially considerable owing to the timing. A heated election campaign in eastern German states culminates in a vote this Sunday in which the anti-immigrant, populist AfD is expected to do well. The debate over relations with Russia and whether and how Germany should continue to support Ukraine are playing an important role in the campaign.

The AfD’s foreign policy spokesperson, Markus Frohnmaier, said he believed “without a doubt” Germany faced hybrid threats but said he would not speculate over who was behind them, calling on the government to “first establish transparency and provide information about the current state of knowledge”.

articles.title: At Venice Film Festival, politics take center stage
articles.summary: With works about Gaza, Ukraine and Elon Musk, political cinema is in the spotlight at the 2026 Venice Film Festival.

image.caption: Penelope Cruz and Javier Bardem (seen here in a photo from 2017) return to Venice as the stars of Florian Zeller's 'Bunker'Image: Domenico Stinellis/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The Venice Film Festival used to be the place where the awards season put on its best tuxedo. This year, it looks more like a war room, with politics and political cinema set to dominate the red carpet.

The 83rd Venice International Film Festival kicks off on September 2 with Danny Boyle's "Ink," a drama about Rupert Murdoch's 1969 takeover of Britain's The Sun tabloid — the origin story of the Murdoch right-wing media empire.

Over 11 days on the Lido, audiences will also get films about Israel and Gaza, Russia's war on Ukraine, the CIA-backed coup in Pinochet's Chile, ICE raids in Minneapolis and a tell-all documentary on the world's richest man.
Festival artistic director Alberto Barbera has called it Venice's "most political" edition ever.

blocks.caption: 'Naza,' a documentary by 'No Other Land' directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, runs in the official competitionImage: Venice Film Festival/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Venice goes political
This year's competition includes "Naza," a documentary from "No Other Land" Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, examining Israeli military killings of Palestinian civilians in Gaza.
US-Russian director Julia Loktev chronicles Russian President Vladimir Putin's crackdown on independent journalism in "My Undesirable Friends Part II — Exile," a sequel to her 2024 doc.

blocks.caption: DW co-production 'Letters From the Silenced Country' portrays life under repression in BelarusImage: DW/ZDF/Arte

blocks.text: Andrei Kutsila's "Letters From the Silenced Country" a DW, ZDF/Arte and TVP co-production about repression in Kutsila's native Belarus, will have its world premiere in Venice.
As will Alex Gibney's four-hour Elon Musk documentary "Musk," a film the richest man in the world has already denounced, sight unseen, as a "hit piece."

And Laura Poitras, the Oscar-winning director of "Citizenfour," will screen what she describes as a "short horror film," the documentary "They're Here," co-directed with Rachel Lauren Mueller and built from previously undisclosed footage of ICE's deportation surge in Minneapolis last January.

blocks.caption: Laura Poitras also won the Golden Lion award in 2022 for best film for 'All the Beauty and the Bloodshed' Image: Domenico Stinellis/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: This is a new look for Venice.

Under artistic director Barbera, the festival had until recently cultivated a reputation as a place for movie stars and Oscar campaigns. You go to Venice to watch Timothee Chalamet on the red carpet, or George Clooney and Brad Pitt yucking it up at a press conference.
Venice let the other big European festivals — Berlin, and to a lesser degree Cannes — be the homes of political movies and the polemical debates that accompany them.
Berlin's political backlash

But Berlin's reputation as a festival for activist cinema has taken a major hit. The past three years have seen political debate, primarily over the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, overwhelm discussions of cinema at the Berlinale, to the point where the future of the festival looks in doubt.

At this year's Berlinale, jury president Wim Wenders was lambasted online for saying filmmakers "have to stay out of politics." Later, when Syrian-Palestinian director Abdallah Al-Khatib called out the German government at the awards ceremony for being "partners in the genocide in Gaza by Israel," the backlash nearly cost Berlinale director Tricia Tuttle her job.
Venice, by contrast, has spent the past two years leaning into political cinema.

blocks.caption: How will she react to political questions? Actor Maggie Gyllenhaal is the president of the international jury this yearImage: Federico Vespignani/AA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Venice leans into controversy

Last year saw the world premiere of Kaouther Ben Hania's "The Voice of Hind Rajab." The harrowing docudrama, which recreates the killing, by Israeli forces, of a 5-year-old Palestinian girl and her family in Gaza City, received a 22-minute standing ovation, a Lido record. The Israeli military has recently announced an official investigation into Hind Rajab's death.

Just days before, thousands marched on the Lido in protest of the war in Gaza. Filmmakers called on Barbera to label Israel's campaign "a genocide." He didn't go that far, speaking instead of his "huge sadness" over the suffering in Gaza and Palestine.
But the Venice boss didn't flinch, then or now, from programming films that address, head-on, the most controversial topics of the day.

blocks.caption: Danny Boyle's Rupert Murdoch drama 'Ink' opens the festivalImage: StudioCanal/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Ukraine objects to 'DAU'
Russian films selected by the festival are also sparking protest.

Ukraine's Foreign Ministry, Culture Ministry and its embassy in Italy have issued a formal complaint over Barbera's decision to include Ilya Khrzhanovsky's "DAU," an art house drama about life under Soviet rule in Ukraine, in official competition. Ukraine objects to the film's Russian connections.

Khrzhanovsky is Russian-born, though he renounced his Russian citizenship and now lives in exile in Berlin. The film's lead, Greek-Russian conductor Teodor Currentzis, still lives and works in Russia and has never publicly condemned Russia's war on Ukraine.

blocks.caption: Greek-Russian conductor Teodor Currentzis, who stars in 'DAU,' has remained silent on Putin's invasion of UkraineImage: Getty Images/AFP/S. de Sakutin

blocks.text: In a statement, the Ukrainian ministries said programming the film "sends a deeply worrying signal" given the war.
Barbera is not backing down. He called the criticism a "smear campaign" from people who haven't seen the film.

Khrzhanovsky took to social media on August 20 with his rebuttal: "'DAU' is not an instrument of Russian state cultural policy," he wrote on Facebook. "It is an artistic statement about the nature of totalitarian evil."
Stars are still coming
Venice hasn't completely abandoned its Hollywood stars.
Robert Pattinson, of "Batman" and "Twilight" fame, will hit the Lido this year with "Primetime," playing a controversial US reality TV producer.

blocks.caption: Robert Pattinson is among the stars expected on the red carpetImage: Luca Carlino/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell play CIA agents in Chile on the eve of the Pinochet coup in "Wild Horse Nine" from director Martin McDonagh ("Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri").
Real-life couple Javier Bardem and Penelope Cruz star as husband and wife in Florian Zeller's "Bunker," about an architect commissioned to build a nuclear shelter for a billionaire.
George Clooney and 93-year-old acting legend Ellen Burstyn will swing by to collect Golden Lion awards for lifetime achievement.

blocks.caption: George Clooney, a Venice regular, will attend this year to receive an honorary Golden LionImage: Stefano Costantino/SOPA Images/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Venice also hasn't abandoned its role as a gathering place for cinema's elder statesmen — several of them German.
Wim Wenders, fresh off the Berlinale storm, brings an altogether gentler work to the Lido, a 3D documentary on the work of Swiss architect Peter Zumthor.

Werner Herzog, the last wild man of '70s German cinema, returns to narrative filmmaking for the first time in seven years in Venice with "Bucking Fastard," starring real-life sisters Kate and Rooney Mara.

And for those who want to forget about the world for a moment and just kick back and sing, pop stars Liam and Noel Gallagher are expected on the Lido for the premiere of the Oasis reunion documentary "Don't Look Back in Anger."
