articles.title: Duterte Impeachment Trial: Who is Prosecution Counsel Amando Virgil Ligutan?
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Lawyer Amando Virgil Ligutan is among the private lawyers assisting the House prosecution panel in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte. Since the trial began,…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Lawyer Amando Virgil Ligutan is among the private lawyers assisting the House prosecution panel in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

Since the trial began, Ligutan has conducted the prosecution’s direct examination of National Bureau of Investigation Regional Director Jeremy Lotoc and Gina Acosta, a former special disbursing officer of the Office of the Vice President who testified as a hostile witness.
The Cebuano lawyer is not afraid to use his native language during trial, even at times translating for Acosta when the latter said she found some Tagalog words quite deep.
Ligutan is the managing partner of SALiGAL Law (Sapayan Lim Alvarez & Ligutan Law Offices) in Cebu.

He is also actively teaching Labor Law, Remedial Law, and Public International Law as a lecturer and law instructor in University of the Philippines, University of San Jose-Recoletos School of Law, and University of Cebu School of Law.
Ligutan was valedictorian when he graduated High School from Sacred Heart Seminary in Palo Leyte in 1999.
Four years later, he completed his undergraduate degree in AB Philosophy from University of San Carlos in Cebu, and was awarded Summa Cum Laude.
He then pursued Law in University of the Philippines Diliman and graduated in 2009.
Among his expertise are civil and criminal litigation, political and administrative law, and public interest cases.
He also has expertise in labor relations law, risk and crisis management, and local government and election law.

This Wednesday, Aug. 26, Ligutan is set to explain his Facebook post, which read, “A principle all lawyers and law students know by heart: Misleading questions are not allowed even on cross-examination.”

The post became a point of concern when defense lead counsel Sheila Sison raised to the impeachment court that the post was seemingly referring to a statement made by defense counsel Kristine Ferrer during her cross-examination of state auditor Xylene del Campo.

articles.title: Mirra Andreeva and her 'crush' Rublev win in US Open mixed doubles
articles.summary: NEW YORK — Mirra Andreeva revealed a secret Tuesday after she and Andrey Rublev ended the reign of the two-time US Open mixed doubles champions. She used to have a crush on her partner. “I’ve never…

blocks.text: Mirra Andreeva, of Russia, and Andrey Rublev, of Russia, react after winning a mixed doubles match at the U.S. Open tennis championships, Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026, in New York. (AP Photo/Yuki Iwamura)
NEW YORK — Mirra Andreeva revealed a secret Tuesday after she and Andrey Rublev ended the reign of the two-time US Open mixed doubles champions.
She used to have a crush on her partner.
“I’ve never said anything, I’ve never told him anything as well, but I used to have a little crush on him as well,” Andreeva said during an interview on the court.
That’s just adorable 🤗 pic.twitter.com/R3bunVJUzj — US Open Tennis (@usopen) August 25, 2026

The French Open champion added that it was “like a dream come true to play with my favorite” before being unable to finish that sentence when Rublev interrupted to give her a hug as the crowd cheered.

The crush is over — the 19-year-old Andreeva said it was when she was 15 or 16 — but their tournament goes on. The Russians will play Wednesday night in the semifinals against Karolina Muchova and Jakub Mensik.
They began the event by outlasting Sara Errani and Andrea Vavassori 1-4, 4-1 (11-9), then emerged from another match tiebreaker to edge Diana Shnaider and Casper Ruud for their semifinal spot.
Rublev, 28, is perhaps most recognizable for his red hair and his occasional outbursts on the court. Andreeva definitely noticed his appearance, but thought he was kind despite the tirades.
“I mean, first of all, his hair, OK?” she responded when asked why she was drawn to him.
What. A. Finish 💥 Andreeva and Rublev stare down match point before dethroning Errani/Vavassori! pic.twitter.com/gYta8R0N8L — US Open Tennis (@usopen) August 25, 2026

“So many interviews I saw and so many things that I heard from other people, I just knew he’s a great person. I didn’t know him at that time yet. I don’t know, I just feel like he’s super kind, very nice with everyone. Again, the hair. I don’t know, everyone said that every time he would step on court, he would look tired. I don’t know, he was looking great every time for me.”
Rublev’s response to Andreeva’s revelation?

“You know this typical moments when the kids, they don’t have taste yet, they need to try some stupid things before they start to have it?” Rublev said. “I was in the part of stupid thing, in the transition moment.”
Rublev has reached 10 Grand Slam quarterfinals, including four at the US Open, in singles. Now he’s in the semifinals at a major.
“We see how Mirra affects me,” he said.

articles.title: From Strategy to Execution: Powering Central Luzon’s AI future through regional digital transformation
articles.summary: The Department of Science and Technology Regional Office No. III (DOST-III / DOST-CL) and WPH Digital, a Singapore-based AI and digital innovation company, have signed a Memorandum of Understanding…

blocks.text: The Department of Science and Technology Regional Office No. III (DOST-III / DOST-CL) and WPH Digital, a Singapore-based AI and digital innovation company, have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) to accelerate regional digital transformation and artificial intelligence (AI) adoption across Central Luzon.

The collaboration brings the Philippines’ National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (NAIS-PH) closer to regional implementation by combining DOST-III’s public-sector mandate with WPH Digital’s expertise in AI, digital transformation, and practical technology implementation.

The agreement was formally signed by Dr. Julius Ceasar V. Sicat, Regional Director of DOST Central Luzon, and Mr. Vincent Leoh, Managing Director of WPH Digital, on 19 August 2026. Held at the opening of the joint program, the ceremony was witnessed by over 50 key delegates and industry leaders representing diverse business, technology, and public sectors from across Central Luzon.

“We believe AI adoption is not a technology challenge — it is a capability challenge,” said Mr. Vincent Leoh, Managing Director of WPH Digital. “Through WPH Academy, we help people build AI capabilities, and through WPH Digital, we help organisations apply those capabilities using practical AI solutions. When capability building and practical implementation come together, organisations start seeing real value from AI.”
Democratizing Generative AI Across Central Luzon

By bringing enterprise-grade digital expertise directly to Region III, the collaboration demonstrates how government and private-sector organisations can work together to democratize access to advanced Generative AI and cloud computing technologies beyond Metro Manila. The initiative positions Central Luzon as a key regional innovation hub, driving competitiveness across local micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs), industries, and public sector operations.
Human Capital and Workforce Readiness First

At the heart of the partnership is a strong emphasis on talent reskilling, practical capability-building, and workforce development. Rather than viewing technology solely as a displacement risk, the collaboration equips local professionals and civil servants to use Generative AI as a productivity multiplier—fostering a resilient, highly competitive regional talent pool equipped for modern, future-ready workflows.

As an immediate step toward putting the partnership into action, DOST-III and WPH Digital conducted the Generative AI for Modern Business Operations workshop. The practical capacity-building session provided business leaders, IT professionals, and regional stakeholders with hands-on exposure to practical AI solutions, cloud-native platforms, and execution strategies designed to deliver practical business value.

Beyond training and capability-building, the collaboration is intended to help organisations translate these capabilities into actual implementation, enabling them to identify practical AI opportunities and develop solutions that can be applied within their operating environments.
International Cross-Border Tech Collaboration

The MOU highlights cross-border technology transfer between Singapore’s private sector and the Philippine government. By bringing Singaporean tech consulting expertise to Central Luzon, WPH Digital showcases how international private-sector solutions can actively contribute to regional development goals in organisations and communities across Southeast Asia.

“AI is already here, and it is becoming part of how businesses plan, create, communicate, and improve their operations,” said Dr. Julius Caesar V. Sicat, Regional Director of DOST Central Luzon. “This training is not just about learning AI — it is about empowering our MSMEs to confidently embrace change and turn technology into opportunities.”
Trusted AI with Certified Governance

The partnership also underscores the importance of responsible and governed AI adoption as organisations move from experimentation to implementation. WPH Digital brings AI governance expertise backed by the internationally recognised ISO/IEC 42001 standard, which provides a structured framework for responsible, secure, ethical, and governed AI adoption.
WPH Digital is one of the first AI and Digital Service Providers in Singapore to achieve ISO/IEC 42001 certification for Artificial Intelligence Management Systems, and is the first in the world

to achieve ISO/IEC 42001 certification for AI systems in the oil and gas industry. This experience supports the company’s approach to helping organisations move beyond AI concepts and strategy toward practical, production-ready solutions.

By combining AI expertise, enterprise technology experience, cloud capabilities, and ISO/IEC 42001-based AI governance, WPH Digital brings an implementation-focused approach to AI adoption. Under the DOST-III partnership, this approach complements workforce training and technical capability-building, helping organisations explore how AI can be applied responsibly and effectively within their operating environments.
A Replicable Blueprint for Regional Action

The alliance establishes a repeatable model for regional government-industry partnerships throughout the Philippines. Moving beyond high-level strategy, DOST-III and WPH Digital provide a structured model for continuous technical implementation, capacity building, and enterprise enablement across provincial economies.

The longer-term ambition is for this model to extend from national government agencies to provincial and local government units (LGUs), and eventually across other regions of the Philippines. By connecting national AI priorities with regional capability-building and practical implementation, the collaboration has the potential to provide a scalable model for AI capabilities.
ADVT.
This article is brought to you by WPH Digital.

articles.title: Spouses Svitolina, Monfils reach US Open mixed doubles semis
articles.summary: NEW YORK — Elina Svitolina and Gael Monfils have both gone far but never all the way to the US Open title. Maybe the married couple can finally win a trophy together. The spouses made quite a pair on…

blocks.text: Elina Svitolina, of Ukraine, left, and Gael Monfils, of France, kiss after winning a mixed doubles match at the U.S. Open tennis championships, Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026, in New York. (AP Photo/Yuki Iwamura)
NEW YORK — Elina Svitolina and Gael Monfils have both gone far but never all the way to the US Open title. Maybe the married couple can finally win a trophy together.
The spouses made quite a pair on the court Tuesday, becoming the first team into the mixed doubles semifinals by edging Katerina Siniakova and Henry Patten 5-4 (6), 4-5 (3) (10-8).
Serena Williams and Carlos Alcaraz won their first-round match but were then ousted after a 5-4 (4), 4-1 loss to Belinda Bencic and Flavio Cobolli.
“Happy wife, happy life.” Gael Monfils and Elina Svitolina are lifting each other up ❤️ pic.twitter.com/7c2NrmHyVq — US Open Tennis (@usopen) August 25, 2026

Svitolina and Monfils will face Bencic and Cobolli in one semifinal Wednesday, with Mirra Andreeva and Andrey Rublev to meet Karolina Muchova and Jakub Mensik in the other. The winning team will earn $1 million.
That would be quite a payday for Monfils to share with his wife in his final Grand Slam tournament before retiring.
“Happy wife, happy life,” Monfils said in their postmatch interview after a kiss and hug on the court.
Williams and Alcaraz beat Erin Routliffe and Lloyd Glasspool 5-3, 4-1 in Williams’ first match at the U.S. Open since 2022.
“It’s always such an amazing place to be here,” Williams said. “I never expected to be back on this court, so it was just a really cool moment. I never thought this would happen.”

But the 44-year-old Williams, a 23-time Grand Slam singles champion, and the two-time U.S. Open champion Alcaraz appeared to run out of steam after dropping the first-set tiebreaker after quickly returning to the court for their second match.
New champions will be crowned and an old crush is revealed

Williams and Alcaraz began their opening match just as the two-time defending champions were eliminated. Andreeva and Rublev saved a match point and outlasted Sara Errani and Andrea Vavassori 1-4, 4-1 (11-9). The 19-year-old Andreeva revealed afterward that she used to have a crush on her partner and fellow Russian, who is 28.
They then recovered after blowing four match points in the second set to beat Diana Shnaider and Casper Ruud 4-1, 4-5 (9) (10-5).
The US Open tinkered with the format of the tournament this year to allow more doubles specialists back in, but it was the singles players who had the upper hand.
Monfils, who will turn 40 on Sept. 1, reached the US Open semifinals in 2016. Svitolina, who is eight years younger, got to the final four in Flushing Meadows in 2019.
Chemistry 💯 Elina Svitolina and Gael Monfils are the first pair into the mixed doubles semifinals! pic.twitter.com/haD8IMSepi — US Open Tennis (@usopen) August 25, 2026
Now it’s another semifinal — and an unlikely one — after they outlasted a team featuring the No.-1 ranked players in men’s and women’s doubles.

Monfils, who is from France, was given a wild card into the singles tournament. He and Svitolina, who is from Ukraine, were given wild cards to compete in mixed. They were married in 2021 and daughter Skaï was born the next year.
Because they were unsure at first they would be in the field in New York, Svitolina said they entered with no expectations, having not even worked on their tactics until Monday.
“I mean, we practice quite a lot together back at home or on the tournaments. Only yesterday we worked on few things for doubles,” Svitolina said.
“When we warmed up this morning, yeah, I told my coach it would be amazing if we can win just a few games.”
Czech duo has the look

Muchova and Mensik reached the semifinals with a 4-1, 5-3 victory over American pair Emma Navarro and Tommy Paul. Mensik texted Muchova on the eve of the tournament so they could coordinate outfits, and both wore pink tops and maroon bottoms.
“It’s definitely one of the most important things, to look good on the court, as well,” Mensik said.
Siniakova and Patten ousted Aryna Sabalenka and Novak Djokovic 1-4, 4-2 (10-2) in the first round. Siniakova ended the match with an ace while serving to Djokovic.

The tournament was overhauled last year in an effort to get more top singles players to compete. It was moved to a two-day event well before the singles main draw begins, with a scoring format that guarantees quick matches that shouldn’t tax the players too much.

The matches in the first three rounds feature sets to four games, with a tiebreaker at 4-all and a 10-point tiebreaker instead of a third set. Only the final will resemble a regular match, with traditional sets to six games.
“I will say if we play until basically regular rules, until six games, will be much more difficult,” Mensik said.

Sabalenka, the two-time defending U.S. Open women’s champion, and 24-time Grand Slam champion Djokovic are exactly the types of players the U.S. Tennis Association was seeking. They had the No. 1 seed based on the lowest combined singles ranking of any team, but their loss was far from an upset.

Doubles specialists such as Siniakova and Patten were shut out of the U.S. Open last year, when teams qualified directly based on the two players’ singles rankings, or were given wild cards by the USTA. Errani and Vavassori, who had won the title in 2024, were the only doubles players in the field after they were given a wild card to return, and went on to defend their title.
An eight-team qualifying tournament was added this year, giving two teams, composed mostly of regular doubles players, the chance to earn their way into the main draw.
Svitolina and Monfils routed Alex Eala and Felix Auger-Aliassime 4-1, 4-1 in their opening match. Muchova and Mensik edged Kristina Mladenovic and Marcelo Arevalo 4-1, 2-4 (10-7) in their opener.

articles.title: P129M abandoned cigarettes destroyed in Bulacan – BOC
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Around 3,000 cases of abandoned cigarettes, amounting to over P129 million, were destroyed from three containers in Santa Maria, Bulacan, according to the Bureau of Customs…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Around 3,000 cases of abandoned cigarettes, amounting to over P129 million, were destroyed from three containers in Santa Maria, Bulacan, according to the Bureau of Customs (BOC).

In its statement on Wednesday, the BOC said its Port of Subic disposed of the assorted-brand cigarettes through shredding and pyrolysis (melting through extreme heat) from July 28 to August 3 at its accredited disposal facility.
The bureau noted that it livestreamed the destruction process through the Port of Subic’s official YouTube account for the public to witness and “to ensure transparency and accountability.”
According to the BOC, the three 40-foot containers are part of the 10 identified containers of abandoned cigarettes with a total estimated value of P413 million that the bureau intends to dispose of.
The bureau said it is also in the process of disposing the contents of the remaining seven containers.
The ongoing destructions are still being livestreamed and conducted according to established disposal procedures, said the BOC.

articles.title: El Salvador, Panama sound alarm on El Niño-fueled drought
articles.summary: SAN SALVADOR — Panama on Tuesday became the latest Central American country, after Honduras and El Salvador, to declare an emergency over El Niño, which has already forced a reduction in…

blocks.text: SAN SALVADOR — Panama on Tuesday became the latest Central American country, after Honduras and El Salvador, to declare an emergency over El Niño, which has already forced a reduction in shipping through the Panama Canal.

Panama’s Interior Minister Dinoska Montalvo said the declaration will allow authorities “to be prepared for what may come with El Niño,” which has fueled a severe drought that is ravaging harvests and sparking fears of famine.
Meanwhile, El Salvador declared a state of maximum alert on Tuesday to activate monitoring, surveillance and aid efforts for affected communities.
“We are declaring a red alert for meteorological and farming drought across the national territory,” the Civil Protection department wrote on X.

El Niño is a weather pattern that raises surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, generating global changes in winds and rainfall as well as erratic weather conditions.
It is also nudging up global temperatures in a year predicted to be the hottest on record.
El Niño occurs on average every two to seven years, but this year’s is shaping up as the most intense in recent years.

Central America is in the throes of a severe drought that has already prompted Honduras to place 80 percent of its territory on alert and caused the Panama Canal to cut shipping traffic because of its dwindling water levels.
In El Salvador, the lack of rain, which is usually abundant at this time of year, has wiped out crops.
The agriculture ministry has announced food assistance for rural families that do not have irrigation systems.
Several municipalities in El Salvador are located in the Central American Dry Corridor, an arid strip that also includes parts of Honduras and Nicaragua and is vulnerable to extreme weather events.
All three countries broke their monthly temperature records in both June and July, exacerbating famine concerns.
So far in August, 14 temperature records have been smashed in El Salvador.
Further south, Peru last week declared a state of emergency in a third of its cities over El Niño and said intense heat and rain could also cause havoc for food production. /dl

articles.title: Drought-hit Danube gives way to fossil hunt in Bulgaria
articles.summary: RYAHOVO, Bulgaria — Volunteers scanned the dried-up bank of the Danube in northern Bulgaria, close to where receding waters laid bare mammoth bones last month, hoping to find more fossilized…

blocks.text: RYAHOVO, Bulgaria — Volunteers scanned the dried-up bank of the Danube in northern Bulgaria, close to where receding waters laid bare mammoth bones last month, hoping to find more fossilized fragments exposed by Europe’s parching drought.
“I’ve found a tooth!” exclaimed Aleksandar Denkov, a 30-year-old amateur photographer, holding up a yellowish fragment protruding from the sand.

Denkov last week joined some 20 other volunteers, many hoping to find more mammoth fossils during the search organised by the regional history museum of the nearby city of Ruse, around 250 km (155 miles) northeast of Sofia.

Though their hopes were not fulfilled, the group found remains of a mammal — “probably an aurochs or a European bison,” according to the museum — a horse jawbone in a subfossil state and a cluster of fossilised oysters dating back around 60 to 65 million years.

Europe’s drought, exacerbated by human-induced climate change according to experts, has seen major rivers slow to a trickle, causing serious problems for cargo shippers and nuclear plants normally cooled by river water.
But the low waters have also revealed remains and historical artefacts not seen for decades — or even millennia.

Finds in recent weeks along the Danube, Europe’s second-longest river, have included World War II shipwrecks in Austria and Serbia and the remains of two German soldiers and a motorbike in the middle of Budapest.
‘Close to history’

Ruse Regional History Museum curator Krasimir Kirov said the museum decided to organize the field day “to teach people how to recognise different finds, show them what they might uncover, and give them safety tips.”
“After the mammoth was discovered, I started getting dozens of calls from people telling me about what they’d found,” he told AFP.

Last month, a resident of the village of Ryahovo — some 30 kilometers from Ruse — spotted by chance what museum specialists then identified as a mammoth jaw bone, fragments of tusks, part of a shoulder blade and a femur.
Announced on social media, the initiative to gather near Ryahovo for a guided search quickly sparked keen interest, with requests already pouring in for the next outing, according to Kirov.
The search began with a few instructions: the volunteers must advance in a line and, if someone spots something, raise a hand so that the whole group stops.
Above all, they must not touch any metal objects, which could be ammunition or explosives.
But the walk had barely begun when the line broke apart: enthusiasm won out over discipline.
“It’s a very rare opportunity to feel this close to history,” Ekaterina Yordanova, a 34-year-old psychologist, told AFP.
“Seeing the Danube in this state is worrying, but it also gives us the chance to discover new things.”
Vladimir Tsvyatkov, a 44-year-old business owner, said he, his wife and their two children mainly came “for the adventure”.
Having grown up on the banks of the river, he said he had “never seen the Danube so dried up.”
WWII remnants
Further upstream in Bulgaria, the low Danube levels have also allowed archaeologists to document the foundations of a bridge, more than two km long, inaugurated under Emperor Constantine I in 328.
And elsewhere along the Danube, World War II weaponry and other remnants have been found.
In central Austria, two wrecks of German warships are protruding from the water.
Damaged in fighting with American tanks in 1945, they were later sunk by their own crews, according to local media.

In Serbia, near Prahovo, the receding river has likewise exposed wrecks of German warships, which were among dozens sunk by their own side in 1944 in an attempt to slow the Soviet Red Army’s advance along Europe’s second-longest river.
And in Budapest, a motorbike and the remains of two German soldiers were found, according to the German War Graves Commission.

The findings come as vast tracts of many of Europe’s largest rivers have fallen to levels never recorded before in the month of July, according to data from European climate observatory Copernicus. /dl

articles.title: 43 gun-related incidents recorded in BARMM despite gun ban
articles.summary: COTABATO CITY – Police reported 43 gun-related incidents in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) since the implementation of the gun ban last July 16 for the historic…
articles.byline: Drema Quitayen Bravo and Edwin Fernandez

blocks.text: COTABATO CITY – Police reported 43 gun-related incidents in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) since the implementation of the gun ban last July 16 for the historic parliamentary elections next month.
Capt. Steffi Salanguit, Police Regional Office-Bangsamoro Autonomous Region (PRO-BAR) spokesperson, said the figure covers incidents recorded as of Tuesday.
Maguindanao del Sur recorded the highest number of shooting incidents at 16, followed by Maguindanao del Norte with 14, seven in Lanao del Sur, four in Basilan and two in Cotabato City.

On Tuesday, a solar panel installer was shot dead in Sultan Kudarat, Maguindanao del Norte, while a man was also shot dead in front of his horrified wife in Barangay Kalanganan 2 in Cotabato City hours earlier.

Also on Tuesday, a village watchman was injured after he was shot by his older brother following a heated argument in Datu Paglas, Maguindanao del Sur, according to Maj. Guissepe Tamayo, Maguindanao del Sur police spokesperson.
Salanguit said the shooting incidents were either due to personal grudge, ‘rido’ (family feud), revenge, or drug-related activities.
These gun related incidents left 14 people dead and eight wounded./coa

articles.title: America 'not at war' with Canada, insists U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent

image.caption: U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says Prime Minister Mark Carney walked away from the best trade deal offered to any county and then turned the ongoing trade dispute with the U.S. 'into a political shouting match.' (Gerald Herbert/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

United States Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent insisted his country is "not at war" with Canada, then proceeded to mock the threat Canada could pose to his country with "submarines from the Edmonton mall."
Bessent says Carney's 'doing what is best for the Liberal party, what's best for Mark Carney' not Canadians
The secretary also suggested Prime Minister Mark Carney was to blame for the current "political shouting match" between the two countries because keeping the fight alive is good for his poll numbers.
Bessent made the remarks Monday in an interview with the U.S. cable news network CNBC, where he was asked if his country is now in a trade war with Canada.
"Well, I don't think you can be in a tit for tat with someone that's 13 times larger than you are," he said.
"I mean we're not at war with Canada. How are we going to be at war with Canada? What, are they going to take their two submarines from the Edmonton mall and sick them on us?"

items: Canada has leverage in this trade fight, but economists warn it comes with a cost
Carney says trade deal became untenable when U.S. 'asked too much and offered too little'

blocks.text: Pointing Edmonton's submarines at the U.S. today would be more than a little difficult.
While the West Edmonton Mall did have four recreational submarines to ferry tourists through an indoor lake, the ride closed in 2005 and the subs were broken up for scrap in 2012.

None of that seemed to matter in the ongoing war of words between the Trump administration and Canada that found renewed vigor this week after a trade deal between the two countries fell apart at the last minute.
Charette says Canada consistently raised auto industry in U.S. trade negotiations
Carney said he pulled Canada's negotiating team back home late on Friday, Aug. 21 after the U.S. team introduced "last-minute changes" that the government deemed "unfair" and "uneconomic."

Those demands, Carney said the day after talks stopped, would have restricted Canada's ability to sign trade deals with other countries and undermined subsidies to French-language media and the requirement for bilingual product labelling.
The prime minister also said that the auto deal the U.S. wanted to strike would have degraded the industry over time, something he could not accept.

The day after pulling back from the table, the U.S. hit Canada with 50 per cent tariffs on about $28 billion worth of Canadian exports to the U.S. Carney followed that up by announcing Canada would match those tariffs dollar-for-dollar beginning Sept. 8.
Carney not doing what's best for Canada: Bessent
Since those trade talks fell apart the U.S. President Donald Trump has taken to insulting Canada on social media and trolling Canadians by renaming Lake Ontario, Lake America.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford and Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew have both pushed back against Trump, with Ford inviting the U.S. president to "kiss my ass" and Kinew comparing Trump to an "over the hill" band playing out their last days in a casino.
Carney has so far avoided joining in with taunts and jeers, but he did confirm that Canada is now in a trade war with its southern neighbour.
"You're at war when you get attacked. We got attacked," Carney said last week.
Bessent said he talks were going well and Canada was "offered the best trade deal of any country on the globe" before Canada walked away "at the last minute."

items: Trump says Canada 'wants the benefits' of being a U.S. state 'without being one' as trade dispute deepens
What went wrong with U.S. trade talks, according to Canada's chief negotiator

blocks.text: "I think it is very unfortunate that Prime Minister Carney has turned this into a political shouting match," Bessent said Monday on CNBC. "He came to power on an anti-American, anti-Trump agenda, he was 20 points behind in the polls and then he started this.

"It's unfortunate he's not doing what's best for the Canadian people, he's doing what is best for the Liberal party, what's best for Mark Carney, and in the long run the Canadian people are going to see through that."

Meanwhile, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith was also on American television Monday arguing that both countries will be hurt in the ongoing trade dispute with the U.S. because "no one wins a tariff war."
Retaliatory tariffs will hurt Alberta: Premier Smith

Smith said that as long as tariffs remain in place, the impact will be felt most deeply by small businesses on both sides of the border, which will be forced to lay off workers to cope with the higher costs of a tariff war.
The premier said the best thing that can happen to both economies is for negotiators to return to the table, even when relations with the two countries remain strained.

"Canadians are confused, I think they're disappointed," she said. "I guess we're a bit confused, because we're such a strong ally, we have such integrated defence, we have such integrated markets, we don't understand why the Americans would want Canada to be weaker."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Peter Zimonjic is a senior writer for CBC News who reports for digital, radio and television. He has worked as a reporter and columnist in London, England, for the Telegraph, Times and Daily Mail, and in Canada for the Ottawa Citizen, Torstar and Sun Media. He is the author of Into The Darkness: An Account of 7/7, published by Vintage.

articles.title: Alto high-speed train would be ‘catastrophic’ for Quebec farmers, federation says

image.caption: Daniel Legault, the owner of Ferme Legault in Rigaud, Que., says he’s concerned the proposed Alto high-speed rail project would separate his property and sever the main road connecting him to the rest of the province. (Chloë Ranaldi/CBC)

blocks.text: Montreal

The proposed train line, designed to cut travel times between Toronto and Quebec City in half, could slice directly through one farmer's property in Rigaud, Que. He says the proposed train route would divide his farm and cut off his access to the main road — making farming operations impossible.
Proposed project could slice through land, isolate communities
Farming has been in Daniel Legault's family since 1929.
For the past 30 years, he's run Ferme Legault, a dairy and cereal farm in Rigaud, Que., alongside his wife and son.
While he hopes to pass the legacy down to his three grandsons, a proposed high-speed rail project threatens to sever his land in two and disrupt business.
“My father and I have worked our whole lives to build a business like this. And we have no control over the future,” he said.

The proposed train line, designed to cut travel times between Toronto and Quebec City in half, could slice directly through Legault's property. He says he received a flyer in the mail about the Alto project, and then a notice asking to study his land – which he says he refused.

Legault says the proposed train route would divide his farm and cut off his access to the main road. He says he’ll be forced to make large detours multiple times a day to get to his fields – severely affecting business.
“It won't be logistically feasible,” he said. “It's going to be impossible to feed all these animals.”
Beyond Legault's farm, Alto says the proposed project will impact about 1,700 properties, including at least 500 farms between Ottawa and Montreal.
Legault says a lack of communication from those responsible for the project has left his family’s future in limbo.
"[My son] doesn’t see the future as clearly as he did before this,” Legault said.
Disastrous for farming communities, says federation

Jérémie Letellier, president of the Fédération de l'UPA de la Montérégie, a regional branch of Quebec's largest agricultural federation, says the rail project would be disastrous for farming communities in Ontario and Quebec.
“It's catastrophic the impact on a single farm,” Letellier said. “A lot of farms will be thinking about reorienting or even terminating their activities because of a project like that.”
He says everyone along the train's proposed path from Rigaud to the North Shore is concerned.

items: Montreal-Ottawa high-speed rail line could cross 1,700 properties, Alto predicts
Could the Alto high speed rail plan be derailed?

blocks.text: Letellier says the train line will cut farmland in two, with no possibility of going over the rails.
“Instead of having a couple 100 metres to go, you might have 15 to 20 kilometres to go. So it changes everything as far as the cost is concerned, and as far as the practicality of it,” he said.
Letellier is also denouncing Alto’s lack of transparency and consultation with his members over the past months, saying people have questions and are worried about their futures.
“I think we have to take a step back. I think we have to evaluate all the possibilities, the alternative possibilities,” he said.
‘We want to do things right,’ Alto says
Caroline Des Rosiers, a spokesperson for Alto, says a more detailed route for the network's initial section between Ottawa and Montreal is expected in the fall.
“We're developing the project at a fast pace, it does not mean that we are going to skip steps,” she said.
“We want to do things right.”
Des Rosiers says from the start, Alto has made a commitment to limit the impacts on agricultural communities.
“This could mean, as much as possible, following the end of the land or existing infrastructure so that, as much as we can, we limit the impacts to the end of a lot,” she said.

items: Kingston probably getting high-speed rail stop, says Alto CEO

blocks.text: Des Rosiers adds that they plan to build overpasses and underpasses when possible, to prevent certain areas from being isolated.
“We know that is a major concern that people have, but we are committed to maintaining that access,” she said. However, it’s unclear where those points will be and what areas will be targeted.
Alto has also promised to ensure businesses that are affected are compensated fairly, looking at long-term impacts and consequences on farming operations, said Des Rosiers.

A first round of public consultations has already concluded, with meetings held in some parts of Ontario and Quebec, however none have been in the Vaudreuil-Soulanges territory, where Legault's farm is located.

A second round of consultations is expected this fall in Pointe-Fortune, once a more detailed route is presented. Alto says it plans to also continue conversations with elected officials in different regions.
But those plans do little to reassure the Legault family, where farming has been their way of life for almost a century.
“It's discouraging to see where we are. Our plans have come to a standstill; our future has come to a standstill,” said Legault.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Chloë Ranaldi is a journalist covering Montreal's off-island communities like Vaudreuil-Dorion, Hudson and Saint-Lazare. Chloë has an office space in Hudson.

articles.title: 'Lake America' change highlights Canada's reliance on U.S. tech

image.caption: A person holds an Apple iPhone Air during an event at the Steve Jobs Theater on the Apple Park campus in Cupertino, California, on Sept. 9, 2025. (Nic Coury/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Business·New
U.S. President Donald Trump's push to rename Lake Ontario "Lake America" underscores Canada's reliance on U.S. tech giants like Google and Apple.
Tech industry experts say Canadian consumers and businesses have few non-U.S. options
"Lake America" labels are live on Google Maps, and U.S. President Donald Trump wants Apple to follow suit with the navigation app preinstalled on every iPhone.

Tech industry experts say the situation highlights an uncomfortable reality for many Canadian consumers and businesses: they're effectively "locked in" to these U.S.-owned platforms, with few, if any, viable non-American alternatives.

"Canadians really do live under the shadow of American tech monopolies, and we often forget that this is a fact until there are these moments of controversy," said Anne Pasek, Canada Research Chair in Media, Culture and the Environment at Trent University.
"Our digital lives, and a lot of our life that extends from that, falls under the jurisdiction of American companies, and therefore American law."
Canadian government sites display ‘Lake America’ thanks to Google
Some Canadian websites, including federal government sites and some of the country's largest banks, have recently displayed maps with Lake Ontario renamed "Lake America."
The changes follow an executive order from Trump directing the U.S. federal government to officially rename one of the Great Lakes separating the two countries amid an increasingly bitter trade war.
Google made the change for users in the U.S. and introduced an option for non-American websites to display "Lake Ontario" by localizing their maps and setting their region to Canada.
"These updates follow our long-standing policy for bodies of water with names that vary from country," the company stated on Saturday.

U.S. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum told Fox Business on Monday that Trump contacted Apple to request that Lake Ontario be changed to "Lake America" on its apps. Apple has not responded to multiple requests for comment from CBC News.
Beyond providing real-time directions to millions of users, mapping tools from U.S. tech giants are woven into the websites and operations of scores of Canadian businesses.

They provide hours of operation, contact information, reviews and other critical details. Behind the scenes, they help e-commerce sites auto-complete addresses and allow rideshare and food-delivery apps to monitor traffic and road construction.
"There is a pretty clear monopoly," Pasek said. "Folks are locked in."
Will Trump seek tech-based 'choke points' against Canada?

Emily Osborne is a policy research associate at the Canadian Shield Institute. The Toronto-based think-tank was launched by BlackBerry co-founder Jim Balsillie to modernize public policy on technology and national security and safeguard Canadian intellectual property.
"We rely on American companies like Google, like Apple for many different digital services and products online, and navigation is certainly one of those," Osborne said.
For basic navigation, she suggested Dutch companies TomTom and HERE Technologies as potential alternatives to Google and Apple.
Until recently, Canada had a homegrown alternative. Toronto-based Avenza Systems was acquired by Maine-based Blue Marble Geographics for an undisclosed sum in a deal that closed in April.

If tension continues to rise between Canada and the U.S., Osborne worries the Trump administration may look for other tech-related "choke points" to pressure Canada. She pointed to payment processing and cloud storage.
"Think of the AWS (Amazon Web Services) outage that happened last fall. So many Canadian businesses were affected by that," she said.
"That's concerning when we contemplate the possibility of that service potentially being, you know, restricted or revoked based on an order made by President Trump," Osborne added.
"Canadian businesses rely on Visa and MasterCard for credit card payments. We don't have a Canadian alternative there."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jeff Lagerquist is a senior writer with CBC News based in Toronto. Originally from Erin, Ont., he studied journalism at Toronto Metropolitan University. Jeff previously worked as a senior reporter for Yahoo Finance Canada. He was also a reporter and digital producer for CTV National News, BNN Bloomberg and The Financial Post. He was also a Columbia University energy journalism fellow for 2025.

articles.title: 3 byelections test Carney government's popularity as U.S. trade war heats up

image.caption: Turnout in byelections is typically lower than in general elections. (Keito Newman/The Canadian Press)

items: September 1Advance voter turnoutTurnout in byelections is typically lower than in general elections. (Keito Newman/The Canadian Press)Elections Canada estimates that nearly 40,000 voters cast a ballot at advance polls across all three ridings.Advance voting was open just a little over a week ago. North Vancouver-Capilano saw the highest turnout with roughly 16,700. Beaches-East York and Chicoutimi-Le Fjord had an estimated 11,800 and 11,000 voters cast an early ballot, respectively.Compared to the 2025 election, advance turnout dropped significantly in both the B.C. and Ontario ridings. Both had over 20,000 voters cast a ballot early.Chicoutimi-Le Fjord also saw a drop off, but to a lesser extent. Just over 14,000 advance ballots were cast in that riding last election.On the whole, byelections typically see an overall lower voter turnout compared to general elections.

Who are the candidates in Beaches-East York?Gabriela Silva PonteSigns for Liberal candidate Tanveer Shahnawaz are seen at his election night party before polls close in Beaches-East York. (Gabriela Silva Ponte/CBC)Hi, I'm reporting from a pub on Queen Street East in Toronto, where members of the Liberal Party will be spending their evening as votes roll in.The Liberal candidate for the Beaches-East York byelection is Tanveer Shahnawaz. The party selected him as the candidate in July, following the resignation of former member of Parliament Nathaniel Erskine-Smith in June. He previously worked as the office manager for Erskine-Smith and as co-chair of a neighbourhood health and community group, according to a news release.Shannon Devine, who also ran in 2025, is the New Democratic Party candidate, while Bruce Livesey is running with the Green Party in Beaches-East York. Jim Syrbos is the Conservative candidate in the riding.

Local versus federal issuesLaurence WattLocal concerns about cost of living and traffic may not be what ultimately decides the vote in North Vancouver-Capilano. Simon Fraser University political science lecturer Sanjay Jeram says federal voters are often influenced more by their views of the national parties and leaders than by local issues. "The truth is local issues, especially in the Canadian context, local issues don't tend to drive outcomes as much as we might think," Jeram said.

A growing community under pressure in North VancouverLaurence WattA local vote with national stakes in North VancouverVoters in North Vancouver–Capilano will go to the polls on Aug. 31. Housing, rent and traffic congestion rank among the top local concerns. The results of the race could affect the balance of power in Ottawa as the Liberals are one seat short of a majority.Hi, I'm a CBC journalist who has lived in North Vancouver for more than a decade.Six candidates are on the ballot in North Vancouver-Capilano: Liberal Braeden Caley, Conservative Stephen Curran, NDP candidate Stephen Tweedale, Green candidate Shelley Luce, People's Party candidate Ehsan Arjmand and Independent Jeff Monds.On the surface, North Vancouver is a scenic and growing part of British Columbia that is voting to replace former Liberal MP Jonathan Wilkinson. But there's a lot more to it than that, including local pressures. North Vancouver was recently ranked the most expensive rental market in Canada by Rentals.ca and Urbanation, with average asking rents above $3,000 a month. And vehicle traffic is another major concern, especially along roads feeding the Lions Gate and Ironworkers Memorial bridges.For a quick overview of what's at stake in this byelection, watch the video above. Or you can listen to our This Is Vancouver podcast here.

Canada's trade war looms large over Quebec raceRhianna SchmunkU.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick accused Carney of manufacturing conflict over French-language regulations for political gain. (Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters)I've been covering trade from Washington, D.C., for the past few weeks. Canada's dispute with the United States became an even bigger conversation in Chicoutimi-Le Fjord after Carney said French language protections were one of several issues that led him to pull the plug on negotiations earlier this month.U.S. President Donald Trump and two of his trade deputies denied that language was a sticking point. They said Carney made up the accusation to gain political support, including from the public in Quebec. "This is politics only. If you think I ever said the word 'French'? Do I care about how the Quebecois speak? I mean, what could matter less to America? We don't care," U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick told reporters in Washington on Thursday. "The fact is, we never brought those words up. This is [Carney's] manufacturing."

The race to watchDarren MajorPrime Minister Mark Carney is seen campaigning with Chicoutimi-Le Fjord Liberal candidate Daniel Gobeil, left, earlier this month. (Jacques Boissinot/The Canadian Press)No disrespect to the candidates in the other ridings, but Chicoutimi-Le Fjord is really the race to watch tonight.North Vancouver-Capilano and Beaches-East York are fairly safe Liberal ridings — the party won both with over 50 per cent of the vote in the last election.But Chicoutimi-Le Fjord is a bit of a toss-up. Martel, a popular former hockey coach who had been considered a sort of star candidate for the Conservatives, had been the MP for the riding since 2018.Martel only beat the Liberal and Bloc Québécois candidates by a few percentage points last year. Without his star power, the Conservatives' share of the vote could drop.That leaves an opening for the Liberals and Bloc, who are both gunning for the seat. Prime Minister Mark Carney and Bloc Leader Yves-François Blanchet have both made stops in the riding over the summer.The fact that this riding saw the least drop off in terms of turnout for advance polls could be an indication that parties are pushing to get out their vote.

Aren't there other vacant seats?Darren MajorPM Carney to call 13 byelections in just 2 yearsPrime Minister Mark Carney is set to be the first prime minister in 75 years to call more than 13 byelections in their first two years. So, what does this mean for the current state of Canadian politics? The founder of The Writ.ca, Éric Grenier, joins Power & Politics to discuss.Keen political watchers will know there are a number of other vacancies in the House of Commons right now that aren't being filled tonight.There are another six seats that will need to be filled in the coming months. But when Carney called these three byelections, there was only one seat where the MP had officially resigned — the other four only stepped down in the past few weeks.The Bloc's Simon-Pierre Savard-Tremblay resigned his seat, the riding of Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot-Acton, back in June and is running for the provincial Parti Québécois this fall.Like Savard-Tremblay, former NDP MP Alexandre Boulerice is shifting to provincial politics and is running for Québec Solidaire. But unlike Savard-Tremblay, Boulerice only resigned his seat, Rosemont-La Petite-Patrie, last week.Although Liberal MP Steven Guilbeault gave notice that he would be leaving elected politics way back in May, the former cabinet minister made it official last Friday. Shaun Chen, another former Liberal MP, gave up his Toronto seat earlier this month.Conservative Cathay Wagantall gave notice of her intention to step down as MP for the Saskatchewan riding of Yorkton-Melville back in May. Her official last day was slated for today.There is a bit of a process and timing rules that come into play once an MP official gives notice of their resignation. The Speaker has to inform the chief electoral officer of the vacancy, at which point the prime minister has 11 to 180 days to call a byelection. For Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot-Acton, the final day to call the vote is in December.There is another vacancy coming down the pipe as well. Ontario Conservative MP Larry Brock has said he will step down on Sept. 19.

Where things stand in the House of CommonsDarren MajorSeveral MPs have either resigned or said they intend to resign since the House of Commons went on summer recess. (Christian Patry/CBC)Carney's Liberals were able to turn what was originally a minority government into a majority earlier this year, although the margin was only a handful of seats.The Liberals officially entered majority status in April with 173 seats to the opposition's combined 169.Even with the slew of resignations, the Liberals haven't dropped out of majority status. When all the vacancies are accounted for, the Liberals currently have 170 seats compared to 167 on the opposition benches. But the Liberal number includes the Speaker, who only votes in the case of a tie.The only way for the governing party to feel a bit of heat in the House of Commons would be if they lose every byelection tonight. But that seems unlikely given two of those votes are in safe Liberal territory. If the Liberals win both North Vancouver-Capilano and Beaches-East York as expected, that would boost their numbers to 172 seats. They would still outweigh the opposition if they lose Chicoutimi-Le Fjord, as an opposition victory would bring the total count to 168 for the other parties.Things are likely to shift in the coming months with a number of other byelections on the way.

Which seats are up for grabs?Darren MajorVoters in the Toronto riding of Beaches-East York voted for their new MP earlier on Monday. (Keito Newman/The Canadian Press)Hi folks, I'm a senior writer with the parliamentary bureau in Ottawa.Add "byelections" to the list of things that come in threes, because this is the second time in 2026 that we have a trio of seats up for grabs on the same night.The B.C. riding of North Vancouver-Capilano is open after former Liberal cabinet minister Jonathan Wilkinson shipped out to Brussels to take up a new job as Canada's ambassador to the European Union earlier this summer.Nathaniel Erskine-Smith, another former cabinet minister, also resigned his Toronto seat in Beaches-East York.And the Quebec seat of Chicoutimi-Le Fjord became vacant after Prime Minister Mark Carney appointed now-former Conservative MP Richard Martel to the Senate.There are a few other vacant seats in the House of Commons at the moment, but only voters in these three ridings are casting ballots today.

articles.title: Russia is rattling NATO’s nerves, but how far will Moscow go?

image.caption: European leaders are growing increasingly concerned that the Kremlin is planning to carry out deliberately ambiguous acts of violence large enough to frighten or destabilize NATO, but deniable enough to avoid triggering the Western military alliance's self-defence clause. (Pavel Golovkin/The Associa

blocks.text: Politics·Analysis

Russia may not be preparing to invade NATO, but something more ambiguous could be coming. Intelligence warnings point to provocations designed to rattle the alliance, sow confusion and test its resolve. With uncertainty surrounding Washington’s response, Moscow may see an opportunity to probe NATO’s most vulnerable point: its political unity.
Incursions may be aimed at testing Western military alliance's resolve

It would be fair to say this summer has been the season of fear and loathing in Eastern Europe, as more signs emerge that Russia could be ready to further test NATO solidarity in the hopes of breaking it.
Poland and Romania have witnessed a series of Russian drone intrusions and at least one missile strike since the spring.
The idea that the Kremlin is preparing some kind of incursion drove speculation surrounding the CIA director's surprise visit to Moscow last week.
What is worrying officials in Poland and the Baltic states is not the prospect of Russian armoured divisions suddenly crossing the frontier.

The concern is that Moscow may believe it can carry out a deliberately ambiguous, limited act of violence — large enough to frighten or destabilize NATO, but small and deniable enough to make invoking the Western military alliance's self-defence clause, Article 5, politically difficult.

In late July, a Russian cruise missile crashed into Poland's Lublin province after travelling deep into Polish territory during a massive strike against Ukraine. Multiple drones have also approached or tested Polish airspace in the weeks since.

A Polish defence expert who specializes in the Russian military and politics said the war in Eastern Europe is rapidly approaching a critical turning point where the Kremlin has reached the conclusion that the only way to defeat Ukraine is to politically break NATO.

"There is frustration [over the] inability to break Ukrainian armed forces and to defeat Ukrainians in the field," said Withold Rodkiewicz, a security expert at the Center for East European Studies at the University of Warsaw.

The Russian "elite," as Rodkiewicz calls them, know they're not winning the war, and Ukraine's increasingly effective attacks on oil and commercial infrastructure have the potential to destabilize the Kremlin's grip on power.

"The analysis that's around in Moscow is that the main reason that Ukrainians are able to resist is because they are supplied from the West," he said, adding that nothing short of total victory in Ukraine will satisfy the Kremlin.
"They're not looking for a way out. They are not looking for … an off-ramp," he said. "When they are thinking what to do next, an escalation is an obvious thing."
Rodkiewicz said he believes the time will be right for Moscow sometime in September, either before or after Russia's parliamentary elections.

There is mounting evidence of Russian risk-taking, but there is no consensus that Russian President Vladimir Putin has decided to start a conventional war with NATO. Estonia’s foreign intelligence service, for example, still assesses that Russia does not presently intend to attack a NATO country militarily in the coming year.
Do I think they'll do something that is so clearly aimed at shaking NATO decision-making and political cohesion? Absolutely.- Kerry Buck, Canada's former ambassador to NATO
At the same time, throughout the summer, U.S., Polish and Baltic warnings about a provocation have become considerably more specific.

In late June and July, reporting emerged that Western intelligence services had picked up indications that Russia could be preparing some form of action against Poland or the Baltic states, designed specifically to test NATO cohesion.

The Guardian newspaper in the U.K. reported that intelligence received by Latvia pointed toward a possible Russian military provocation, and subsequent reporting said the United States had warned Poland about the possibility of an armed incident on Polish territory.

By early August, the warning sharpened even further. U.S. intelligence was reportedly telling Poland and the Baltic countries that Putin could be prepared to authorize provocative action against NATO while the Ukraine war is still underway, rather than waiting for Russia to regenerate its conventional forces after the war.
That is a significant change in the threat conversation.

Canada's former ambassador to NATO, Kerry Buck, said Russia has been out to destroy the alliance since its invasion of Crimea in 2014, and the conditions have only improved since U.S. President Donald Trump returned to power last year.

The constant berating of allies, the new fiscal demands placed on them, the cutting of U.S. forces earmarked for an emergency, and now Washington's review of American troop posture in Europe have created the conditions for a major political crisis, should there be a provocation.
It is, Buck said, "a window of opportunity where Russia was emboldened to poke NATO more, poke NATO territory, airspace and space more."
While she doesn't believe an outright attack on NATO is in the offing, she also believes Russia is prepared to try something ambiguous.
"Do I think they'll do something that is so clearly aimed at shaking NATO decision-making and political cohesion? Absolutely," Buck said.

Trump told reporters last week that he's "not concerned at all" about Russia attacking NATO territory. He said he's spoken to Putin and has been assured he "is not going to be attacking a NATO territory."

At a meeting of the North Atlantic Council in Brussels last week, U.S. defense policy chief Elbridge Colby insisted Washington is not abandoning Europe. He said it wants a new vision of NATO built around European-led conventional defence.

Buck said most of what Russia is likely planning falls below the threshold of a direct attack. She also accepts at face value what Colby has said. Rather, her concern lies within the reality of NATO politics.
In the past, whenever there's a crisis, the U.S. has stepped up to organize the allied response. Will that happen under the current administration?
"All signs from President Trump are that they are not as committed as they used to be, so who would step in and lead the preliminary response?" Buck asked.

"And would it be held up by U.S. reluctance? So we're dealing not just with a lack of U.S. leadership, but potentially U.S. reluctance to fall into whatever it is NATO is doing or might contemplate doing."
Just recently, Lithuanian intelligence raised another disturbing possibility: Russia using captured Ukrainian drones in a false flag operation against a Baltic country.

Lithuanian Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said that intelligence indicated Russia might employ captured Ukrainian UAVs in an operation intended to look as though Ukraine had attacked NATO territory.
The objective would be political rather than military, creating confusion inside the alliance and undermining support for Kyiv. Russia dismissed the allegation.
But that scenario becomes more plausible because something very similar happened in Latvia last spring.
Ukrainian strike drones have repeatedly wandered into NATO airspace, apparently in some cases because Russian electronic warfare has disrupted their navigation.
The incident in Latvia caused a political crisis that cost the defence minister his job, and eventually cost the prime minister her job.
Buck said there's a range of disturbing scenarios for Moscow to make mischief.
"It's in their interest to do it now," she said. "And I don't think NATO's quite ready to respond in a way, particularly because of the uncertainty about the U.S. response."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Murray Brewster is the senior defence writer for CBC News, based in Ottawa. He has covered the Canadian military and foreign policy from Parliament Hill for over a decade. Among other assignments, he spent a total of 15 months on the ground covering the Afghan war for The Canadian Press. Prior to that, he covered defence issues and politics for CP in Nova Scotia for 11 years and was bureau chief for Standard Broadcast News in Ottawa.
